News.title: United Nations votes to adopt new world map that reduces size of Britain and US and shows Africa much bigger
News.content:
WORLD VIEW United Nations votes to adopt new world map that reduces size of Britain and US and shows Africa much bigger

A NEW world map has officially been adopted after a UN vote – with the fresh model reducing the size of Britain and the US while making Africa bigger.

The landmark resolution means the traditional Mercator map – which the planet has been using for 500 years – will be replaced with a 2018 version.



The Mercator greatly exaggerates the size of several countries and continents based on how far they are from the equator.

Africa‘s true size for example, is not properly represented compared to countries like Russia, Canada and Greenland.



The US was the only nation to vote against the resolution.

Washington said the new map was designed to fit an “ideological agenda” and distracted from “genuine problems of international peace, prosperity or good relations”.

The new ruling was hailed by the Africa Union – who said the old map’s distortions had given the continent a “symbolic minimisation”.

Negotiations were led by Togo, who argued the Mercator map had made “lasting cognitive, educational, cultural, geopolitical and socioeconomic effects, contributing to a drastic reduction in the perceived size of Africa and other regions of the world in the global collective imagination”.

Governments, schools, and international groups are being encouraged to adopt the new map, named the Equal Earth projection, which was made in 2018.

But the new ruling does not force nations to abolish the old format.



The map the world is used to seeing was devised by Gerardus Mercator, a Flemish cartographer, in 1569.

It allowed sailors to navigate using straight lines that correspond to compass directions.

But the maps format means landmasses appear larger the further they are from the equator.

Greenland is roughly the same size as Africa on the old map – despite the Danish territory being 14 times smaller than the continent.

Robert Dussey, the foreign minister of Togo, said: “A map is never neutral.



“It shapes perceptions, influences how the place of peoples and continents in the world is understood and may, sometimes from the earliest years of schooling, perpetuate representations that do not correspond to geographic reality.”

Before the vote on Friday, Jean-Noël Barrot, the French foreign minister, spoke in support of the resolution.

Many saw it as an attempt to show solidarity with France‘s former colonies.

He said: “[We] will abandon the Mercator projection in favour of map representations tailored to specific uses, more faithful to actual surface areas and in line with the recommendations of cartographers and scientists.”

News.title: I made a deal with God and until my last breath I’ll make sure the world never forgets 9/11, says miraculous firefighter
News.content:
AS the Twin Towers fell around him and whipped up winds of 160mph, firefighter Tim Brown clung to a pillar and “made a deal with God”.

He vowed that if he lived through the deadliest terror attack in history, he would dedicate his life to sharing the heroism he saw that day.



Now, 25 years on from his miraculous survival and living with 9/11– induced prostate cancer, he has made good on his promise.

Tim, 64, said: “Until my last breath I will do everything I can to make sure the world never forgets.



“We have at least one full generation now of people who were not alive and don’t remember 9/11.

“The narrative has to come from us, the people who were witnesses, otherwise the truth will get lost in history. I’m determined that won’t happen.”

At 8.46am on September 11, 2001 Tim was eating breakfast in 7 World Trade Center, a 47-storey office block next to the Twin Towers, when al-Qaeda terrorists crashed American Airlines Flight 11 into the North Tower.

As office workers streamed out on to the street, Tim raced towards danger and quickly began helping to evacuate the shocked masses.

As he did so, he bumped into two of his closest firefighter friends, Chris Blackwell and Captain Terry Hatton.

Terry pulled him into a tight embrace, telling him: “I love you, brother. I may never see you again.” Sadly, he was right.



Tim said: “Terry and Chris were just two of the fallen heroes that day.

Terry took his men and they went up the stairs just like all of the firefighters and police officers.

“Chris went up alone. Every one of them said, ‘Send me’. They all knew they weren’t coming back.



“It was my job to stay in the lobby in the command post, to co-ordinate the enormous response.”

Then at 9.03am, United Airlines Flight 175 struck the South Tower.

Tim hurried into the building’s lobby and helped hundreds to flee.

He recalled: “There were injured people immediately in the lobbies of both towers. The scene was as horrific in the South Tower.

“Jet fuel had poured down the elevator shafts, creating a fireball.



“It was a scene of utter horror as that fireball burned a lot of people very quickly. There were bodies everywhere.

“While the worst of humanity led to this attack, I noticed that for every person who needed help, four or five people helped them.

“In them I saw the goodness of humanity — it was already a fight back of good against the evil that had struck.



“One elevator had free-fallen 70 floors, as when Flight 175 crashed, it snapped the cable.

“The emergency brakes had kicked in and stopped it from hitting the concrete. But now they were trapped, getting burned in front of me.

“Out of nowhere appears Firefighter Michael Lynch, from Ladder Four, who managed to save three women.

“I told his widow Denise that he was an angel that appeared out of nowhere to save their lives.

“He was killed when the South Tower collapsed. He ran out of time saving them.”



The collapse, 56 minutes after impact, sent thousands of tonnes of debris and hurricane-force winds surging through the streets.

As it collapsed, Tim ran to the lobby of the neighbouring Marriott hotel, and recalled: “I was getting pummelled by debris.

“The wind was so strong it blew the helmet off my head. I crawled, trying to find a vertical column as I knew it was my best shot at living.



“You can’t breathe or see due to the dust. You are at God’s mercy.”

Finally he saw a column, and he said: “I held on to it in 160mph winds which were created when the South Tower collapsed on to the hotel, and then the hotel collapsed around me.

In a building collapse, all the air on all floors of the hotel creates a hurricane of wind. I was in the eye of the storm.

“I made a deal with God during those 20 seconds — ‘Please let me tell my family that I love them one more time, and then I will come to your side whenever you ask me to’.

“That’s why 25 years later, I speak out as much and as often as I can about all the innocent people — the heroes of the day, the firemen and the cops who lost their lives.”



‘MY BID TO TEACH KIDS ABOUT ATTACKS’ AMONG the 67 Brits who died in the 9/11 attacks was Michael Egan, 51, who was an executive at insurance giant Aon on the 103rd floor of the World Trade Center’s South Tower. His sister Christine, 55, who had grown up with Michael in Hull, was visiting his office that day, and she also died. Michael’s son Jonathan, 43, who lives in Manhattan, was then an 18-year-old student. He said: “My father was able to call my mum and tell her they were stuck on the 103rd floor and trying to get to the roof.” Jonathan, pictured with his dad and Christine, later heard his father helped staff escape, returning twice. He added: “Reading that made me proud.” Today he is an ambassador for UK charity since911.com, which aims to get the terror attack on the school curriculum. He is also a volunteer CEO of The Queen Elizabeth II 9/11 Garden in downtown Manhattan, which he will attend for a memorial on Friday.

At 10.28am, the North Tower fell, with a total death toll of more than 1,400.

In all, 2,977 people died, including 343 of Tim’s New York City Fire Department colleagues.

He is still haunted by their loss and says he thinks of them “from the time I wake up to the time I pass out”.

On Friday’s anniversary, Tim will take his place at the September 11 National Memorial, on the site of the World Trade Center, to honour them.



He said: “I will stand shoulder to shoulder with some American heroes from the intelligence and military community who worked in silence over the past 25 years to serve justice for the murder of my friends and colleagues and the innocent civilians.

“It was an intentional murder of the innocent.”

Since the attacks, more than 2,000 deaths have also been attributed to 9/11 illnesses, caused by toxic smoke and dust exposure that day.

Tim was diagnosed with prostate cancer in 2023, and said: “We found it early as I’ve been watching very closely for it.

“Mine is what they call a slow spreader. I know a close friend who died very quickly from the same thing.



“So I am blessed — and until my last breath I’ll work to make sure people don’t forget.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“I am focused on my friends and their families who lost their lives — and my life’s work until the day I die will be ensuring that the world remembers the truth.”

News.title: TV presenter, 39, among 11 other people sentenced to death in Egypt for manufacturing and trafficking drugs
News.content:
DEATH SENTENCE TV presenter, 39, among 11 other people sentenced to death in Egypt for manufacturing and trafficking drugs

AN EGYPTIAN television presenter has been sentenced to death by hanging after being convicted of drug trafficking.

Sarah Khalifa, 39, and 11 others were handed the sentence after being accused of running a criminal gang and producing narcotics.



The well-known presenter, recognised for her work on Egyptian crime show Mission Impossible, was sentenced to “death by hanging” in a Cairo court on Saturday.

Khalifa, who has 2.5 million Instagram followers, and the 11 defendants faced charges of manufacturing narcotics and possessing firearms.



Egyptian authorities reportedly seized more than 750kg worth of narcotics and raw materials.

Cops also allegedly discovered two apartments used as laboratories, as well as unlicensed firearms and ammunition during their investigation.



Khalifa and her co-accused were given a guilty verdict after the Grand Mufti of Egypt was consulted.

His religious opinion is required by Egyptian law in capital punishment cases.



The defendants still have the option to appeal the ruling.

Khalifa was also sentenced alongside others to five years in prison over a separate case involving the kidnapping and assault of a young man.

When asked by the judge about her alleged role in the group, Khalifa said she had never seen any drugs before until she was photographed with them in a police station, according to state media.

Egypt reserves the use of the death penalty for premeditated murder, terrorism, some rape offences and drug trafficking.

Last year, 541 people were sentenced to death in the North African nation, according to the Egyptian Commission for Rights and Freedoms.

News.title: Green Party deputy leader owns two buy-to-let properties despite party’s vow to crack down on landlords
News.content:
THE deputy leader of the Green Party owns two buy-to-let properties despite his party’s vow to crack down on landlords.

It has emerged Mothin Ali, 44, bought a former council house for £165,000 in 2022, and a second for £157,000 in 2025 through his company MA Holdings.



Both are in Gipton, Leeds, and are thought to be occupied by tenants.

Ali, who shouted “Allahu akbar” when elected a Leeds councillor in 2024, became co-deputy leader of the Greens in England and Wales a year ago.



In October, they passed their “Abolish landlord” policy.

It would use taxes to make it hard for landlords to make a profit.

In March, leader Zack Polanski said tenants were seen as “cash cows”.

A Green Party spokesman said: “Councillor Ali has acted solely in the interests of vulnerable close family members.”

Ali, ADD who has previously been criticised over his views on Israel sparked outrage when he shouted “Allahu akbar” as he was elected as a Leeds councillor in May 2024.

He apologised for “any upset” caused, but was criticised again after social media posts about Hamas’s October 7 2023 attacks emerged.



He also insulted a Leeds-based rabbi for serving as a reservist with the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) in Gaza last year.

He got denounced for “inciting division”.

News.title: Daughter of Brit couple killed in Spanish wildfire ‘finds their bones inside burnt-out car they died in’ after funeral
News.content:
BLAZE TRAGEDY Daughter of Brit couple killed in Spanish wildfire ‘finds their bones inside burnt-out car they died in’ after funeral

A BRIT daughter of a couple who were killed in the Spanish wildfires allegedly found her parents bones in the charred car they died in.

Pete and Fran Gillam were killed when a ferocious wildfire ripped through the Brit-expat hotspot in Bédar in Spain’s Almería province.



The couple were among 14 people – including seven British nationals – who died as blistering 40C heat helped fuel a devastating inferno that tore through the countryside and ravaged two towns.

But now their daughter Danielle Gillam-Kirton claims she has uncovered multiple bones inside the burned-out vehicle – along with keys, jewellery and loose change.



The 42-year-old says Spanish police had previously told her the car was so badly gutted by the flames that virtually nothing remained inside.

According to Danielle, officers said the only trace of human remains they recovered was a tiny fragment of bone.



That fragment was later cremated at a funeral service this summer.

But when Danielle travelled to the wreckage herself, she claims she immediately spotted what appeared to be several bones inside the vehicle.

She said the discovery included what she believed was a hip bone – raising a chilling question over what happened to the remains previously handed to the family.

Recalling the moment she picked up the suspected bone, Danielle told the Guardian: “I honestly can’t describe what that felt like.



“I remember staring at what was in my hand, and the slow realisation of what I thought I was looking at hit me. I shouted out in shock.”

The grim discovery has now plunged the family into fresh anguish as they question whether the wreckage was properly searched in the first place – and where the remains they cremated came from.



Danielle said the ordeal had compounded the family’s grief and left them asking: “Who or what did we cremate?”

The newly discovered bones have since been sent for DNA testing.

Danielle claims that came only after repeated pleas to local authorities, who initially dismissed the remains as animal bones.

She said subsequent assessments indicated they were human.



The family’s nightmare comes amid mounting questions over the handling of the catastrophic blaze and whether more could have been done to protect those caught in its path.

Danielle had previously criticised what she claimed was a failure to issue adequate warnings to people in Almería as the inferno raced through the region.

She is now calling on the Foreign Office in London to pile pressure on Spanish authorities and demand answers from local police.

Families of the 14 victims are also reportedly considering launching a private prosecution against the local government.

According to Spanish media, such a move could give the families’ lawyers direct access to judicial files examining how prepared authorities were for a major wildfire of the kind that engulfed Almería.



One major flashpoint is the emergency mobile phone alert system, which was never activated during the inferno.

Regional officials defended the decision, claiming the blaze moved so rapidly and the technology was too limited when targeting small areas.

They argued that sending alerts could have caused confusion and blocked crucial routes needed by emergency crews.

Pete and Fran had lived in Bédar, the village at the centre of the fast-moving inferno.

The couple had disappeared on the day of the blaze, July 9, with their last contact coming in a text message to Danielle at around 7pm.



Fran had messaged her daughter to say that she and Pete were evacuating.

But contact was then severed and subsequent calls failed to connect.

Police later confirmed the devastating news that the couple had perished in the fire.

Danielle shared the heartbreaking confirmation on Facebook, writing: “We are heartbroken to share that we have received confirmation from the police that Mum and Dad did not survive the fire.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“Thank you for all your love, support and prayers over the past few days. They have meant more to us than we can ever express.”



The inferno was among the worst wildfires to hit Spain this year, scorching more than 16,000 acres and forcing 1,448 people to flee their homes.

News.title: ‘King of the North’ Andy Burnham plans to make his wife ‘Queen of the South’ with First Lady-style role in No 10
News.content:
ANDY Burnham plans to make his wife the Queen of the South with a First Lady-style role in No 10.

The PM — known as the King of the North — wants to hire a media adviser and assistant for Marie-France van Heel, who’s known as Frankie to friends.



The marketing executive, a mum of three, faced scrutiny over her appearance and views in the run-up to him becoming Prime Minister in July.

A source revealed Downing Street aides had been asked to look out for a potential recruit for the aide job — the salary for which will come out of existing budgets.



They said: “Spouses of Prime Ministers have made public appearances and championed causes in the past.

“But this would be a new step. Frankie has always been instrumental behind the scenes. However, this shows that she is going to take a more formal role in future.

“Hers will be more like you see in the US where the First Lady is an official role.

“Burnham is not scared to do things differently.”

Marie-France, 56, attended her husband’s meeting with France’s President Emmanuel Macron and his wife Brigitte when they visited Downing Street last week.

Burnham first met his future wife at Cambridge University in 1989 — soon before she famously appeared on Cilla Black’s Blind Date.



A source said: “There is plenty Marie-France would like to do. She’s passionate about charity work and has worked with Marie Curie, the ­Alzheimer’s Society and Great Ormond Street Hospital on brand and marketing strategies — so more like that should be expected.”

In the past, there has been controversy about the role of the PM’s wife.

During his years in power, Tony Blair’s missus Cherie was embroiled in a number of rows over her commercial activities.

More recently, Boris Johnson’s now-wife Carrie was accused of influencing key government policy.

News.title: Influencer, 43, dies after having penis enlargement surgery in Thailand during holiday with his wife
News.content:
VACATION TRAGEDY Influencer, 43, dies after having penis enlargement surgery in Thailand during holiday with his wife

AN INFLUENCER died after undergoing penis enlargement surgery at a clinic in Thailand while on holiday with his wife, an inquest has heard.

Igho Ubiribo, 43, was injected with 40 milliliters of hyaluronic acid and lidocaine before suffering chest pain and passing out.



He was on holiday with his partner, Danielle Simba Allen, at the time of the operation in Bangkok.

The British-Nigerian businessman went for a massage after going under the knife on March 5.



The influencer then started saying he was suffering chest pain – and soon after he passed out twice.

The popular social media star, who had 185,000 followers on Instagram, was rushed to hospital.



He was taken to the emergency room in the Sukhumvit Hospital where he was seen by doctors who recommended a CT scan.

But the Brit lost consciousness before they could carry out the scan.



Dr Thongchai Chansirirattingkul, of Sukhumvit Hospital, said: “He had had two cases of syncope (fainting) earlier, when he was having a massage.

“He had had 40 milliliters of penile filler injections earlier that day.”

Assistant coroner Jean Harkin said: “Igho Ubiribo was having a massage with his wife when he started to complain of chest pain.

“When he was in the ambulance he was able to answer questions normally. His wife was able to confirm that he had passed out two times.

“When he got to the hospital, his wife confirmed that he had filler injections in the penis.”



Ubiribo’s wife had told doctors at the hospital about her husband’s surgery.

They told her he had suffered a pulmonary embolism – a blood clot in the lungs.

His primary care doctor in London confirmed Ubiribo had an operation on his joints, was pre-diabetic and suffered from gout but had no other medical issues.

Pathologist John du Parcq carried out a postmortem in the UK and also confirmed Ubiribo had suffered a pulmonary embolism.

He said: “Cellular material found in Mr Ubiribo’s lungs matched the hyaluronic acid used in his penis filler jab, in keeping with a pulmonary embolism.



“This matches the Thai autopsy.”

The couple had been staying at the Marriott Hotel in the Thai capital, an inquest at Inner West London Coroners’ Court heard.

It is unclear which exact clinic Ubiribo had his operation done at.

The influencer owned a Los Angeles home and a £450,000 flat in Shepherds Bush.

He married his Anglo-Zimbabwean socialite wife in 2022.



Ubiribo, who was also known as “Tiny”, was laid to rest in London in May in a gold coffin which reportedly cost more than £500,000.

Reports suggest a growing number of Brits are getting penis fillers every year.

During the procedures, patients have hyaluronic acid injected into their penis before having it massaged to spread it out.

They are then advised to continue spreading the acid out evenly at home.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

The penis width increase lasts about six months on average.



Warnings have been issued against the procedure – which is said to cost around £6,000.

News.title: Five arrested after man in his 50s found dead as cops discover body that had been ‘lying in house for days’
News.content:
MURDER PROBE Five arrested after man in his 50s found dead as cops discover body that had been ‘lying in house for days’

COPS have made five arrests after a man was found dead “lying in a house for days”.

The man, in his 50s, is thought to have died several days before his body was discovered, according to Northamptonshire Police.

Officers went to the home on High Street in Burton Latimer on Wednesday after receiving a “concern for welfare call.



Detectives launched a murder inquiry after a forensic post-mortem examination which was carried out at Leicester Royal Infirmary on Thursday.



The investigation is being led by the East Midlands Special Operations Unit.

Three men, aged 43, 48 and 54 have been arrested on suspicion of murder, while two people, a woman, aged 38 and a man aged 53, have been arrested on suspicion of assisting an offender.

All remain in police custody.

Detective Inspector Cheryl Thompson, said: “This is a fast-paced investigation with three people now in custody on suspicion of murder.

“In recent days we’ve been speaking to local people and businesses and would still like to hear from anyone who may have seen any suspicious activity in the High Street area of Burton Latimer in the last week or may have captured anything suspicious on dashcam, CCTV or a doorbell camera.”

Cops have urged witnesses or anyone with information to contact Northamptonshire Police via their online portal or by calling on 101.

You can also call the independent charity Crimestoppers anonymously on 0800 555111.



Please quote incident number 26000526485.

News.title: Disruption at Port of Dover as masked 'stop the boats' protesters block roads
News.content:
There has been major disruption at the Port of Dover due to a large group of masked men holding a demonstration.

Hundreds of protesters, dressed in black and wearing face coverings, blocked roads and were heard chanting "stop the boats".

Traffic was stopped from going in and out of the port, with the government saying it condemned "the behaviour in Dover and the travel disruption it has caused".

Kent Police, which made no arrests, described it as a "spontaneous" protest, while Mike Tapp MP said questions need to be asked around why it appeared the police "didn't know about it".

Officers moved the crowd from the port to Dover Priory railway station at about 11:30 BST and said "all involved had dispersed by 12:00".

Paul King, Reform UK councillor for Dover West, said he had been told it was a "stop the boats protest".

Kent Police has not yet commented on who was behind the demo.

Anti-hate organisation Hope Not Hate claims that the Patriot Platform network arranged the protest, saying the group began meeting in July and has brought together members of anti-migrant groups from around the country.

Demonstrators told the BBC they did not want to talk to the media, although one said "send them back" and another said "stop the boats" when approached.

Far-right activists Tommy Robinson and Danny Thomas both posted about it on X, praising those involved.

Thomas wrote: "The experience on the ground today, was the overwhelming majority of the women and local people we spoke to were thankful that people were actually doing something."

News.title: Nigel Farage tells BBC he 'wasn't listening' during foreign donor talks filmed undercover
News.content:
There's no question the allegations in the Channel 4 film have been embarrassing for Reform, and disrupted what they hoped would be a conference about their plans for office if they win the next General Election.

Everywhere around the huge, draughty exhibition hall in Birmingham are giant posters and placards saying, "Reform - the first 100 days".

They wanted to herald their deal with a serious contender to be the next French President, Jordan Bardella, to deal with small boats.

They were keen to highlight the promise to cut income tax if they win the election, scheduled to be in 2029.

They wanted to talk about their proposals for education, welfare, planning, and the rest.

Party members, delighted to have a reason to get together, have taken part in those sessions, applauded and cheered in the hall; gone wild for Farage on stage.

But for the rest of the country, most of the noise from the conference will have been the huge and awkward story about the toxic mix of politics and money.

What is harder to assess is the impact this mess will have on Farage's standing with the public, after a tricky summer and a recent poll slump.

At the top of the party there is a quiet admission that what has happened here is a genuine mistake.

One senior figure told me they could brush off other claims of murky funding, confident nothing had gone wrong - but they conceded these claims do matter, and that for a certain vital percentage of voters, it would "cause them to ask questions".

No one is pretending it's just what Farage tried to joke was a "little, local difficulty".

And there is a private acknowledgement that stories like this can be off putting to voters beyond Reform's no doubt very enthusiastic base.

Another party source told me they were "totally blindsided" by the revelations; stunned "there'd just been no diligence" and in disbelief at how Jukes and Orr, who both say they'd done nothing wrong, seem to have behaved.

A different member of the party's top team said, "hopefully, it's just growing pains". In other words, Reform's developed so fast that sometimes mistakes are made. But they told me: "The party has to step up â sometimes the people that got us here, aren't the people for the next stage".

Among Farage's fans at the conference, I found different views. One member was convinced the party is treated unfairly: "It's the blob, it's all against him," she said.

But another young Reform enthusiast rejected that, telling me: "It's all documented and there on camera â Nigel has to be more careful about what party members say."

But there is a sense of "here we go again". When I asked another member what they thought of the financial scandal, a weary answer, "Which one?"

This time last year in the same conference complex, Reform felt like they were simply sweeping all before them. Twelve months on, they are having to work harder, the scrutiny is more intense, and the pressure only growing.

Farage's claim that he "wasn't listening" to the conversation was telling â to get to power without more of these kinds of serious embarrassments, he may have to pay more attention to what is going on.

News.title: Aviation faces hotter, stormier skies – and passengers might have to accept more disruption
News.content:
As the country sweltered through one of the many heatwaves of a baking summer in late June, towering thunderclouds were gathering over the south of England and across much of northern Europe. It was a Saturday, and with the holiday season getting under way, thousands of passengers were heading to London's Heathrow and Gatwick airports to catch flights abroad. It was always going to be a very busy day.

What followed, however, was chaos for travellers. As air traffic controllers struggled to route aircraft around the storms, airspace became heavily congested and many planes due to fly were simply forced to wait on the ground. In the end, some 900 flights to and from both airports were delayed, some by up to 11 hours. Dozens more were cancelled. At airports across Europe, passengers expecting to fly into London also faced long waits and uncertainty.

The weather in the UK may now have cooled, and passengers may soon forget their experiences. But some within the industry believe what happened in June should be seen as a warning.

The timing in this case was clearly unlucky. But there are concerns that such incidents are only going to become more common as the effects of climate change mount up around the world and weather systems are likely to become increasingly unstable, making disruption more likely and adding to costs for airlines, airports and travellers.

Tim Atkinson, an airline risk consultant and former pilot, says the very crowded skies over the UK and northern Europe mean the region is particularly exposed.

He thinks there is a real risk, for example, that all of London's airports could be affected by storms at the same time, potentially with major consequences in the air and on the ground.

"What we're seeing now is very rapid climate change," he says.

"We're going from the kind of weather activity which takes out an airport, and which the system kind of copes withâ¦ to a situation where, with very little predictability, it would be possible to lose all of the London airports from real-time operation quite swiftly and with little notice".

Such a scenario, he thinks, would make the disruption for passengers caused by the incident in June seem relatively minor â and could even put lives at risk. But how likely is it?

News.title: Major disruption as grass fire halts all trains to Heathrow Airport
News.content:
Trains to and from Heathrow Airport have been halted after a trackside grass fire caused delays and cancellations.

National Rail said "major disruption" was expected until the end of Saturday following the incident which began shortly after 16:00 BST.

A statement said all lines were blocked between London Paddington station and Heathrow's terminals, as well as Reading, due to "a failure of the electricity supply caused by a fire next to the track".

An update from Network Rail Western late on Saturday said the fire had been extinguished, but warned that disruption would continue, possibly into Sunday morning for some services.

It comes hours after a separate grass fire on Heathrow's airfield shut a runway earlier on Saturday.

Pictures on social media showed crowds of stranded passengers at Paddington, one of London's main rail hubs.

London Fire Brigade said six fire engines and around 40 crew members were tackling the blaze near Scrubs Lane, North Kensington.

Great Western Railway, external cancelled its services to Reading and no Elizabeth line or Heathrow Express services were running between Paddington and Heathrow on Saturday night.

The airport advised passengers to leave extra time for their journeys, adding that the Piccadilly line, which runs services to the airport, also has delays.

Network Rail Western said some services on Sunday morning could face delays and cancellations, caused by trains being displaced by the disruption.

Earlier on Saturday, Heathrow's southern runway was closed while crews tackled a grass fire on the airfield.

It caused some disruption with at least two flights diverted elsewhere. Heathrow apologised for any disruption and said the fire was extinguished quickly.

That comes weeks after another grass fire near Heathrow's southern runway which forced 18 flights to divert and destroyed a large area of grassland.

While weather has cooled across much of the UK in recent days following record-breaking heat over the summer, fire crews have still been warning of wildfire risks.

The Met Office's Fire Severity Index, external shows that if a wildfire was to occur, it would have a "high" fire severity in most of south-east England and some of the Midlands.

The fire severity is "exceptional", the highest level on the index, in some parts of London including Heathrow, as well as on the Essex and Suffolk coasts.

News.title: Why more women carry the 'mental load' - and how couples can share it
News.content:
"My head's always full," says mum-of-three Stacie Matthias. "I go to sleep with a mental to-do list."

She's talking about the concept of the "mental load" - the burden of planning, organising, remembering and anticipating tasks that keep a household running.

These tasks include: remembering school trips, checking for updates in parents' WhatsApp groups, noticing which parts of the house need cleaning, monitoring how much sleep children get, scheduling doctors' appointments and buying school uniforms.

According to academics, this is work that in heterosexual couples disproportionately falls to women - particularly mothers - alongside the bulk of physical household labour.

All relationships and households are different, of course, but studies suggest clear patterns.

Children in the UK have just gone back to school from the summer holidays, and Stacie, 37, from Stockport, says her mind often feels especially busy in September.

"It's that feeling of always having something to remember, organise or worry about that makes this time of year particularly full-on," she says.

For Stacie this list of responsibilities leaves her mind feeling like a washing-up bowl that's being filled up throughout the day.

"If someone's not helping you remove those pots and pans, your water's overflowing by the end of the day," she says, "and you're at tipping point."

News.title: Majority Russian-speaking city in Ukraine considers language ban in the arts
News.content:
Ukraine's third-biggest city Odesa will decide this week whether to back a controversial plan to ban the Russian language in the arts.

The proposal being considered by councillors in Odesa on the Black Sea coast aims to add to existing restrictions on Russian imposed by national legislation.

It is particularly significant because Odesa is overwhelmingly Russian-speaking, although the ban would only affect public spaces and everyday usage of Russian would remain unaffected.

For millions of Ukrainians, Russian is their first language including many of the troops defending the country in its war with Russia. But Ukrainian is the only state language and spoken by the majority, and some see Russian as a tool of Russian influence.

The proposal in Odesa, which is targeted daily by Russian drone and missile strikes, calls for a complete halt to Russian-language content in music and literature, in streets, parks, public institutions and state-run arts and entertainment venues. It would also recommend a ban in privately owned spaces.

In a city famous for Russian-language writers and musicians, it has provoked strong passions.

The ban would extend in public spaces to old Odesa songs almost universally known throughout the former Soviet Union. All Russian-language books would be removed from display in public libraries. Currently, they can be shown, but not prominently.

News.title: The next James Bond: the (00)7 questions fans want answered
News.content:
Back in May, Amazon MGM Studios who now control the Bond franchise confirmed the casting process was under way, external. But little detail beyond that was given, the statement only saying: "While we don't plan to comment on specific details during the casting process, we're excited to share more news with 007 fans as soon as the time is right."

It now seems that the right time is fast approaching. In an interview with Deadline, external Amy Pascal, one of the next film's producers, was asked whether we might have news on who would be playing Bond by the end of the year. She replied: "I would say the end of the year is a good bet."

Last month entertainment writer Daniel Richtman said, external on social media: "I hear they're in the final round of casting for James Bond and might have already found their guy."

His post on X was followed up by journalist Jeff Sneider, external who said: "Heard the same rumour. First it was down to seven, then three. Now 'they may have found their guy'. Who knows at this point? But for some reason, I don't think it's any of the so-called frontrunners, including the Aussieâ¦"

The Aussie is almost certainly a reference to Euphoria and Wuthering Heights star Jacob Elordi, who was brought up in Brisbane and Melbourne before moving to the US to pursue his acting career.

News.title: Why Munya Chawawa is 'jumping ship' from socials to Shakespeare
News.content:
Comedian, content creator and documentary maker Munya Chawawa became a star in the "golden era" of online video, but says his stage acting debut in Shakespeare is part of a move to "jump ship" from social media.

Recently, he has been immersing himself in footage of the UK's 1990s illegal rave scene.

It was a time of hedonism and freedom surrounded by political and media panic - and is the setting for a modern take on Shakespeare's A Midsummer Night's Dream, in which Chawawa will appear.

"I've obviously done a super-deep dive into rave culture and watched loads of rave footage from all these little free parties where they would find an empty field," he says.

While some footage exists of those illicit outdoor parties, they came before everyone had phones and cameras - and Chawawa, 33, feels a pang of nostalgia for that age of analogue abandon.

"I absolutely miss an era where we were dancing for ourselves and not for a digital world somewhere," he says.

News.title: Jaguar Land Rover confirms planned job cuts
News.content:
Car manufacturer Jaguar Land Rover (JLR) has confirmed it is opening a voluntary redundancy programme, a year on from a cyber attack which brought production to a halt for more than a month.

The firm said it needed to save about Â£1.7bn over the next two years as it seeks to adapt to "evolving global market conditions".

It was reported by The Times on Saturday that as many as 4,000 jobs may be lost due to the impact of tariffs and a drop in sales.

The firm told the BBC it had not confirmed the numbers. It said the decision to cut jobs was to help "simplify" the organisation as well as "improve efficiency and build greater resilience".

"Today, we informed our colleagues, and trade union partners that JLR is opening a voluntary redundancy programme offering salaried and management team members the opportunity to leave the business," a spokesperson said.

"We will share further information with our colleagues first."

Unite general secretary Sharon Graham said the union had been warning about a "perfect storm" hanging over the automotive industry for some time.

"Death by a thousand cuts has been going on under the nose of successive governments," she said.

She added there had been "intensive" discussions over the weekend about mitigating jobs losses adding that she and Business Secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, would be meeting JLR's chief executive, PB Balaji, next week.

"This is an incredibly worrying and stressful time for JLR workers," said Unite national officer, Des Quinn. "Unite is working round the clock to deliver the best possible outcome."

News.title: King and Queen join Highland games fans at Braemar Gathering
News.content:
King Charles and Queen Camilla have joined cheering crowds watching Highland games events at the annual Braemar Gathering in Royal Deeside.

The event, which draws spectators from around the world, is held on the first Saturday of September every year and coincides with the monarch's annual summer holiday at nearby Balmoral.

Among the events watched by the spectators were tug-of-war, caber tossing, hammer throwing, Highland dancing and a parade of pipe bands.

This is the fourth Games that the King has attended since his coronation.

News.title: Lauryn Hill, Wyclef and Giggs among surprise guests at Jay-Z's long-awaited UK show
News.content:
Jay-Z's first headline solo show in the UK in more than a decade saw him celebrate hip-hop culture alongside a host of special guests, including Lauryn Hill, Wyclef Jean and Giggs.

The US rap superstar rolled back the years for more than two hours - playing hits like 99 Problems, Empire State of Mind and Dead Presidents - as he took to the stage at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium on Friday night for the first of two shows in London this weekend.

The run is part of his Jay-Z 30 tour, which is marking the 30th anniversary of his debut album, Reasonable Doubt, and his culture-shaping career that followed.

Fans of his wife BeyoncÃ© had hoped she would join him on stage, like she did at two of his three New York shows this summer, as she was also celebrating her 45th birthday on Friday.

News.title: UK support for Falkland Islands 'unwavering' after Argentina restates claims, No 10 says
News.content:
It is not yet clear how or to what extent the sanctions will be imposed or tightened. In Argentina, a current law already allows for restrictions of activities of oil companies participating in projects considered unauthorised on the islands.

Two oil companies â Britain's Rockhopper Exploration and Israel's Navitas Petroleum â are due to begin extracting oil in the Sea Lion oilfield off the Falklands coast within two years, something Milei said Argentina could not allow.

A joint statement from the two firms on Friday said it had the valid licences granted by the government of the Falkland Islands, "and with the full support of the UK government."

The project is due to deliver its first oil in 2028, Rockhopper and Navitas said the partnerships' timetable would not be affected.

The Sea Lion oilfield, around 130 miles from the islands, contains an estimated 1.7 billion barrels of oil - described by Rockhopper as a field containing "highly marketable crude".

Milei also announced plans for a naval base in Tierra del Fuego in the south of Argentina, saying Trump and the US were "assessing their historical position in regard to the Falklands", which Argentina refers to as Las Malvinas.

"That is not empty words as they understand that Argentina is a reliable partner and a valuable ally for decades to come," he said, describing the UK as a nation "in decline".

On Thursday, President Trump hinted the US would not help the UK in any future Falklands conflict because Britain "had not been there to help me" during his war with Iran.

Trump's latest remarks on the islands come after he previously said the US position on the Falklands is one of many under review.

On Friday, Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said the UK would "resolutely uphold" the self-determination of the islands.

Writing on X on Friday, Miliband said the Islands would remain British as that is the "overwhelming position of the islanders."

Defence Secretary Wes Streeting also said Britain's commitment to the Falkland Islands was "absolute and unshakeable".

"Milei's statement overnight tells us more about domestic politics in Argentina than it does about the Falkland Islands," he wrote in his own post on X.

In an earlier statement, Downing Street said it was "not the first time" the Argentine government had made economic threats against the Falkland Islands.

"We are clear that the Falkland Islanders' right of self-determination extends to the right to exploit their own natural resources," it said.

Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch said "Britain does not surrender to bullies".

"If (Milei) wants a stronger Argentina, he should build its economy, not threaten others."

Although the US is formally neutral, Washington provided support for Britain's campaign to retake the islands after the Argentinian invasion in 1982.

Argentine forces landed on the Falklands to stake a territorial claim in 1982, sparking a 74-day war over the territory as a British military task force ejected them.

The conflict led to the deaths of 255 British military personnel, three islanders and 649 Argentine military personnel.

In a sign of the ongoing tensions between the two countries over the issue, Argentina players celebrated their victory over England in the World Cup by waving a banner in support of their country's territorial claim.

News.title: Police probe after child dies in woodland
News.content:
A police investigation has been launched following the unexplained death of a child in woodland.

Emergency services were called to reports of a child in cardiac arrest on land near Strawberry Lane, Cheslyn Hay, Staffordshire, at about 08:45 BST on Saturday.

An air ambulance was sent to the scene, but the child was pronounced dead by paramedics a short time later, Staffordshire Police said.

The force, which has not confirmed the age of the child or any other details, is currently treating the death as unexplained.

Roads in the area were closed throughout the day while investigations took place and officers were expected to remain at the scene throughout the evening.

News.title: Cleveland police chief proud of force but being 'let down' by funding
News.content:
A Volkswagen Passat carrying five young men drove the wrong way down the motorway near Middlesbrough in the early hours of the morning before colliding with a marked police car.

Officers had been pursuing the car for almost seven minutes after it was connected to earlier alleged criminal activity, but the pursuit was abandoned 10 seconds before the crash when the Passat turned on to the dual carriageway, the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) said.

Fuller, whose force covers an area of north-east England that includes Middlesbrough and Teesside, recalled being asleep when the duty commander rang her with the news.

"No matter how tragic and devastated you feel, we swing into action and we do what we need to do," she said.

The home secretary announced this week that Cleveland Police would be given an extra Â£2m to deal with the fallout from the crash, with 200 officers drafted in from elsewhere.

Fuller told the BBC on Friday that she was grateful for the support the force had been given, but added: "I need that all the time."

Cleveland's Labour police and crime commissioner has previously said the force needed an extra Â£20m a year to hire more officers and crack down on organised crime.

Cleveland Police is grappling with the highest recorded crime rate of anywhere in England and Wales, Office for National Statistics (ONS) figures for the year to March show.

It also ranks highest for burglary, sexual offences, violence with injury, and criminal damage and arson.

Fuller said Cleveland Police had also experienced the largest decrease in the number of officers since 2010 and was staffed as if it were a rural force.

"It absolutely needs to change," she said.

Fuller expressed hope that reform to policing across the country was on the horizon, and that Cleveland Police would become one of the "big, strategic forces that have the resource, the flex and the capability to surge when they need to surge".

She added: "In the meantime, we need additional funding... to take us to that point."

Recent inspections show Cleveland is one of the most improved forces in England and Wales, with performance levels also judged to be some of the best in the country.

The force has recently arrested 87 people for offences linked to organised crime gangs and over the past two years 16 people have been jailed for such crimes.

Fuller denied that gangs had control over parts of Middlesbrough, describing it as a "complex" area to police, with high rates of school absence, drug addiction and mental health issues.

"We're doing the very, very best with what we've got - and we absolutely do need more."

Authorities say high deprivation and unemployment in the area are fuelling organised crime.

"When young people have little aspiration or hope, who don't have confidence in the state, then unfortunately criminals exploit these people," Fuller said.

"They give confidence, and they give them hope, and they give them aspiration. And sadly what that means is young people doing things without thought of consequences."

News.title: 'I'd rather die than ring the police': Distrust and fear in Middlesbrough after A66 crash
News.content:
All but one of the residents who speak to us do so on the condition of anonymity. They are worried that showing their faces could place them or their homes at risk.

What message do the attacks send to people on this street, I ask one.

"Well, they should be scared, shouldn't they, that something's going to happen to their property if they say anything or get involved. So we don't."

Victoria, who moved here several years ago, says the escalating violence cannot be separated from the wider condition of the town.

"This is a social problem, especially in this area. Teesside has been massively neglected and ignored," she says.

The attack in Acklam is far from Middlesbrough's only recent case of a vehicle being used as a weapon. Back in May, a tractor was driven into a house on Priory Road, and since the A66 crash Cleveland Police has investigated at least two further rammings.

Detectives have also linked their wider investigation to a caravan fire on Attlee Road in Grangetown.

"It's getting worse," a nearby resident says. "They're always balaclava-ed up as well, do you know what I mean?"

He blames drugs.

"It can't be anything else. Why would you be like you are unless it was drugs?" he says.

Whether every incident is part of a single feud has not been established. But taken together, the rammings, fires and arrests have created a powerful sense that violence is being used to intimidate, punish and send messages.

What is most unsettling for these residents is the sense that nobody is fully in control.

Grangetown and South Bank are communities still living with the void left by the decline of heavy industry. Both now rank among England's most deprived neighbourhoods.

In South Bank, we see a group of teenagers tend three ponies tethered on the grass. Two perform wheelies on electric scooters while another uses a long stick to scatter rubbish.

On the adjoining estate, more than a dozen homes have boarded-up windows.

On a wall are the words "RIP 2UZZI", said locally to have been the nickname of Jakub Matusiak, who lived one street away.

One 17-year-old boy tells us he knew him. "He was my best mate," he says. "It's sad."

Elsewhere, three letters are repeated: "FTP" - an expletive directed at the police.

I ask the teenager if he would call the police if another young person approached him carrying a knife.

"No," he says. Before adding: "I've never needed the police in my life. I'd rather die than ring the police."

Again and again, the young people we speak to express a profound distrust of the police.

Cleveland's Chief Constable Victoria Fuller said what we'd heard was "horrifying".

"Yes, there are a small minority of people in the Grangetown area who blight those communities. But we will continue relentlessly to serve our communities."

The scale of the challenge facing the force and the community it serves is not new.

The area has some of the highest police-recorded crime rates in England and Wales.

Its leaders have been warning for years that its resources did not match the demands placed upon it.

But recent inspections show Cleveland is one of the most improved forces in England and Wales, with performance levels also judged to be some of the best in the country.

The force has recently arrested 87 people for offences linked to organised crime gangs and over the past two years 16 people have been jailed for such crimes.

Since the crash, more than 200 additional officers have been deployed in Middlesbrough and surrounding communities. Their immediate task is to suppress the violence and identify those directing it.

There is also the question of restoring order and rebuilding trust and confidence.

News.title: New police team to crack down on illegal number plates across England
News.content:
A centralised crackdown on illegal number plates will target organised crime groups and drivers who dodge fines by bringing together data and information from police forces across England, the government has said.

The newly-created National Roads Policing Coordination Centre (NRPCC) will see improved collaboration across forces as well as new technology, such as specialist goggles that can detect number plates that have been made unreadable to cameras.

Illegal number plates are often used by organised crime groups to move stolen goods and to evade speeding, parking and clean air zone penalties, the Department for Transport (DfT) said.

Drivers with incorrectly displayed or missing number plates can be fined up to Â£1,000.

Illegal number plates can come in many forms including cloned plates - which copy the registration of a legitimate vehicle - and ghost plates - where a transparent film is used to make them undetectable to cameras.

Vehicles that hide from number plate recognition cameras are harder for police to track down when they are stolen or linked to crimes.

Policing and crime minister Sarah Jones said: "Illegal number plates are not a victimless offence.

"They are used by criminals to avoid detection, move illegal goods and stay one step ahead of law enforcement."

She said by bringing forces together and making better use of technology the new team would track down offenders faster and disrupt gangs.

Ch Supt Marc Clothier, deputy national co-ordinator for the NRPCC, said: "The police forces involved in our ghost plates operation have shown how effective a targeted and intelligence-led approach is in tackling offenders as well as educating and supporting drivers in ensuring their number plates are compliant."

Katie Taylor acclaimed becoming a three-time undisputed world champion in her farewell fight at Croke Park as the most special moment of her decorated career.

Taylor outclassed Flora Pili in a unanimous points victory in front of a crowd of 80,000 to ensure her three decades as an amateur and professional boxer ended in fairytale fashion.

Wild celebrations followed the announcement she had overwhelmed the previously unbeaten Pili 100-90 100-90 98-91 on the scorecards.

For Taylor the feeling of signing off in front of her fans bettered winning Olympic gold at London 2012, headlining Madison Square Garden and her trilogy against Amanda Serrano.

open image in gallery Katie Taylor won in front of her home crowd (Brian Lawless/PA) ( PA Wire )

The 40-year-old said: “This was definitely the highlight of my whole career.

“I didn’t think anything could get bigger than London 2012 and then MSG came along.

“I didn’t think anything could get bigger than that first fight with Serrano and then here we are at Croke Park.

“I ended my career on top, like every athlete wants to do, on my terms, and I ended it as the undisputed champion.

“That’s exactly how I wanted it to end. It was so important to me all along to end my career well.”

Taylor thrilled Croke Park with a spine tingling ring walk and also delivered in the ring by outclassing Pili across all 10 rounds.

She finished the fight by launching an all-out assault in the final 10 seconds that was roared on by the crowd and once the bell sounded, she smiled and hugged her opponent knowing she had thrown her final shots.

open image in gallery Katie Taylor secured victory (Brian Lawless/PA) ( PA Wire )

Taylor said: “This night was everything I expected and more. Thankfully I was able to hold my emotions together because I was getting emotional all week speaking about this event.

“And over the last few months, the preparation for this has been so emotional. But the atmosphere was so special. It was beyond my wildest dreams. It was unbelievable.

“What an amazing night. Looking back on an amazing career, this was just a dream ending to a dream career for me. What a way to end.

“I don’t think there’s another country in the world that would sell 80,000 tickets for a female athlete. I’m convinced Ireland was the only country that would actually do that.

“What a way to end this amazing journey. I started off this career and I had the dream of becoming an Olympic champion.

“I achieved that, but then these last 10 years have been beyond my wildest dreams. It’s been a remarkable 10 years.”

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has promised to protect military members who deliver religious greetings at New Mexico’s Kirtland Air Force Base.

Hegseth wrote on X Friday that the Pentagon will “never cave” to the Military Religious Freedom Foundation after the nonprofit intervened to stop the religious greetings. The nonprofit’s president, Mikey Weinstein, had a five-word response to the Pentagon chief in an interview with The Independent: “Tell it to the judge.”

The Military Religious Freedom Foundation announced Thursday that it put an end to a “weeks-long blitz” of religious greetings from guards at the front gate of Kirtland.

The press release included two emails that a member of the Air Force wrote to the nonprofit’s president, Mikey Weinstein. The initial email sent Wednesday morning read, in part, “I’m writing because something is happening at the front gate of my base that is absolutely unacceptable, and frankly I’m stunned it’s been allowed to continue.

“For multiple days over the last couple of weeks, the guards have been greeting me with ‘God bless you’ every single morning as I come through. Not once, not twice... repeatedly, consistently, as if it’s an officially sanctioned script.”

open image in gallery Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has promised to protect military members who deliver religious greetings at New Mexico’s Kirtland Air Force Base ( Win McNamee/Getty Images )

The unnamed Air Force member said they want this “blatant violation of the separation of church and state” stopped.

While the Air Force member who wrote the email disclosed that they are not Christian, the nonprofit said they were one of 34 people who wanted the religious greetings stopped and that 24 complaints came from Christians.

The Military Religious Freedom Foundation also shared the “thank you” email that the Air Force member sent Wednesday afternoon, by which time the nonprofit said the issue was resolved.

“I have gone through the same gate a couple times without hearing the religious greeting. After dealing with it repeatedly for weeks, seeing that change happen within hours is honestly incredible,” the email read.

The nonprofit says it has helped nearly 100,000 individuals, including active-duty troops and veterans, with issues of religious freedom in the military — 95 percent of whom are Christians.

open image in gallery The Military Religious Freedom Foundation announced Thursday that it put an end to a 'weeks-long blitz' of religious greetings from guards at the front gate of Kirtland ( Todd Berenger via Kirtland Air Force Base )

But the issue of religious greetings at Kirtland is far from over with Hegseth now interjecting.

“The MRFF is a radical anti-Christian, pro-atheist group that attacks any/all faith inside the @DeptofWar,” Hegseth, who is a Christian, said in his Friday X post.

“We will never cave to them. The @usairforce will confront this. God bless our Airmen.”

The Independent has reached out to the Pentagon for comment.

Hegseth has been known to insert his religious beliefs into the military, whether it’s through monthly Christian worship services at the Pentagon or quoting scripture at a press briefing in March, telling reporters, “Blessed be the Lord, my rock, who trains my hands for war and my fingers for battle.”

open image in gallery The nonprofit’s president, Mikey Weinstein, has threatened legal action against the federal government if the religious greetings continue ( Kent Nishimura/AFP via Getty Images )

“Just tell it to the judge, little Petey,” Weinstein told The Independent in response to Hegseth’s X post.

Weinstein called Hegseth a “Christian nationalist” whose “favorite thing to do is to defecate all over the U.S. Constitution.”

The nonprofit pointed to a clause in Air Force Instruction, which states, “Leaders at all levels must balance constitutional protections for free exercise of religion and the constitutional prohibition against governmental establishment of religion.

“They must ensure their words and actions do not discriminate against any individual or group because of their faith, belief, or absence of belief, or extend preferential treatment for the same.”

Weinstein has threatened legal action against the federal government if the religious greetings continue, and against Hegseth himself, claiming libel over his X post calling the nonprofit “anti-Christian” and “pro-atheist.”

“Hegseth is spewing complete and total lies, and it's reckless disregard of the truth. And why is that important? Because I'm a public figure. For public figures in America to win a libel suit, you can't just show regular defamation. You have to show reckless disregard,” Weinstein said.

Prince Hisahito turned 20 on Sunday as he faces growing attention as a future monarch in Japan following the government's unpopular revision to the Imperial House Law that reinforces male-only succession rules.

Hisahito, the nephew of Emperor Naruhito, is second in line to Japan's 1,500-year-old Chrysanthemum Throne and the youngest of 16 members of the rapidly shrinking and aging imperial family.

The child who loved animals and bugs, especially dragonflies, is now a sophomore majoring in biology at the University of Tsukuba near Tokyo. He has been often spotted on campus with friends, sometimes carrying a bug-catching net or on his bicycle.

While he mostly concentrates on his studies, Hisahito started taking on some official duties. He attended a palace banquet for Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. in May, prayed for the atomic bombing victims in Hiroshima and joined a teenagers' camp in the southwestern Japanese city in August.

Hisahito is often compared to his hugely popular cousin, 24-year-old Princess Aiko, who has impressed everyone with her ability to interact with people and make them smile. She is the emperor's daughter and most Japanese want her to be his successor, even though as a woman she is ineligible.

The revised succession law enacted by Japan's Parliament in July lifts a ban on the adoption of male offspring from extremely distant former royal families. It lets female royals keep their status after marrying a commoner, so they can continue to undertake official duties, but their future partners and offspring won't be royals.

The revisions to the 19th-century law have been criticized as anachronistic and sexist and led to protests from Japanese who see the changes, which were backed by conservative Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, as an attempt to eliminate Aiko from ruling while justifying discrimination against women and a patriarchal system.

Experts say the measures will put Hisahito and his eventual wife under enormous pressure to bear a male child as they determine the future of the imperial family.

Asked about his future and marriage plans at his debut news conference last year, Hisahito said his main focus was to study and expressed hopes to spend some time overseas to gain new perspectives and meet people from different backgrounds and cultures.

“About marriage, I haven't thought about an ideal timing or a partner yet,” he said.

A television game show in Nigeria’s commercial hub of Lagos has an unforgiving rule: Speak English and you lose. For a U.S.-born millennial in the audience and a student of her parents' mother tongue, the high-stakes setting is a perfect classroom.

Meanwhile, a 15-year-old Canadian speaks to a teacher about 13,000 kilometers (8,000 miles) away in Zimbabwe, learning a language her parents feared she would never speak.

“Mhoroi,” Nyashadzashe Machingura says cheerfully with a pronounced Canadian accent while greeting in Zimbabwe's vernacular Shona.

The scenes capture a new generation of interest and entrepreneurship around African languages once pushed to the margins by decades of colonialism. Often seen as secondary to English, French and Portuguese, they are enjoying a renaissance that is also creating business opportunities.

There are between 1,500 and 3,000 languages in Africa

Africa is home to over 1 billion people speaking roughly a third of the world’s languages, with between 1,500 and 3,000 across 54 countries, according to UNESCO.

Experts say the revival in some of them is driven partly by second- and third-generation Africans in the diaspora finding it easier to reconnect with their roots and communicate with older relatives, thanks to social media, online learning and entertainment.

“There were times I definitely felt left out because my family around me were all speaking Shona. And I just couldn’t understand them,” Nyashadzashe said after a lesson covering traditional greetings, proverbs and ancestral clan symbols. She said she had eaten the food and worn the traditional clothing but still felt left out.

But now her conversations with her grandparents in Zimbabwe are growing longer.

“Being able to connect with them on that level makes me really proud of my heritage,” she said.

African languages were never ‘modernized’

Her Zimbabwe-based tutor, Shungu Chidovi, left her banking career in January to focus full-time on ZimbOriginal, an online platform that teaches Shona through storytelling, book clubs and “buddy pairing” exchanges.

Now she teaches about two dozen learners in Zimbabwe, Canada, Australia, South Africa, Ireland and Scotland, charging $50 a month.

The business, part of a small but growing number of online initiatives teaching African languages, emerged almost by accident. Chidovi began writing a blog about Zimbabwean traditions in 2016. Readers began asking whether she taught Shona.

“I didn’t see it at the time that I was really writing about the Shona language,” Chidovi said.

Western languages were prioritized

Like many in Africa, she grew up with the understanding that to get ahead she had to embrace Western languages instead of her mother tongue. English remains the dominant language for education, business and government affairs in the southern African nation that officially recognizes 16 mostly Indigenous languages.

“When you talk of Africa, you talk of English, French, Portuguese,” said Believe Mubonderi, a linguistics lecturer at Zimbabwe Open University. His research notes the importance of ensuring that African languages have a place in technologies shaping how people communicate, learn and trade.

“In most cases, African languages were sidelined. They were never exposed or modernized to be used in commerce, science and technology," he said. "When a language has a very low status, there’s a danger that that language eventually becomes endangered.”

Culture and connection are driving the new interest

Governments and international organizations are trying to reverse that trend.

The African Union’s 2022 decision to adopt Kiswahili, spoken in much of east Africa, as an official working language has raised its international profile. The United Nations declared 2022-2032 the International Decade of Indigenous Languages.

And the AU continental body and UNESCO are supporting efforts to document and revitalize African languages, including using artificial intelligence to generate and translate children's books and teacher guides.

But there's a steep digital disadvantage. UNESCO says only 10 languages around the world dominate the "internet ecosystem,” while less than 2% of African languages have a meaningful online presence. That leaves many with too little data to train artificial intelligence systems.

Still, momentum for change is growing, with much of it from Africans abroad.

“People of African descent have come to realize that we also have our own identity which we need to embrace and be proud of. You go on Facebook, you go on TikTok, you are seeing many different efforts,” Mubonderi said. Younger diaspora Africans "are trying by all means to revive, to revitalize, to make use of these languages.”

Chindovi said she hears that desire from children and their parents.

“When people are away from home, they long for home more than when they are home," she said.

Nigerian game show penalizes English speakers

That hunger for connection is also reshaping culture.

In Nigeria, a game show called “Masoyinbo,” meaning “Do not speak English,” has turned Yoruba, one of the country's most widely spoken languages, into prime-time entertainment. Contestants, including diaspora Nigerians, are tested on Yoruba language and culture, with prizes reaching thousands of dollars.

Host Olalekan Fabilola, who started the show in 2024, sees its popularity as part of a wider shift.

“If ‘Masoyinbo’ had started like 10 years ago, it wouldn’t have been what it is now," he said. “But we are in the age of cultural resurgence. People want to go back to their roots. Everyone wants to know why, where they are from, and so it’s timely.”

Tomi Adeshokan, a New Jersey resident who is learning to perfect her Yoruba with Fabilola as a tutor, was part of the audience during a recent recording of the show. She said she lost daily exposure to Yoruba after moving out of her father’s home before the COVID-19 pandemic. During the pandemic, she joined Clubhouse just to hear the language and later began taking classes. Now she was back visiting family.

“It’s very important for us to immerse ourselves in our culture and not to fully identify with other cultures, like the American, the Western culture," Adeshokan said.

___

Ikpoyi reported from Lagos, Nigeria.

Just days before two teenagers carried out a mass shooting at a San Diego mosque, federal law enforcement officials warned the parents of one of the shooters that their son was making concerning comments about school shootings on the dark web, according to new details included in a recently filed lawsuit.

The mother of Caleb Vazquez alleges in her lawsuit that Park Mental Health Treatment of San Diego failed to intervene despite signs that her 18-year-old son posed an imminent threat to himself and others. Vazquez was living there and receiving treatment for a range of mental health conditions, including depression and psychotic episodes, the lawsuit says. The court filings follow a number of high-profile convictions of guardians who provided teenagers with weapons that were later used in mass shootings.

The FBI called Vazquez’s mother on the evening of May 14, and she said she immediately left a message with the treatment facility to notify its staff, according to the lawsuit, filed in a San Diego court on Aug. 31. Vazquez’s mother again shared the FBI’s warnings with her son’s therapist on May 15 and with a program director later that night.

On May 18, the morning of the shooting, employees at the facility contacted Vazquez’s mother to tell her that he was missing. Video surveillance footage subsequently showed Vazquez leaving the property at 8 p.m. the night before.

Vazquez’s parents were driving around looking for him on the morning of the shooting. Vazquez and another teenager killed three people at the San Diego mosque that day before taking their own lives.

It is unclear whether Vazquez was allowed to leave the previous evening or whether he broke facility rules by doing so. Park Mental Health offers a range of treatment options, some of which advertise 24-hour surveillance, while others provide more limited counseling.

The center did not immediately respond to an emailed request for comment Saturday afternoon. In a previous statement to radio station KPBS, Park Mental Health disputed the assertions in the lawsuit.

“While it is understandable that his parents might seek to blame someone in their time of loss, this lawsuit is misguided in that neither Park nor its employees are responsible for Mr. Vazquez’s actions,” the statement to KPBS read. “Only he and his coconspirator bear responsibility for their conduct and, ultimately, his death.”

An FBI spokesperson declined to comment Saturday, citing agency policy.

The FBI’s alleged contact with Vazquez’s parents was not the first sign of his mental deterioration.

Vazquez had been hospitalized for roughly three days in January 2026 after telling a classmate that he wanted to carry out a school shooting.

Almost exactly a year earlier, Vazquez was flagged to law enforcement for exhibiting alarming behavior and idolizing Nazis, prompting police to confiscate 26 guns from his father under a 2014 California law allowing firearms to be taken from people considered dangerous.

Authorities have said Vazquez met the other shooter, Cain Clark, 17, online and that both were radicalized there. Police have not shared more details about how they knew each other or specified whose weapons were used in the shooting.

The lawsuit was filed on the same day that North Carolina authorities announced the indictment of a 17-year-old in connection with the shooting.

New details about the FBI’s push under the second Trump administration to investigate Dr. Anthony Fauci and find evidence Covid-19 came from a Chinese lab have emerged.

Fauci, the former director of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases, was thrust into the political spotlight during the pandemic.

As health officials scrambled to find the source of the outbreak, a theory emerged that the deadly virus was leaked from the Wuhan Institute of Virology while scientists were researching bat coronaviruses. Many Trump supporters even believed Fauci and other researchers covered up the leak.

There is still no definitive answer as to what caused the pandemic — and no concrete evidence of a cover-up — but, according to a New York Times report, the FBI and Justice Department are still investigating.

Early last year, then-Deputy FBI Director Dan Bongino met with dozens of agents at the bureau’s Washington, D.C., headquarters, demanding to know why investigators had stalled a probe into the origins of the pandemic and why they were not more heavily scrutinizing the role of government scientists, current and former officials told the Times.

open image in gallery New details about the FBI’s push under the second Trump administration to investigate Dr. Anthony Fauci and find evidence Covid-19 came from a Chinese lab have emerged ( Getty Images )

Under this renewed push, FBI agents and DOJ prosecutors have sought evidence — including phone, email and payment records — related to at least eight scientists, including Fauci, according to the Times.

When reached by The Independent about the new reporting, the FBI’s national press office said, “We don't have any comment.” The Independent has also reached out to the DOJ for comment.

Dr. David Morens, a former adviser to Fauci, pleaded guilty last month to conspiring to conceal federal records related to research on the pandemic’s origins. He was accused of using his private email account to intentionally get around public records laws while working at the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases.

DOJ prosecutors in Maryland subpoenaed documents in Morens’ case in September 2025 as they sought evidence about Fauci, including any emails he sent to certain researchers from his personal account, according to documents reviewed by the Times.

The FBI’s Cleveland office also recently examined whether Fauci and other government scientists pressured virologists in early 2020 to understate the possibility that Covid-19 came from a lab, according to the Times.

open image in gallery FBI agents and DOJ prosecutors have reportedly sought evidence — including phone, email and payment records — related to at least eight scientists, including Fauci ( AFP via Getty Images )

Just before leaving office in January 2025, then-President Joe Biden issued a preemptive pardon to Fauci for any federal crimes he may have committed or taken part in since January 2014 as NIAID director or in service to the White House during the pandemic.

Despite his protection from Biden, Fauci invoked the Fifth Amendment more than 100 times during a Senate hearing in late July, refusing to answer questions about the origins of the COVID-19 pandemic.

Ahead of the hearing, Republican Senator Rand Paul of Kentucky, who chairs the Senate Homeland Security and Government Affairs Committee, released more than 1,000 pages from a long-running diary Fauci kept.

In an April 2021 entry, Fauci wrote that members of the “radical right wing” like Paul were trying to “connect me with the virus from WUHAN.”

“They are saying that I deliberately worked with the Chinese together with [zoologist] Peter Daszak to create a virus that would be released to the world,” he wrote at the time. “This sounds very much like a way-out conspiracy theory, which it is. However, there are enough crazy people around to make this a problem.”

The Homeland Security and Government Affairs Committee voted to hold Fauci in contempt of Congress in early August after he refused to answer questions at the Senate hearing.
