What the government is asking for

On September 3, the Finance Ministry sent a request to the Legislative Assembly, which is El Salvador’s Congress. The request asks to reform the national budget and add US$97 million for the second half of 2026.

The Finance Ministry calls the costs ‘priority and unavoidable obligations’ for 11 state institutions. The full list is not public, but the largest items are known.

Where the money comes from

The US$97 million is not new borrowing. It comes from two domestic bond issues that Congress approved earlier but were not fully used.

The first issue was approved in November 2025 for US$344 million. The government used US$267 million, leaving US$77 million.

The second issue was approved in April 2026 for US$100 million. It left US$20 million unused.

Together, those leftovers make up the US$97 million. This is an important distinction.

The funds are pending authorizations, not surplus from bonds that were already sold. The government is asking for permission to use the remaining borrowing capacity it already has.

How the money would be spent

The largest single item, US$37 million, goes to the Ministry of Agriculture and Livestock. Reports differ on the exact use, from farm markets to running costs.

The next largest, US$30 million, is for prisoner rehabilitation. About US$19 million goes to the interior and territorial development ministry, split between running the ministry and social programmes.

Smaller sums go to the Attorney General’s office, the economy ministry and public works. The National Registry of Natural Persons gets US$1.19 million to issue free national ID cards for first-time applicants.

Other recipients include the environment ministry, tourism ministry, and CORSATUR, the state tourism promotion corporation. The decree does not say how long the bonds would run or what interest they would pay.

Why Congress must approve it

In El Salvador, changes to the national budget require approval by the Legislative Assembly. This includes using existing bond authorizations.

The request reached the Assembly as a formal letter from the Finance Ministry. The Assembly’s finance committee has been called to take up the request early next week.

A plenary vote would follow if the committee backs it. The Assembly could still change the request or reject it.

The IMF program behind the budget

El Salvador is under a 40-month Extended Fund Facility (EFF) with the International Monetary Fund, approved in February 2025. The program provides about US$1.4 billion in loans.

In exchange, the government agreed to cut spending and raise revenue. The goal is to reduce public debt to about 83% of GDP by 2028.

That means running a primary surplus, which is revenue minus spending before interest payments. The IMF program also limits new debt.

Under the deal, the government cannot issue Bitcoin-linked bonds or other crypto-related guarantees.

El Salvador’s approved 2026 national budget is US$10,555.6 million. The request would move money inside that total.

How this request fits the IMF deal

Using leftover bond authorizations is a way to get cash without going to international markets. Fitch Ratings, a credit rating agency, said in May 2026 that it does not expect new Eurobond sales before 2027.

Instead, El Salvador relies on domestic borrowing and multilateral lenders like the IMF and World Bank. This request fits that pattern.

The IMF’s 3 September statement on the second and third reviews does not mention this request. The two are separate steps.

The bigger picture: fiscal consolidation

The IMF program requires deep spending cuts. El Faro, an independent Salvadoran outlet, reported that the IMF-backed plan implied social spending cuts of about US$623 million in 2025.

It put the cuts at over US$1 billion in 2026 and US$1.4 billion in 2027. The government says it is committed to fiscal consolidation.

In December 2025, an IMF staff statement praised the government’s ‘strong’ commitment. It said the 2025 primary balance target was on track.

But some targets have been missed. Fitch notes that the 2025 domestic debt reduction goal was not met.

A Q1 2026 indicative target was also missed. The end-2025 primary balance target, however, was achieved.

What this means for foreigners

For investors and expats, this request shows how El Salvador manages its public finances under the IMF program. It is a mix of domestic borrowing, multilateral support, and strict spending controls.

The US$97 million is under 1% of the 2026 budget. It is a small sum, but the government still needs permission to spend it.

The request also signals that the government is avoiding new international debt for now. It also means less new debt sold abroad this year.

It also means the IMF programme sets the limits.

What to watch next

The key date is when the finance committee meets, likely early next week. If approved, the money will be distributed to the 11 institutions.

Also watch for the IMF’s final approval of the second and third reviews. That would release the next tranche of loan funds.

The government has not said when it will issue the remaining bonds. The interest rate and the term of the bonds have not been published.

How El Salvador’s budget process works

El Salvador’s national budget is a law passed by Congress each year. The Finance Ministry proposes it, and lawmakers approve it.

If the government needs more money mid-year, it must ask Congress to amend the budget. This request is a formal step in that process.

The Legislative Assembly has 60 seats. The ruling party, Nuevas Ideas, holds 54 of them, so approval is likely.

Mid-year top-ups are routine. In June the Assembly approved a separate US$118 million reinforcement funded by higher tax collection.

What the numbers do and do not prove

The US$97 million is under 1% of the 2026 budget. It is a small sum, but the government still needs permission to spend it.

The request is significant because it shows the government’s cash flow challenges. It needs to use leftover borrowing authority to pay for basic services.

The numbers do not prove that the government is in crisis. They show that it is managing within the limits set by the IMF program.

However, the missed targets on domestic debt reduction suggest some strain. The government is walking a tightrope between spending needs and fiscal discipline.

Who is affected and how

The US$97 million would reach several groups. Farmers would benefit from the agricultural market programs.

Prisoners would get rehabilitation services, which the government lists as a priority cost. First-time applicants would get their national ID card, the DUI, free of charge.

Tourism agencies would organize international events to attract visitors. The money is still borrowed, and it is borrowed at home.

Local banks and pension funds are the usual buyers.

The role of domestic bonds in El Salvador

Domestic bonds are debt securities sold to local investors, such as banks and pension funds. They are a key source of funding for the government.

In 2025 and 2026, Congress authorized two domestic bond issues. The government did not sell all the bonds, leaving US$97 million in unused authorization.

Now it wants to use that leftover permission to borrow. This is a common practice in many countries, but it requires legislative approval.

Domestic bonds are different from Eurobonds, which are sold on international markets. Eurobonds are more expensive and subject to foreign investor sentiment.

What is still missing

The specific terms of the bonds, such as interest rates and maturity dates, are not public. The government has not released that information.

It is also not clear whether the IMF has explicitly approved this budget reform. The staff-level agreement does not mention it.

Only the largest recipients among the 11 institutions have been named so far. The Assembly could still change the request or reject it.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is the US$97 million a surplus from an existing bond? No. It comes from unused balances of two domestic bond issues approved in 2025 and 2026. The government is asking for permission to use that remaining borrowing capacity. What will the money be used for? The largest amounts go to agriculture (US$37 million) and prison rehabilitation (US$30 million). Smaller sums go to ID card issuance, environment programs, and tourism events. Why does Congress need to approve this? In El Salvador, any change to the national budget requires approval by the Legislative Assembly. This includes using existing bond authorizations. How does this relate to the IMF program? The IMF program requires fiscal consolidation and limits new debt. Using leftover bond authorizations helps the government avoid new international borrowing, which fits the program’s goals. When will Congress vote on this? The finance committee was due to take it up in the week of 7 September. A plenary vote would come after that.

World.title: São Paulo Builder You,Inc Faces Negative Equity
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

The morning intel from across Latin America. Free.

BRAZIL · REAL ESTATE

Key Facts —What happened: You,Inc, a São Paulo developer, is delaying deliveries and has negative equity of R$312.7 million (about US$61 million). —How big it is: The company’s net debt reached R$779.8 million (about US$153 million) in the second quarter. —What it means: Negative equity is an accounting measure, not a finding of insolvency. —The catch: You,Inc is not in judicial recovery. —Who it hits: Buyers in several You,Inc projects in São Paulo report stalled works and late deliveries. —What comes next: Brazilian law allows buyers to seek contract termination and refunds, but recovery depends on the company’s finances.

You,Inc’s own second-quarter accounts show it burning cash. Buyers on several projects say deliveries have slipped.

What negative equity means for You,Inc

Negative equity sounds technical. It is not.

It means a company’s debts are bigger than its assets.

For You,Inc, that gap was R$312.7 million at the end of June 2026. That is about US$61 million.

At R$5.11 to the US dollar, the Banco Central do Brasil PTAX rate of Friday 4 September 2026.

A year earlier, You,Inc had positive equity of R$2.4 million (about US$0.5 million). The swing took just 12 months.

You,Inc’s financial troubles in numbers

You,Inc’s net debt rose from R$663.1 million to R$779.8 million between the first and second quarters of 2026. That is about US$130 million to US$153 million.

Equity turned more negative in the same period. It went from minus R$221 million to minus R$312.7 million (about minus US$43 million to minus US$61 million).

The company burned R$116.7 million of cash in the second quarter, about US$23 million. That was up from R$71.7 million (about US$14 million) in the first quarter.

Gross sales fell 68.1% year on year in the second quarter, to R$94 million (about US$18 million). Contracted sales are not the same as booked revenue, but the fall shows how little new money is coming in.

Delayed deliveries and stalled works

Buyers have protested over works that Brazilian outlets report as stopped or slowed on several projects. Portas, a Brazilian property title, names one specific site: Authentique Perdizes, stopped since March 2025.

You,Inc has not launched any new projects in 2026.

There is no public total for how many buyers are affected. Portas counted at least 15 court cases specifically over delivery delays.

Dozens more over contract revision and damages, and at least 106 complaints on Reclame Aqui in six months.

A consumer law site lists about 19 You,Inc worksites. These are ordinary civil disputes, not a formal bankruptcy process.

What happens to your money if a Brazilian developer fails

Brazilian developers can ring-fence a single project under a rule called ‘patrimônio de afetação’. It walls that project’s assets and buyer payments off from the rest of the company.

Ring-fencing is optional, not automatic. Buyers should check their own contract and the project’s registry record to see whether it applies.

Where a project is not ring-fenced, buyers rank alongside other unsecured creditors if the developer fails. That is the general rule in Brazil.

If the developer goes bankrupt, you may have to join a queue of creditors to get your money back. Protection is not absolute.

Your rights as a buyer in Brazil

Under Law 13.786/2018 a buyer may terminate and seek a refund. Developers may keep a penalty, and there is a 180-day grace period on delivery.

How much is refunded depends on the contract.

This process is called ‘distrato’. You can also demand compensation for delays.

Lawyers who handle these cases say the first step is written notice. Timing and the exact contract terms then decide what follows.

If the developer does not respond, you may need to go to court. Legal action can be slow, but it is often the only way to enforce your rights.

Is You,Inc in judicial recovery?

Judicial recovery is a Brazilian process similar to Chapter 11 bankruptcy. It gives a company protection from creditors while it tries to restructure.

No court has placed You,Inc in judicial recovery, and no filing has been reported. This is a cash and delivery problem, not an insolvency case.

Being in judicial recovery would freeze most lawsuits against the company. It would also give You,Inc time to negotiate with creditors.

Without that protection, buyers can pursue their claims individually. Nothing in the public record indicates the company plans to file.

What the company says

You,Inc has not published a project-by-project response to the delays. Its chief executive, Abrão Muszkat, has described an operational and financial restructuring at the company.

The financial figures come from the company’s own disclosures.

Estadão has reported that builders in this segment, You,Inc among them, are selling projects to cut debt. You,Inc has not confirmed any sale.

Commentators quoted in the Brazilian press. Including Roberto Pereira of ATEX Investimentos and Adenauer Rockenmeyer of Corecon-SP, describe the company as heavily indebted.

Selling land or projects is the usual route out for a developer in that position.

What buyers should do now

If you have a contract with You,Inc and the delivery is delayed, you can send a formal notification to the company. This is the first step in a distrato process.

You may also want to seek legal advice. A lawyer can help you understand your rights and the best way to get your money back.

Keep all documents related to your purchase, including contracts and payment receipts. These will be essential if you go to court.

The company has announced no new delivery dates and no refund schedule. This is general information, not legal advice.

The bigger picture for Brazil’s real estate market

Estadão has reported that builders which bet on the middle class are now heavily indebted and selling projects. You,Inc is one of them.

The pattern is a warning for foreign buyers. A big market does not make a small developer safe.

The middle-class segment was once seen as a growth area. But economic downturn and high interest rates have hit these developers hard.

Some of these companies are selling projects to reduce debt. Others may need to restructure or face bankruptcy.

How You,Inc got here

You,Inc expanded in the São Paulo market. The company targeted middle-income buyers with residential projects.

The company’s debt grew as it financed new projects. When sales slowed, the debt became harder to manage.

Net debt kept rising while sales fell. The company has launched nothing new in 2026.

You,Inc reported a landbank of about R$1.8 billion (roughly US$352 million). One account of the same results puts inventory at R$1.58 billion (about US$309 million).

What is not yet known

Neither the company nor the courts have published a figure for affected units. The exact number of buyers remains unknown.

You,Inc has not published a detailed response to the delays. Its plans for new delivery dates or refunds are not public.

The negative equity figure of R$312.7 million (about US$61 million) comes from You,Inc’s own financial reports. These are public documents filed with regulators.

Frequently Asked Questions

What does negative equity mean? It means a company’s liabilities are bigger than its assets. For You,Inc the gap was R$312.7 million, about US$61 million, at the end of June 2026. Can I get my money back if You,Inc delays my property? Brazilian law allows a buyer to terminate and seek a refund once the delivery date and grace period have passed. A process known as distrato. Is You,Inc bankrupt? No. You,Inc is not in judicial recovery as of 5 September 2026, and no filing has been reported. How many buyers are affected by You,Inc delays? There is no public total. Portas counted at least 15 active delay cases, and a consumer law site lists about 19 worksites. What protections do Brazilian buyers have? Some projects are ring-fenced under ‘patrimônio de afetação’, which separates that project from the developer’s other business. It is optional, so buyers need to check whether their own project has it.

Connected Coverage We have also reported on Brazil’s Vinci Takes Over Navi’s Property Funds.

World.title: National Geographic Germany Devotes 11 Pages to Costa Rica
World.content:
National Geographic Traveler’s German edition has given Costa Rica eleven pages in its September issue, describing Costa Rica as a treasure of nature and taking readers on a route that runs from the Pacuare River to the Osa Peninsula. The photographs reaching German newsstands this month include hummingbirds, beaches, forest canopy, a sloth and rafters on whitewater.

The written feature follows a journey through the Nairi Awari Indigenous Territory, San Gerardo de Dota and Los Quetzales National Park before moving south to Carate Beach, Corcovado National Park and the Gulf of Nicoya. The Costa Rican Tourism Institute (ICT) said the article is the product of a partnership with National Geographic Germany. Under that agreement, Costa Rica covered airfare, lodging and production costs for the assignment.

As of Saturday, the institute did not have figures available on how much it spent on those items. The ICT said that in exchange, Costa Rica appeared in a publication where the equivalent advertising space would have cost €207,900, or about ₡109 million. That works out to roughly $240,000 at today’s exchange rate.

Marcos Borges, executive president of the ICT, said partnerships of this kind let Costa Rica put its attractions in front of thousands of potential travelers and encourage them to turn what they see on the page into a trip. The magazine printed 35,000 copies for distribution across Europe and the feature will also run in National Geographic’s digital edition.

Journalist Amelia Duggan wrote the piece, which is structured as a first-person account of her time here. Her framing is that Costa Rica’s natural wealth is not something to be looked at from a distance but something to be walked into and taken in through all five senses.

The article also spends time on conservation, on seeing wildlife in its own habitat, and on how easily a single trip can cross between sharply different ecosystems. According to the ICT, the report presents Costa Rica as a country that has built the protection of its natural heritage and its sustainability commitments into the tourism product itself, reinforcing a reputation the institute describes as global leadership in sustainable travel.

Beyond landscapes and wildlife, the feature argues that understanding Costa Rica means spending time in local communities and engaging with its culture, food and people. Pura vida is presented as shorthand for that identity, and as a way of valuing simple, unpolished experiences over packaged ones.

Germany remains one of Costa Rica’s more important European source markets. Between January and August 2026, it received 50,000 German visitors by air, part of the roughly 300,000 European arrivals by air over the same stretch. Placements like this one sit at the center of how Costa Rica competes for attention abroad, and they carry a cost the public underwrites.

The value of the exposure will be measured against those European arrival numbers over the coming season, and the price paid for it is a figure the ICT has said it will need to look up.

World.title: Thousands of Olive Ridley Turtles Come Ashore in One of the Year’s Largest Arribadas
World.content:
One of the largest arribadas of the year began in the early morning hours this morning at the Ostional National Wildlife Refuge in Guanacaste, as thousands of olive ridley sea turtles emerged from the Pacific to nest on the beach long known as their favorite stretch of Costa Rican coastline.

Guides and residents alike described this week’s event as among the biggest seen so far in 2026. More turtles were expected to continue arriving through Friday night and into Saturday morning. The spectacle draws both Costa Ricans and tourists eager to watch the turtles come ashore, dig their nests, lay their eggs and return to the sea. That cycle has made Ostional one of the most closely watched nesting sites in the world.

The timing fits a well-established seasonal pattern as well as arribadas occur throughout the year at Ostional, but September, October and November typically bring the largest events, when more than 100,000 turtles can come ashore in a single night and a single arribada can stretch on for up to two weeks.

Dry season arribadas, running roughly from January through July, are considerably smaller. Those events usually bring fewer than 20,000 turtles over three or four nights. Friday’s event also arrived on schedule as arribadas at Ostional cluster around the last quarter moon, which fell on September 4, and can begin two days before or after that phase.

The refuge is patrolled daily by park guards who track nesting activity along the beach. When the number of turtles climbs to around 1,000 in a given arribada, the Asociación de Desarrollo Integral de Ostional, the local community development association, can declare what is known as an arribada aprovechable.

That designation sets several things in motion at once. It triggers Costa Rica’s official monitoring operation and allows members of the local community to carry out a legal, regulated harvest of a portion of the eggs. It also closes the beach to anyone not accompanied by a certified local guide, with groups capped at nine visitors.

The guide rule is not a formality but a nesting female that is startled will abandon the attempt and return to the water without laying, and a beach at this density is packed with fresh nests that are easily crushed underfoot. Flash photography and white flashlights are prohibited for the same reason.

The harvest itself is limited to the first days of an arribada, when eggs laid early are likely to be dug up and destroyed by the waves of females arriving behind them. The model has operated at Ostional for more than three decades and remains one of the only sites in the world where a regulated harvest of sea turtle eggs is permitted.

The refuge covers 468 hectares (1,156 acres) of land and 8,000 hectares (19,768 acres) of ocean along 16 kilometers (10 miles) of coast, taking in not only Ostional but also the beaches of Nosara, Pelada and Guiones. Final turtle counts and nest totals for this week’s arribada were not yet available. Those figures are typically released by Costa Rican wildlife authorities and the local association once monitoring concludes, generally a few days after the largest nightly arrivals taper off.

Anyone planning to travel to Ostional in the coming days should confirm tour availability with the local guide association before setting out. Access during an arribada is by guided group only, and slots fill quickly when a large event is underway.

World.title: Belizean Cacao makes its way to Chocolate makers around the world
World.content:
Belizean Cacao makes its way to Chocolate makers around the world

By Zoila Palma: Maya Mountain Cacao (MMC) has announced that its final container of Belizean cacao for the 2026 U.S. market is now on its way, marking another milestone for Belize’s growing fine-flavor cacao industry.

The company said it will also ship its final container to the European Union market next week, officially bringing the 2026 export season to a close.

MMC sources premium Belizean cacao for fine chocolate makers while supporting farmers and creating social impact in cacao-growing communities.

The company said the end of the 2026 export season also signals a new chapter, as beginning in 2027, international exports will be managed by the Maya Mountain Cacao Co-operative Society Limited, placing farmers at the center of the business and its future growth.

World.title: Teach them to plant! Why Agriculture could transform Belize’s schools and future
World.content:
Teach them to plant! Why Agriculture could transform Belize’s schools and future

By Zoila Palma: As Belize looks toward a future of greater food security, entrepreneurship and economic resilience, agriculture should be given a much stronger place in the secondary school system.

Every high school student should have the opportunity to learn how to plant, cultivate, harvest and care for crops—not simply as a school subject, but as a practical life and business skill.

Teaching agriculture can help young Belizeans understand where their food comes from while developing skills that can become sources of income.

Students can learn vegetable production, livestock rearing, soil management, composting, irrigation, greenhouse farming, aquaculture and even the business side of agriculture.

Such knowledge can encourage young people to see farming not as an outdated occupation, but as a modern industry with opportunities in food production, agribusiness, technology and entrepreneurship. Belize’s education planning has previously identified the reintroduction of gardening and agriculture into primary and secondary education as a way to better connect education with the country’s needs.

An excellent example of this demonstrating what is possible is Mopan Technical High School in Benque Viejo del Carmen.

Its agriculture program provides students with hands-on experience in areas including soil and organic-matter management, planting, crop care, harvesting, greenhouse production and animal husbandry.

Mopan’s model demonstrates that agriculture education can extend far beyond a classroom.

The school has historically utilized its campus for agricultural activities, including crop fields, greenhouses, poultry and pig production and aquaculture.

Students have also participated in community activities such as World Food Day, giving tours and providing plant seedlings. The school’s own history notes that it was among the first high schools in Belize to enter students in CXC Agriculture examinations.

Imagine if more high schools across Belize had productive school farms.

Students could grow vegetables used in their school feeding programs, raise chickens or fish, learn to propagate fruit trees and sell surplus produce to help finance school projects.

Every Belizean eats, and every Belizean benefits when the country can produce more of its own food.

If Belize wants a generation that is more self-sufficient, entrepreneurial and prepared for the challenges of food security and climate change, our high schools should be teaching young people not only how to pass exams, but also how to grow something, produce something and build something of their own.

World.title: Belize Coast Guard Commandant completes strategic leadership Seminar in South Korea
World.content:
Belize Coast Guard Commandant completes strategic leadership Seminar in South Korea

By Zoila Palma: Coast Guard Commandant Rear Admiral Gregory Soberanis has completed a Senior Leadership Seminar in Strategic Studies in South Korea, focusing on lawfare and the evolving geopolitical environment.

The engagement provided senior military leadership with greater insight into the legal, geopolitical and security dynamics shaping today’s operating environment.

The Belize Coast Guard said participation in strategic engagements of this nature strengthens leadership awareness and helps prepare commanders to anticipate emerging challenges.

As Belize’s maritime security environment continues to evolve, the Coast Guard remains committed to developing strategic leaders capable of safeguarding Belize’s national and maritime interests.

World.title: Minister of Home Affairs seek to expand BPD’s K-9 unit
World.content:
Minister of Home Affairs seek to expand BPD’s K-9 unit

By Zoila Palma: Minister of Home Affairs Julius Espat has indicated that the Ministry is seeking the expand the Belize Police Department’s K-9 unit.

“ And right now I’m looking at the K-9 Unit, and we only have two dogs nationally, and I believe we should have at least 20, so we will work on that. I’ve been looking at other things within the force. We’ve been looking at the infrastructure, which is for us the easiest part of it. So, we did a national analysis of all the substations that we have, and we did an evaluation as to what is needed to bring them up to an acceptable level. That report has been sent to Ministry of Finance already, sent to the Prime Minister. And then we’re looking at vehicles,” Espat said.

Espat says that the Ministry is also looking at acquiring ATV so that the police are able to reach urban areas.

“We just signed the contract to roof the Raccoon Street station, and we’ll be doing another part to do the cladding of it. That’s by MIDH. We just had a bid out for purchasing of weapons; we are awaiting that bid to come in. So, the transfer of personnel is just a part of what the Police Department needs.

There’s a lot of work that has to be put in, and I think we have very good police officers who are frustrated,” Espat added.

Espat says that the Ministry continues to seek ways to improve the Belize Police Department.

World.title: International News: Deported to a country they’ve never called home: The 8 top ICE destinations
World.content:
International News: Deported to a country they’ve never called home: The 8 top ICE destinations

By Zoila Palma: The U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) has been deporting thousands of people to their countries of origin, but an increasing number are being sent instead to third countries—nations where they are not citizens. The practice has raised concerns about deportees being left in unfamiliar countries where they may not speak the language or understand local customs.

Mexico has emerged as the largest destination for third-country deportations, with about 20,000 people without Mexican heritage reportedly sent there during the second Trump administration, according to Refugees International’s Third Country Deportation Watch. Mexican authorities reportedly give many third-country nationals only 10 days to remain, leaving asylum systems under significant pressure.

Other Central American countries have also become destinations. Guatemala has received several thousand deportees, including 2,284 Mexican nationals between April and August 2026, while approximately 360 non-Panamanians have been deported to Panama.

Costa Rica has received about 331 people, while approximately 250 non-Salvadorans have been sent to El Salvador since ICE transfers to that country began in July 2026.

Honduras has also received about 170 non-Honduran deportees under a transfer agreement with the United States. Officials have indicated that sending some Mexican nationals farther south could serve as a deterrent to irregular migration, while Mexico has objected to its citizens being deported to other countries.

The policy extends beyond Central America, with more than 130 people sent to Uzbekistan and over 100 people without Ghanaian heritage deported to Ghana, according to the Third Country Deportation Watch.

Human rights organizations have raised concerns about the treatment and legal protections of people transferred to countries where they have no established ties.

World.title: Tracy Panton, saddened by murder of young Brianna Myvett, calls for action against gun violence
World.content:
Tracy Panton, saddened by murder of young Brianna Myvett, calls for action against gun violence

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Leader of the Opposition Tracy Panton has extended condolences to the family and friends of young Brianna Myvett.

“I heard every word you shared, and I felt the words you could not bring yourself to say. The shock, disbelief and pain of it all are simply too much, not only for you, but for every parent who has lost a child to senseless acts of violence.

By all accounts, Brianna was a beautiful, intelligent, talented and ambitious young woman with plans for her life. She kept herself out of harm’s way, yet harm still found her. Her life mattered. Her contributions to our Belizean society mattered.

We may never understand why bad things happen to good people,” Panton said.

“We MUST find solutions to gun violence that is robbing the lives, potential and future productivity of our young people. Belize’s very survival depends on how well we protect them and create opportunities for them not merely to survive, but to thrive and to triumph,” Panton added.

Myvett was a recent graduate of Wesley Junior College. In June, Anglican Cathedral College congratulated her on graduating from the institution, noting that she was a distinguished alumna of ACC’s Class of 2023.

Myvett was laid to rest on September 2, 2026.

World.title: Public Utilities Minister apologizes for remarks on electricity costs
World.content:
Public Utilities Minister apologizes for remarks on electricity costs

By Breaking Belize News Staff: During an interview with Love FM, Minister of Public Utilities Michel Chebat apologized for comments he made on households’ ability to manage increased electricity costs, following widespread criticism on social media.

His remarks at an August 24 press conference were criticized by many as insensitive to families facing financial pressures and the rising cost of living.

Chebat had indicated that savings from government initiatives including free education, increases in the minimum wage and expanded National Health Insurance coverage could be used to cover expenses including light bills.

Chebat said his intention was to address the broader issue of the cost of living, rather than dismiss the financial struggles being experienced by Belizeans.

“So that was unfortunate. I was really addressing, my intention was really to address the overall cost of living. I mean, we know it’s a very serious issue, we know it is something that our citizens complain about. So, my idea was really to address it on a whole as to the cost of living issue,” Chebat said.

“Unfortunately it did not come off that way. And you know what? I must apologize because I think a lot of people were offended by the comments made. It made me look insensitive and it made the government look like if we’re not in tune with what is happening. And so, I do apologize for those comments and the way it came off,” Chebat added.

World.title: Jamaican defender Brown’s Macedonia transfer hinges on late FedEx package
World.content:
Richard Brown

JAMAICAN centre-back Richard Brown’s chances of playing professional football with Macedonian top-flight outfit FK Skopje has taken a dramatic turn, his signing stalled by a FedEx package sitting in a closed office with a transfer deadline of midnight Sunday, September 6, looming.

Jason McKay, owner of the McKay Security Football Group, which includes McKay New Raiders, said on Saturday that Brown’s signing has been left in a precarious position, held up by a FedEx package sent from Jamaica on August 26.

“It has been nine days,” McKay bemoaned. “I have no idea why it has taken so long. The package is now verified to be in Macedonia. However, FedEx isn’t open on weekends.

“All it takes is for some store owner to open his door for a few minutes so the federation there can get the documents. These are important documents such as police and school records, which the federation requires to be original copies,” McKay added.

“The package was sent on August 26 via FedEX after being verified by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs to meet the transfer window of midnight, September 6,” he emphasised.

Reports out of newly promoted FK Skopje, who lost their third match of the new season Saturday, 1-2 to Bashkimi, indicated that Brown was on the verge of signing for the club now sitting at the bottom of the 10-club First Football League on three points from six games.

FK Skopje, who won promotion to the First League, June 1, after finishing as runners-up in the

Second League, are bolstering their squad for a third stint in nine years among North Macedonia’s top-tier teams.

Meanwhile, Brown, raring for a shot at his first international break, said he has been giving his

best with his family back home in mind.

“A lot of sacrifice has been put into this. I am here trying to make myself, McKay Raiders and

my family proud,” he said during a break from training.

Brown has been a feature player in Jamaica’s Premier League since age 18, first representing Cavaliers. The 25-year-old has also donned the colours of Tivoli Gardens, Dunbeholden, Racing and St Catherine Police.

World.title: Tina Clayton joins list of Jamaican 100m Diamond trophy winners
World.content:
Jamaica's Tina Clayton celebrates winning the women's 100m final during the World Athletics Diamond League athletics meeting at the King Baudouin Stadium in Brussels, on September 5, 2026. (Photo by NICOLAS TUCAT / AFP)

KINGSTON, Jamaica—Tina Clayton joined an impressive list of Jamaicans to win the women’s 100m Diamond League trophy after she sped to 10.93 seconds on Saturday’s second and final day of the Wanda Diamond League Final in Brussels, Belgium.

Clayton became the fifth Jamaican woman to take the trophy, joining four-time champion Shelly-Ann Fraser-Pryce, three-time champion Elaine Thompson-Herah, Shericka Jackson and Veronica Campbell-Brown.

She was also the fourth Jamaican to win Diamond trophies at this year’s meet after Rajindra Campbell threw a national record 23.08m to win the men’s shot put, Oblique Seville won the men’s 100m and Tajay Gayle the men’s long jump on Friday.

Great Britain’s Amy Hunt was second in the women’s 100m in 11.06 seconds, American Sha’Carrie Richardson was third in 11.07 seconds, and Jamaica’s Jonielle Smith was fifth in 11.08 seconds.

Three Jamaicans placed third in their respective events: Nickisha Pryce in the women’s 400m, Megan Simmonds in the 100m hurdles and Jordan Scott in the men’s triple jump.

Pryce ran 49.36 seconds for her podium finish as Marileidy Paulino of the Dominican Republic set a meet record of 48.64 seconds to win her fourth Diamond trophy in five years and complete an unblemished Diamond League season. Henriette Jaeger of Norway was second with 49.20 seconds.

Simmonds ran a season’s best 12.43 seconds (1.0m/s), for third in the 100m hurdles, which was won by world record holder Masai Russell in a meet record 12.20 seconds, under the 12.27 seconds set in 2022 by Jasmine Camacho-Quinn.

Devynne Charlton broke her own Bahamian national record with 12.33 seconds to take second place.

Scott jumped 17.18m (0.2m/s) in the first round to finish behind Italy’s Andy Diaz Hernandez, who had a meet record of 17.74m (-0.6m/s), bettering Christian Taylor’s 17.66m set in 2019, with Pedro Pichardo of Portugal second with 17.51m (0.0m/s).

Lamara Distin was sixth in the women’s high jump with a best clearance of 1.88m.

Sabrina Dockery won the women’s invitational 100m in 11.17 seconds (0.1m/s), beating Australia’s Torrie Lewis- 11.24 seconds with Jael Bestue of Spain placing third with 11.28 seconds.

Kadrian Goldson was second in the men’s invitational 100m in 10.05 seconds (-0.2m/s), just beaten by Ghana’s Abdul-Rasheed Saminu with 10.04 seconds, with American Max Thomas third with 10.23 seconds.

-Paul A Reid

World.title: Campbell throws over 23m to claim Diamond trophy, extend national record
World.content:
Jamaica's Rajindra Campbell competes in the women's Javelin Throw during the World Athletics Diamond League athletics meeting at the King Baudouin Stadium in Brussels, on September 5, 2026. (Photo by JOHN THYS / AFP)

Jamaica’s Rajindra Campbell stunned the track and field world on Saturday when he threw a stupendous 23.08m to win the men’s shot put on Saturday’s second day of the Wanda Diamond League Final at King Baudouin Stadium in Brussels, Belgium.

It was the third Diamond trophy won by a Jamaican at the meet after wins by Oblique Seville in the men’s 100m and Tajay Gayle in the men’s long jump on Friday’s opening day.

Campbell’s mark is the fourth best ever in the history of the event, shattering the 22.62m he had thrown in the second round to break the Jamaican national record, the meet record and take over the world lead.

Only three Americans have thrown further- Ryan Crouser- 23.56m in May 2023, Joe Kovacs-23.23m in September 2022, and Randy Barnes-23.12m in May 1990.

Campbell, the Olympic Games bronze medalist who was breaking his own Jamaican national record for a fifth time this year, dominated the contest. His 22.25m in the first round would have still won as American Jordan Geist was second with 22.23m and Kovacs third with 22.09m.

He had extended his own Jamaican record to 22.34m in China in May, then threw 22.44m in June in Zagreb, Croatia and 22.59m in Brescia, Italy last weekend.

-Paul A Reid

World.title: Cop among five dead in separate crashes
World.content:
KINGSTON, Jamaica—The carnage on the nation’s roads has resulted in the deaths of five people, including a police constable, within a 12-hour period.

Police said four fatal crashes happened between Friday afternoon and Saturday morning in Clarendon, Westmoreland and St James.

In the first incident, about 3:00 pm on Friday, Opheal Hyman, 41, a groundsman of Santa Hill district, Spalding, Clarendon, succumbed to injuries he sustained during a collision with a truck on the Nine Miles main road near Spalding. The Manchester police division, which has jurisdiction over Spalding, is investigating the incident.

In the second incident about 8:45 pm on Friday Jevoy Wheatle, otherwise called “Pepe”, 23, a labourer of Gravel Hill in Milk River, Clarendon and Ackeem Thomas, 24, a labourer of Race Course in Toll Gate, Clarendon died from injuries they sustained when the two motorcycles they were traveling on collided with a Nissan Tiida on the Swansea to Four Paths main road in Clarendon.

In St James, police said about 11:50 pm, a pedestrian whose identity has not yet been ascertained died from injuries he sustained after he was hit by a Mark X motorcar on the Rose Hall main road.

In the wee hours on Saturday, police Constable Chadrick Cooke succumbed to injuries he sustained on the Farm Pen Road in Westmoreland in a two-vehicle crash. He was assigned to the Frome Police Station.

Statistics from the police show that up to 6:00 am on Saturday, 232 fatalities were recorded from 199 crashes on the nation’s roads, compared to 263 fatalities from 229 collisions for the corresponding period last year.

— Kasey Williams

World.title: ‘Unfair and illegal’
World.content:
The Jamaica Gazette, dated April 1, 2014, states that all certified motor vehicle dealers must ensure that the warranty provided on motor vehicles imported and sold by them is not materially less than that offered by the manufacturer.

PRESIDENT of the Jamaica Used Car Dealers’ Association Lynvalle Hamilton is headed to court to challenge what he says is an unfair and illegal policy being implemented by the Trade Board to govern warranty that players in the sector must give their customers.



Hamilton, who is the owner of Auto Channel Limited, told the Jamaica Observer that it is important for him to seek to block the policy from taking effect any further as it is a big setback for businesses.

According to Hamilton, other players in the industry are running scared and even though they are not happy with the policy, they refuse to join him in protest over fear they may become targets.

“With this policy in particular, the Trade Board compels us to give a certain warranty and that is not consistent with the law, the Sale of Goods Act. This clearly gives us the right to choose the warranty that we want to give to the customer,” said Hamilton.

“The customer can also rely on our expertise to get warranty, but the Trade Board’s policy wants us to give warranty on every occasion and outlines a particular warranty that we are to give, which is totally unfair. That’s unlawful. They are acting as if they are a law unto themselves as is the case with many agencies and entities in Jamaica. This has to be challenged,” added Hamilton.

He charged that because of his refusal to comply with the policy, his certification has been blocked.

“They use the certification as a weapon [and] it is ruining business. This is my livelihood. This is an abuse of power. The other players in the industry are afraid because, listen, not everybody will stand up to the Government in situations like this. You have to stand up for your rights and also get the Government to abide by the law,” he argued.

“The Government can’t make the laws and then want to be a law unto themselves, and that’s what they are doing now. The dealers, although they know it is wrong, they still comply just to keep their business going,” lamented Hamilton, who is being represented by attorney Hugh Wildman.

Wildman, who has filed the challenge in the Supreme Court, told the Observer that the warranty policy has been proving difficult for players in the industry to adhere to and even more than that, it is illegal.

“The Sale of Goods Act is what governs the buying and selling of goods. When they import motor vehicles from abroad and they are going to sell it to the customer, the customer examines the vehicle before to see whether or not they wish to buy it. Whatever warranty is given to them by the dealer, that is it,” argued Wildman.

“They have come up with this motor vehicle policy now, where they will try to impose warranties on the dealers, but that is not contained within the Act. They are saying that they must prescribe what warranty the dealer must give the customer, outside of what the legislation is saying. Mr Hamilton is challenging that policy which affects him,” added Wildman.

He charged that players in the industry are not pleased, especially because those who disagree with the policy and wish not to adhere to it could find themselves without a licence to operate, as is the case with his client.

“If they don’t get with this policy then they will not certify them to import vehicles,” Wildman said as he told the Observer that an application to challenge the policy was filed on Tuesday.

On Friday, the Observer visited Jamaica Trade Board to get a reaction from Chairman Sean Azan. However, he declined to comment, noting that the matter is now before the court and as such he did not wish to prejudice the case. At the same time, he shared a copy a section of the Jamaica Gazette dated April 1, 2014 that outlines the policy on motor vehicle imports.

Under the section that deals with warranty, the document states that all certified motor vehicle dealers must ensure that the warranty provided on motor vehicles imported and sold by them is not materially less than that offered by the manufacturer. According to the document, manufacturer’s warranty on labour, parts, time owned, or distance driven must be passed on to the consumer. This requirement applies to dealers certified as importers of new motor vehicles and those certified as importers of used motor vehicles but who wish to participate in the importation and sale of new motor vehicles.

The gazette also states that all certified used motor vehicle dealers and brokers must provide warranties in accordance with guidelines determined by the vehicles’ age and odometer reading.

Class A warranty is applicable to vehicles manufactured fewer than four years before the sale date with an odometer reading of less than 53,000 kilometres (km)/32,934 miles.

Class B Warranty is applicable to vehicles manufactured more than four years but fewer than seven years before the sale date, with an odometer of less than 106,000km/65,867 miles.

Class C warranty is applicable to commercial vehicles manufactured more than six years but fewer than 11 years before the sale date with an odometer reading of 178,000km/110, 607 miles.

The warranty covers vehicle parts such as the engine, transmission, differential, steering gear, drive chain, front end, major electronic components including computers, air conditioning system, general electric system, and suspension system.

World.title: Distress signal
World.content:
Researchers have compared data from 2010, 2017 and 2026 showing that mental health indicators have worsened over time with more students reporting suicidal thoughts, suicidal planning, suicide attempts, anxiety and depression.Photo: Adobe stock

BY ALICIA DUNKLEY-WILLIS Senior staff reporter dunkleywillisa@jamaicaobserver.com

THE 2026 Global School-Based Student Health Survey’s finding of increased suicidal thoughts and attempts among students in grades nine to 11 — with girls outpacing boys in both — is “a distress signal from our children” and a warning of a crisis that “did not happen overnight”, according to a child and adolescent development expert.

“When more than one in three grade 11 girls says she has thought about ending her life, and nearly one in three grade 9 girls says she has actually tried, we are not looking at an anomaly, we are looking at a generation in crisis,” Therrain Davis, lecturer in the Child and Adolescent Development Programme at the University of Technology, Jamaica’s College of Health Sciences, told the Jamaica Observer on Friday.

According to researchers, in comparing the 2010, 2017 and 2026 survey results, “mental health indicators have worsened over time with more students reporting suicidal thoughts, suicidal planning, suicide attempts, anxiety and depression”.

For Davis, the crisis now unveiled had been announcing itself from over a decade ago.

“The survey compared data from 2010, 2017, and 2026. Each wave brought worse news. More suicidal thoughts, more anxiety, more depression. That means this has been building for at least 16 years while, as a society, we have largely looked away,” the scholar noted.

She said several factors account for the findings.

“Many of our young people are carrying wounds they cannot name — abuse, neglect, violence in the home or the community. These experiences do not stay in the past. They follow children into classrooms, into friendships, into the way they see themselves and the world. Research tells us that children who grow up in these conditions are significantly more likely to experience depression, anxiety, and suicidal thoughts. Jamaica’s own data confirms this pattern. Yet our systems, schools, health services, communities are rarely set up to recognise or respond to this kind of pain,” the educator reasoned.

According to Davis, the “enormous amounts of time” spent online with almost no guidance is another fatal factor.

“The survey found that nearly nine in 10 students have a mobile phone, and two in three spend three or more hours on screens every single school day. Only 39 per cent have parents who set rules around social media. This matters because the research is clear: Heavy social media use, especially for girls, is linked to rising depression, anxiety, sleep problems, harmful comparisons, and cyberbullying. The Internet is not neutral territory for a hurting teenager,” the university lecturer declared.

She also argued that the stigma attached to people experiencing mental health challenges in Jamaica is another hurdle.

“In Jamaica, mental health struggles are still too often treated as weakness, madness, or something to hide. That silence costs lives. Young people who need help are not getting it, not because they do not want it but because the judgment is too great and the services too few,” Davis said.

She, however, noted that while dire, the problem is “not without solutions” as “other countries and communities have faced similar crises and pulled back from the edge”.

“Here is what the evidence shows works: Start in schools. Schools are where our children spend most of their waking hours [so] they are the most logical places to provide early mental health support: counselling, safe spaces to talk, trained teachers who can spot a child who is struggling. A school counsellor should not be a luxury. Right now, it largely is,” Davis said.

Other proven solutions, she said, include training parents and communities how to talk about mental health, recognise warning signs, and set healthy boundaries around screen time.

Additionally, Davis advanced as another solution making it easier to ask for help through anti-stigma campaigns that speak in the language and culture of Jamaican communities, with buy-in from churches, community organisations, schools, and media.

Creating clear pathways for children in crisis to find help, so that referrals actually work with minimal wait times and service availability across communities, is another strategy.

In addition, Davis said “what lies beneath” must be addressed, as mental ill-health does not exist in a vacuum and is fed by poverty, violence, and unstable homes.

“The release of this survey is an opportunity not to write reports that gather dust, but to act. Every child who checked ‘yes’ to suicidal thoughts on that questionnaire is someone’s daughter, son, niece, nephew, student, or neighbour. The question is not whether Jamaica can afford to respond. The question is whether we can afford not to,” Davis emphasised.

“Policymakers must move beyond awareness to investment in school-based mental health services, in trained professionals, in community programmes, and in the families — who are the first line of support for every young person. But this is not only a Government responsibility; it belongs to all of us. Check on the young people in your life. Have the hard conversations. Ask directly, ‘Are you okay?’ and mean it. Remove the shame. Create space. Listen,” she added.

Said Davis: “Our children are telling us something. The only question is whether we are willing to hear it — and to act before more lives are lost.”

World.title: ‘Something doesn’t sound quite right’
World.content:
.

MONTEGO BAY, St James — Five people walked free from the St James Parish Court on Wednesday after the prosecution offered no evidence in a case stemming from a police operation at a Montego Bay nightclub.

The accused include three women from the Dominican Republic who were charged with working without permits and two Jamaicans, alleged to be their employers, who were charged with aiding and abetting the offence.

The case arose from an August 1 operation conducted by members of the St James Police Division and the Trafficking in Persons Unit. The team went to a nightclub on Barnett Street in Montego Bay following reports of suspected human trafficking activities at the establishment.

The five individuals appeared before Parish Judge Kaysha Grant-Pryce on Wednesday. They are Marsol Beaz Beaz, Yahaira Jimena Tejeda Sanchez and Naiomi Perez, all from the Dominican Republic, along with Jamaicans Camoy Spence and Nicholas Ricketts. They were represented by attorney-at-law Adrian Dayes.

The three women were charged with working without a permit, while Spence and Ricketts faced charges of aiding and abetting that offence. However, the matter took an unexpected turn when the court was informed that the prosecution would not be proceeding with the charges.

Judge Grant-Pryce asked what had changed.

“How it was explained to me, your honour, is that they entered the club and were dancing but several other persons were dancing around them as well,” the clerk of court responded.

The judge then asked the clerk what the prosecution intended to do. The clerk reiterated that the prosecution intended to offer no evidence, but explained that the difficulty was that defence counsel Dayes had indicated that he would provide his own translator, who was not available on Wednesday.

“I was not prepared to have our translator today. They do understand, though, the difference between guilty and not guilty and if the court wishes to proceed we could do so,” Dayes said.

The five accused were subsequently called upon to plead and each pleaded not guilty.

The prosecution then offered no evidence against all five, bringing the proceedings to an end.

However, before allowing the accused to leave, Judge Grant-Pryce issued a stern warning.

“Something doesn’t sound quite right, Madam clerk, but I am going to tell the two Jamaican nationals that these girls are not supposed to be working here,” the judge said.

She further warned the locals that they could find themselves before the court not only in relation to the women working without permits, but also on matters involving trafficking in persons.

“Trafficking in persons is a serious offence. The world is having an issue with that. Vulnerable persons are being used for work of all kinds. You can find yourself on the other side of the law. You are lucky this morning; these girls were dancing,” she added.

According to the allegations, when the police entered the nightclub, several patrons were seen dancing and consuming alcoholic beverages. Several female exotic dancers were also observed, including the three women from the Dominican Republic.

The women were reportedly dressed similarly to the other females at the establishment.

The police subsequently communicated with the women using

Google Translate on their mobile phones and asked whether they had valid work permits. The women reportedly indicated that they did not. The managers were also questioned and allegedly confirmed that they were not in possession of the required permits. The five were subsequently arrested and charged.

During an earlier hearing, Dayes had told the court that his clients were lawfully in Jamaica and were not working at the time of the police operation.

The prosecution’s decision to offer no evidence on Wednesday resulted in the matter being brought to a close.

World.title: Saint International crowns male and female Fashion Face of the Caribbean winners
World.content:
Rajae Shirley (left) and Talleta Gregory were crowned male and female winners of the Saint International Fashion Face of the Caribbean at AC Hotel on August 29, 2026. .

Rajae Shirley, a 25-year-old resident from the hilly community of Thompson Town in Clarendon, and 17-year-old Ascot High School sixth-form student Talleta Gregory of Portmore were last Saturday night chosen as Fashion Face of the Caribbean Male and Fashion Face of the Caribbean Female, respectively, in the Saint International Fashion Face of the Caribbean competition.

The finals of the competition, which saw 45 females and 38 males competing for the titles, took place inside the ballroom of the AC Hotel in New Kingston.

During the event, nine designers showcased 10 collections in the segment dubbed ‘Riddim Runway Fashion Collections’ and which was sponsored by the Ministry of Culture, Gender, Entertainment and Sport.

Designers included UK-based Jamaican designer David Newell, Kaydian Nicely, Janseen Graham, Lucien Harrison, Tamia Carey, Errice Alicia, Nina Levy, Shades of Africa, and Andre Shirley.

The judging panel tasked with selecting the winners consisted of some of the world’s most powerful agents. Corrie Caster – Elite World (Europe); Price Stephen – Soul Artist Management (New York); Agel Raya – No Smoking Period (New York, London, Milan, Paris); and Monika Kielczewska – The Society Models (New York).

And when it came down to the announcement of the winners, you could feel the tension in the air.

“I honestly did not expect to win, but I knew for sure that my presence in the competition would make an impact because of my confidence. Everyone else had time to prepare their outfits, while my clothes were actually purchased by my wife on the same day of the event,” Rajae told the

Jamaica Observer post-event.

Rajae, who said he felt unprepared, had decided to withdraw from the competition due to financial and personal challenges.

“I felt a bit unprepared and out of place. So coming back on the day of the competition after the Saint coordinator called and told me that Mr Peters requested my presence, I decided to show up, be myself, and give it my best,” he shared.

He recalled that when his name was announced as the winner, it made him reflect on events leading up to the finals.

“My mind immediately went back to what Mr Peters had said to me that very same morning. For about three mandatory sessions leading up to the event, I was not present because my daughter had gotten sick and was in the hospital. At that point, I had decided to withdraw from the competition because of the personal difficulties I was facing, and I was still without a sponsor. Then, on the very same day of the event, they had secured a sponsor. I came to Kingston for prejudging, and when I arrived, he told me very firmly that I must never give up on myself and that he believed in me. He said I should give it my best shot because this could be a life-changing moment for me and my family. So when my name was called, all of those words came back to me. I couldn’t help but think about everything that had happened just to get me there. It was a very emotional and unforgettable moment for me,” he said.

Rajae said that it was his wife who encouraged him to enter the competition.

“We were at home one evening and she said, “They like you.” I asked her, “Who?” and she told me it was the agent from Saint International. She went ahead and submitted my picture to their

Instagram post where they were searching for new faces. She knew that modelling had always been a dream of mine, and she wanted to see me finally bring that dream to reality. I decided to take the chance and see where it could lead me,” said Rajae, who described the experience as transformative.

“It challenged me mentally, physically, and emotionally. I had to learn how to take directions, work with the other contestants, and remain composed under pressure. The training sessions were very intense, and I learnt a whole lot. The experience also gave me the opportunity to meet some very talented people and learn more about the fashion industry. Most importantly, it showed me that I am capable of much more than I initially thought, and that sometimes you just have to step out of your comfort zone and give yourself a chance.”

Talleta described being named as the winner of Fashion Face of the Caribbean Female as surreal.

“Honestly, it feels surreal. I was surprised that I won, so hearing my name announced as the Fashion Face of the Caribbean Female was definitely a ‘wait…did they just call my name?’ moment. I’m extremely grateful for the opportunity and proud of myself, especially because I entered mainly to enjoy the experience, meet new people, and grow as a model. Winning was just the beautiful surprise at the end,” she shared.

“When I heard my name announced, I immediately started crying! I was honestly shocked because I really didn’t expect to win. Earlier, I had been chosen as the winner for the Blue Denim Remix Challenge [for all the Fashion Face of the Caribbean competitors] so I thought that would probably be my only big moment for the night. My family and friends had been telling me that they believed I could win, which gave me some confidence, but I still wasn’t expecting it. It was a tough competition, many amazing people; I went into the competition mainly for the experience, to have fun, meet new people and grow as a model.”

Talleta explained her decision to enter the competition.

“I’ve always loved art and fashion, and modelling is something I’m genuinely passionate about. When Saint discovered me at my school, Mr Peters told me that he believed I could be a star, but he did say it required a lot of work and discipline. So when I heard about Fashion Face of the Caribbean, it felt like an opportunity I couldn’t pass up. I wanted to challenge myself, gain more experience, and step outside of my comfort zone. I definitely wasn’t going into it thinking I’m coming home with the crown. I was really just there to enjoy myself and see where the experience would take me. Every training session was different, I realised I was lucky to be with Saint,” she reasoned.

Deiwight Peters, founder, CEO of Saint International is pleased with the turn of events.

“I thought this year’s pool of talent was extraordinary. There were such diverse looks and interesting backgrounds. We had an Italian, Jamaicans, Cubans, British Jamaican, and a Jamaican American. But in terms of the different looks, very interesting. I am confident a number of them will be developed to become international stars using the tried and proven and unmatched Saint formula for making fashion stars. I am very excited to see what the future holds for these wonderful young people,” said Peters.

World.title: Nigel Farage wants to be a global statesman. First he needs distance from Trump.
World.content:
The pair signed a “memorandum of understanding” pledging to stop the flow of small boats trafficking migrants across the English Channel to British shores. For Farage, it was a chance to prove he can cut a deal with a foreign political leader even before he’s elected to office.

The surprise was that the leader wasn’t Donald Trump.

Showing off a French connection — and even suggesting he would speak in French when he repays the visit — might just help dilute the impression that Farage is a disciple of the world’s most divisive and disruptive head of state.

Farage has long made a point of his ideological kinship with the American president, but these connections to the “Make America Great Again” universe now pose perhaps the most serious threat to his campaign to win power in the U.K.

Goodbye to the ‘British sherpa’

Farage’s set-piece Friday press conference alongside Bardella was overshadowed by a storm of controversy over an alleged funding scandal that hours earlier had claimed the scalps of two of his most senior aides.

One of them, policy chief James Orr, is almost as well plugged into Trump’s world as the Reform leader himself. Orr has nurtured a friendship with U.S. Vice President JD Vance, whom he has described as a kind of “mentor.” For his part, the vice president has called Orr his “British sherpa.”

World.title: Farage would use military to ‘crush’ Argentina in any Falklands dispute, senior ally says
World.content:
But last week, U.S. President Donald Trump suggested he was reconsidering Washington’s support for Britain’s sovereignty over the islands. “I always review every position — that’s just one of many,” he told reporters.

Days later, on Friday, right-wing Argentinian President Javier Milei, a Trump ally, escalated the rhetoric over his country’s enduring claim to the islands, pledging to levy sanctions against companies drilling for oil nearby without approval from Buenos Aires.

Britain’s center-left Labour government immediately rejected Milei’s threat. A Downing Street spokesperson said the islanders have a right to self-determination and that the U.K. supports their right “to develop their natural resources for their own economic benefit.”

Jenrick told journalists at the Reform UK conference in Birmingham: “If Nigel Farage was our prime minister, Milei would not be doing what he’s doing. This is happening because Milei is weak, and he senses that we have a weak government too.”

He added: “If Nigel Farage was our prime minister, we would use every lever of the British state — our armed forces, our economic sanctions, everything — to defend the Falklands, and we would crush Argentina.”

Reform UK’s decision to turn on Milei over the issue contrasts with Farage’s previous praise for the Argentinian leader for his right-wing, small state ideology. In 2024, Farage described Milei’s agenda as “amazing,” “incredible” and “like Thatcherism on steroids,” adding: “I’m beginning to think about buying Argentinian bonds.”

“This is due to the preparation and conduct of American contacts in Kyiv,” Peskov said. Witkoff and Kushner are expected to travel to the Ukrainian capital on Sunday.

Russian drone attacks on Ukrainian cities have intensified in recent weeks. Ukraine, meanwhile, has stepped up its hits on Russia’s oil infrastructure, in August reaching a monthly record for strikes since the start of the war in 2022.

Saturday’s pause order followed a broad Russian overnight attack across Ukraine that killed at least five people and injured six others, according to the Kyiv Independent.

“They were deliberate, for the first time in a long while,” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky wrote on Telegram of the strikes targeting airports in Kyiv and Boryspil. “Clearly, Russia’s strikes on the airports are a reaction to discussions and preparations concerning the possibility of the American side using an aircraft to arrive in Ukraine.”

The U.S. emissaries are scheduled to meet with Putin later on Saturday.

World.title: UN backs effort to depict Africa correctly on maps despite US opposition
World.content:
Mercator, the world’s most commonly used map projection, was devised by Flemish cartographer Gerardus Mercator in 1569 to help sailors navigate using compass bearings. | iStock

The American delegation dismissed the resolution as part of a “much larger and more radical ideological project.”

The United Nations on Friday largely endorsed a resolution to promote maps that reflect the true scale of continents after an African-led campaign to move away from the ubiquitous 16th-century Mercator projection.

The United States was the only country to vote against the initiative, denouncing it as part of a “much larger and more radical ideological project” and urging “countries to instill common sense to this body.” Estonia, Georgia, Lithuania, Moldova, Serbia and Ukraine abstained.

Mercator, the world’s most commonly used map projection, was devised by Flemish cartographer Gerardus Mercator in 1569 to help sailors navigate using compass bearings.

World.title: Ein Spaziergang mit Sahra Wagenknecht
World.content:
Endspurt im Wahlkampf in Sachsen-Anhalt: Zwischen Plattenbauten in Halle-Neustadt steht für das Bündnis Sahra Wagenknecht (BSW) weit mehr auf dem Spiel als nur der Einzug in den Landtag. Sahra Wagenknecht skizziert ein Klima der extremen Polarisierung, in dem ihre Partei von zwei Seiten unter Beschuss gerät. Fällt die Brandmauer, oder zwingt das BSW die etablierten Parteien in völlig neue Bündnisse?

Im Spannungsfeld zwischen der AfD um Ulrich Siegmund und den Altparteien kämpft das BSW um Sichtbarkeit und beklagt eine mediale Blockade. Wagenknecht zieht scharfe rote Linien zu Björn Höcke, fordert eine leistungsgerechte Aufstiegsgesellschaft und rechnet mit der Agenda-Politik von Gerhard Schröder ab. Was bedeutet der Begriff „links“ heute überhaupt noch, wenn die einstige Linkspartei ihr traditionelles Milieu verliert?

Neben landespolitischen Fragen geht es um die große geopolitische Linie, von der Kritik an teurem US-Gas bis zur Forderung nach mehr Diplomatie. Ein Spaziergang, der die strategischen Ziele des BSW offenlegt und in der Gordon Repinski mit Wagenknecht auch ihre persönliche Prägung zwischen DDR-Vergangenheit und dem Bruch mit ihrer alten Partei beleuchtet.

Das Berlin Playbook als Podcast gibt es jeden Morgen ab 5 Uhr. Rixa Fürsen, Maximilian Stascheit und das POLITICO-Team liefern Politik zum Hören – kompakt, international, hintergründig.

That being said, it’s impossible now to bring back the Russian teams. Because of the way they are used, the national teams, it’s so hard to separate from the propaganda. That is the aim, that they could play with each other and not be affected by the war. But that’s not possible now, football would stop and Ukraine would not play. So then we are there, and that’s a sad situation, but happening because of war.

When it comes to the Israel situation, we have always said, and we will always say, when you have a breach of FIFA statutes, it needs to be treated. It was delayed, delayed, delayed for many years, that they play with teams from [settlements in] Palestinian territories, which is not allowed by FIFA statutes. And then it’s politically very difficult, but legally not so difficult. So then you need sanctions, and then what the sanctions should be. You’ve got to look at precedents. Do you have any similar cases where you play in other people’s territories? What about Crimea? What about former Yugoslavia? Maybe you have some precedent. What’s the sanction? If it’s not changed, you increase the sanctions, because you need a rules-based system. And you need territory lines.
