World.title: Why Macron’s space summit risks blowing up on the launchpad
World.content:
Six participants with first-hand knowledge of the summit's organization described it to POLITICO as a poorly coordinated event with an unclear outcome. They were granted anonymity to discuss sensitive matters.

“It’s falling behind schedule, it hasn’t really been coordinated with the major players in the European space sector, and it’s not entirely clear what its purpose is,” said a senior space expert involved in the summit’s preparation.

“And now that the White House has effectively decided to use it against Emmanuel Macron, it’s becoming even more awkward — it shows that, from a diplomatic standpoint, they didn’t do what they should have done,” they added.

Next week’s event aims to gather the international community — including leaders, large corporations, startups and researchers — to discuss issues including the regulation of space activities, competitiveness, security and defense, and space exploration.

Macron is keen to ensure that France and Europe remain credible space powers, with an independent launch capability and their own global satellite communications system, in an effort to reduce dependence on U.S. technology.

The French president's office insisted Friday that the absence of SpaceX and Blue Origin — two of the world's leading space companies — will have little impact on the summit.

World.title: Witkoff and Kushner set to visit Moscow then Kyiv on Sunday
World.content:
Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff listen as Vice President JD Vance speaks during a news conference. | Pool photo by Jacquelyn Martin/Getty Images

The men have been key U.S. mediators in the stalled Ukraine peace talks.

U.S. President Donald Trump’s special envoys Steven Witkoff and Jared Kushner will visit Moscow and Kyiv in the coming days in an apparent attempt to restart stalled negotiations to end the Ukraine war, Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Telegram.

“We discussed today that Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner will visit Moscow and then Kyiv on Sunday,” the Ukrainian president wrote.

No details about the substance of the meetings have been released, but a U.S. official told CNN Friday that Witkoff and Kushner intend to press for a diplomatic solution to end the conflict.

World.title: Two pilots killed in Phantom  F-4 jet crash during Greek air force annual show
World.content:
A twin seat Phantom F-4 jet crashed at Tanagra air base during an air show held as part of Athens Flying Week 2026, killing the two pilots, according to officials.

 

The crash occurred during a display, in front of thousands of people, the circumstances of the crash remain unclear.

According to information from ERT, the aircraft suddenly began to lose altitude and plunged to the ground. An explosion followed immediately after the impact.

Athens Flying Week, taking place this year on 5 and 6 September, is one of the largest air shows in south-eastern Europe.

The programme features formation flying, high-difficulty manoeuvres and parachute jumps.

In the wake of the crash, Defence Minister N. Dendias is cutting short his schedule at the Thessaloniki International Fair and is returning to Athens. Organisers have also cancelled remaining events planed over the week end.

Wildfire in forested area

The crash of the fighter jet sparked a fire at Tanagra, which spread to the surrounding forested area.

Some 115 firefighters and 36 vehicles are operating at the scene with three ground teams. Meanwhile, nine aircraft and four helicopters are being deployed periodically, one of them coordinating the operation.

Firefighting aircraft and vehicle operate at the crash site of the Hellenic Air Force F-4 Phantom fighter jet ΑΠΕ ΜΠΕ

During Saturday afternoon, an alert was sent via the 112 emergency number to inform people in the wider area of the fire.

Later on Saturday afternoon, the situation of the fire had improved.

At the same time, because of the fire, police closed the service road of the Athens–Lamia national motorway and the Oinoi provincial road at Oinoi.

World.title: Paris drops Mercator projection: France now looks smaller on world maps
World.content:
A shrunken Africa, a Greenland and a northern Russia that seem to stretch into infinity: that is about to disappear from the maps used by French diplomacy.

 

Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot announced on Friday that his department is abandoning the so-called Mercator projection, which artificially enlarges polar regions and visually downplays the size of equatorial areas. France will now use instead the Eckert IV projection, which reflects the true proportions of the continents more accurately.

As a result, France will appear smaller on the map compared with countries close to the equator, just like the United States or Russia.

'A map is never entirely neutral'

In a speech at the Sorbonne university during the public event "La Fabrique de la diplomatie" or "The making of diplomacy", the French minister said that "the time has come" to "correct" how the world is perceived through maps inherited from 16th-century Western navigators.

In a speech delivered at the Sorbonne for the public event "La Fabrique de la diplomatie", the French minister said that "the time has come" to "correct" how the world is perceived through maps inherited from 16th-century Western navigators.

"A map is never entirely neutral. Take the Mercator projection, the one every one of us has known since childhood. The areas we see on it do not correspond to actual areas: (...) The United States, Russia, China take on a disproportionate visual importance compared with Africa, Latin America or South-East Asia," the French foreign minister said.

Jean-Noël Barrot also cited the example of Greenland, which is roughly the same size as the Democratic Republic of Congo or Algeria, even though it "seems almost as vast" as the entire African continent.

"Changing the map obviously does not change the world. But correcting a representation that distorts it is already an act of truth," he stressed.

The ministry began reducing its use of the Mercator projection in 2021

Meanwhile, French diplomatic maps will not change overnight but the process is already underway, Euronews has learned from a diplomatic source. The ministry began reducing its use of the Mercator projection in 2021, "with the aim of providing a more accurate geographical representation of the world."

The projection has been "gradually phased out" across all public diplomacy websites, the source said.

"The advantages and biases associated with each type of representation are presented at various events attended by the ministry's cartographers," the Quai d'Orsay added, citing the European Heritage Days and the International Geography Festival in Saint-Dié-des-Vosges.

"France will continue this work, prioritising map projections suited to different purposes and providing a more accurate reflection of geographical realities in its diplomatic communications."

French diplomats nevertheless acknowledge that the Mercator projection remains relevant "in a limited number of cases", including regional or local uses around the equatorial zone, as well as for navigation charts.

At the UN, a cartographic victory for Africa

The announcement in Paris comes as, in New York, the world map is also being redrawn. A few hours later, the United Nations General Assembly officially abandoned the Mercator projection in favour of a projection based on the Equal Earth model, created in 2018 and closer to the real proportions of the continents.

The non-binding resolution, entitled "Correcting the map"and sponsored by Togo, was backed by 164 member states. The African Union had already adopted Equal Earth in March, and the text now encourages countries to do the same.

Only the United States voted against, denouncing what it called a "radical ideological project", notably because of a passage in the resolution stating that "correcting cartographic distortions relating to the size of continents constitutes an act of cognitive justice and memorial reparation".

Six countries – Estonia, Georgia, Lithuania, Moldova, Serbia and Ukraine – abstained.

The United Nations General Assembly adopts an African proposal for a new world map In favor: 164 Against: 1 Abstentions: 6

The UN stresses that the resolution does not ban the Mercator projection, "nor does it impose a single map". The resolution "encourages governments, educational institutions, international organisations and technology companies to make use of the Equal Earth projection, or of other so-called 'equal-area' maps that preserve the true proportions of surface areas.

France has therefore joined this movement, but has opted to adopt the Eckert IV projection, created in 1906. It is similar to the Equal Earth projection recommended by the UN, though not identical. Both represent the size of the continents much more faithfully than the Mercator projection, but they differ slightly in the shapes they give to the landmasses.

As the UN points out, Mercator mapping will not disappear altogether. Digital platforms such as Google Maps also currently use a version of this projection.

In French schools, most world maps are still in Mercator. "You can find Eckert or Peters* in some textbooks, but that is very rare," says Grégory, a senior history and geography teacher in Rennes, speaking to Euronews.

It remains to be seen whether the maps used in schools will also follow the shift launched by the foreign ministry.

*another equal-area projection, which provides a better representation of the continents' true surface area – Euronews.

World.title: US drafting post-war plan for the Middle East, report says
World.content:
The Trump administration has begun working on a post-war strategy for the Middle East, aimed and reshaping the balance of power in the region by tightening pressure on Tehran and expanding normalisation between Israel and neighbouring countries, Axios reported, citing two US officials and two other sources familiar with the matter.

 

The US outlet said that the plan remains in its early stages but that it could set out US policy towards the Middle East for the remainder of US President Donald Trump's time in the White House.

The unnamed sources told Axios that three key pillars had been discussed as part of the plan - building "regional alignment" among US allies to deter and constrain Iran, working to wind down the regional consequences of the 7 October 2023 attacks on Israel, and broadening the Abraham Accords while pursuing normalisation of relations between Israel and Saudi Arabia.

Discussions over the plan, which are likely to be impacted by the US' upcoming midterm elections as well as Israel's October legislative elections, have also looked at the possibility of the US acting as a guarantor for the so-called regional alignment, working towards a security agreement between Israel and Syria, and implementing the next part of Trump's Gaza plan.

President Donald Trump disembarks Air Force One at Morristown Airport, Friday, Sept. 4, 2026, in Morristown, N.J. Julia Demaree Nikhinson/Copyright 2026 The AP. All rights reserved.

The regional alignment strategy would not represent a major shift in US policy, as successive administrations since the 1979 Iranian Revolution have sought to curb Tehran's regional influence by strengthening relations and alliances with Gulf states.

But Washington may seek to turn these efforts into a more structured framework that includes closer defence and security coordination among allies, against the backdrop of what the US sees as a shift in the regional balance of power amid the Iran war.

A push for a normalisation agreement between Saudi Arabia and Israel is a goal Washington has been pursuing for years but which has stalled as Riyadh has tied any move in such a direction to tangible progress towards resolving the situation in Gaza and the creation of a Palestinian state.

These efforts build on the "Abraham Accords" agreed to in 2020 under Trump's first administration, which normalised relations between Israel on the one hand and the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain, Morocco and Sudan on the other.

Since then, Washington has worked to widen the circle of countries joining these accords, seeing them as one of the tools for reshaping relations and alliances in the Middle East and reducing the influence of Iran and its allies in the region.

The other pillar, which focuses on addressing the regional repercussions of the Hamas militant group's 7 October attack and the ensuing war in the Gaza Strip, could see the issue tackled in three main ways.

Firstly, moving to the next phase of Trump's plan for Gaza, which, according to previous reports, includes arrangements for the reconstruction of the Strip, the disarmament of Hamas and the establishment of a transitional administration.

The second could be an effort to reach a security agreement between Israel and Syria, which would come amid sweeping political changes in Syria since the fall of Bashar al-Assad's regime at the end of 2024 - as well as new authorities' attempts to recast the country's regional and international relations.

And thirdly, implementing an agreement between Israel and Lebanon that would limit Hezbollah's military capabilities. This comes as part of efforts linked to the ceasefire deal reached by Israel and the group in 2024, which provided for the withdrawal of Hezbollah fighters to north of the Litani River and the deployment of the Lebanese army in the south of the country.

Israel has since accused Hezbollah of trying to rebuild its military capabilities, however, while Lebanon has continued to report Israeli air strikes on its territory.

A final plan has yet to take shape

While the planning continues, one of the sources told Axios that it had not yet fully come together.

"They are cooking it, but it is not yet cooked," they said, adding: "The idea is to tie a whole lot of things in the region together — how you create a regional alignment after the war. It is still unclearif all U.S. allies in the region will be on board."

World.title: Spain to maintain border checks on arrivals from Italy until 22 September
World.content:
Spain is extending its border checks on travellers arriving from Italy by air or sea for a further 15 days, pushing the measure's expiry from 7 September to 22 September.

 

The decision follows the same pattern that has defined the stand-off between Madrid and Rome since the summer. Spain introduced these checks for the first time on 8 August, through Order INT/846/2026, as a direct response to Italy's earlier suspension of the free-movement regime for travellers arriving from Spanish territory.

Italy, for its part, had already extended its own checks until 15 September — a further 15-day extension of the deadline previously set by the Meloni government. Italy's interior minister, Matteo Piantedosi, conveyed this to Spain in a telephone call with his Spanish counterpart, Grande-Marlaska.

Ceuta's migration crisis at the root of the dispute

The diplomatic tussle began in late July, when Giorgia Meloni's government announced the suspension of Schengen arrangements with Spain on national security grounds, in the context of a mass arrival of migrants in Ceuta. Italy has argued, and repeated with each renewal, that the migration situation remains unresolved and continues to justify the checks.

Spain responded first by unsuccessfully demanding that the restrictions be lifted, then by mirroring them with an equivalent measure targeting Italian travellers. Since then, both countries have kept renewing their respective checks in parallel, in 15-day increments, without resolving the dispute.

What it means for people travelling between the two countries

The extension does not amount to a border closure and does not affect the right to travel between the two countries. These are identity and nationality checks, carried out on passports at random in ports and airports; for third-country nationals, they also include verification of residence permits.

Flights and sea links continue to operate as normal, though travellers are advised to allow extra time for these checks.

World.title: Beer production in the EU: rankings, trends and curiosities
World.content:
According to the latest data published by Eurostat (31 August 2026), EU member states produced 34.4 billion litres of beer in 2025. Five countries alone control more than 60% of total production.

 

This figure confirms that beer remains one of the most important agri-food industries on the continent, though with an interesting twist: overall production of traditional beer is edging down slightly, while alcohol-free beer continues to grow.

Ranking of the largest beer-producing countries (2025)

The EU's largest beer producers in 2025 Eurostat

Germany remains by far the EU's brewing powerhouse, while Spain holds on to second place and is still one of the few markets that are growing. According to the Socioeconomic Report on the Beer Sector in Spain 2025 (Cerveceros de España and the Ministry of Agriculture), Spanish production reached 41.5 million hectolitres — 0.5% more than in 2024 and 5.1% above 2019 levels.

It's worth noting that the figures in the Spanish sector report don't always match Eurostat's exactly, since Eurostat measures "production sold" (PRODCOM), whereas national trade associations use their own methodologies. Either way, Spain still ranks as the EU's second-largest producer.

Eurostat methodological note: for the Netherlands and Poland, the ranking is based on "own-account production," since the figure for total production sold isn't published, for reasons of statistical confidentiality.

Key figures for 2025

Total EU production: 34.4 billion litres produced in the European Union.

34.4 billion litres produced in the European Union. Change compared with 2024: -0.7% (a slight decline), to 32.7 billion litres.

-0.7% (a slight decline), to 32.7 billion litres. Change compared with 2020: +2.2% (production is now at or above pre-pandemic levels).

+2.2% (production is now at or above pre-pandemic levels). Beer with alcohol (more than 0.5%): 32.3 billion litres.

32.3 billion litres. Alcohol-free or low-alcohol beer (below 0.5%): 2.1 billion litres.

In other words, alcohol-free beer now accounts for just over 6% of everything brewed in the EU — a share that has been rising steadily in recent years.

Trends in recent years

The same story has played out over the last four or five years: traditional beer output is flat or edging down slightly, while the alcohol-free segment is the only one growing steadily, year after year.

On the trade front, the recent trend is less encouraging: European beer exports fell in 2025 to their lowest level since 2014, reflecting weaker international demand.

In 2024, the EU's largest exporter was the Netherlands (1.5 billion litres, though down 12% on 2023), followed by Germany and Belgium (1.4 billion litres each), Czechia (600 million) and Ireland (500 million).

Beer with or without alcohol: who brews and who drinks the most "0.0"?

This is where one of the most striking findings emerges: the country that produces the most alcohol-free beer isn't the same one that drinks the most of it.

The biggest producer: Germany also leads the EU in alcohol-free beer production — a segment that has exploded there over the past decade, with German alcohol-free beer output nearly doubling in ten years.

The biggest consumer: Spain is, by some distance, the country that drinks the most alcohol-free beer in Europe. According to the 2025 Spanish sector report, one in every four alcohol-free beers consumed in the entire EU is drunk in Spain.

In 2025, sales of alcohol-free beer in Spain rose 4.6% year-on-year, to 3.3 million hectolitres (330 million litres) — a record that now represents 14% of all beer consumed in the country. Notably, 90% of those who drink alcohol-free beer are also regular drinkers of regular beer, suggesting they aren't replacing beer with alcohol but complementing it.

World.title: Fitch upgrades Portugal's rating to A+ and says outlook is "stable"
World.content:
Ratings agency Fitch has upgraded Portugal's sovereign debt rating from "A" to "A+", with a "stable outlook", the company said in a notice published on its website (source in Portuguese), keeping pace with the recent wave of confidence shown by other ratings agencies and investors in the country, according to Portugal's Agency for Investment and Foreign Trade (AICEP). According to the Portuguese government, "all financial ratings agencies" assign Portugal an "A" rating.

 

In August, Standard & Poor's (S&P) (source in Portuguese) confirmed its unsolicited sovereign credit ratings for Portugal of "A+/A-1" for long- and short-term foreign and local currency debt, and maintained the positive outlook. Morningstar DBRS also confirmed, in July 2025 (source in Portuguese), the Republic of Portugal's rating at "A" (high), with a "stable outlook".

Fitch Ratings' announcement on Friday is based on the strengthening of Portugal's public finances, in particular the projected reduction in debt and more robust economic growth than in other countries, underpinned by a "strong political commitment to fiscal prudence".

"The upgrade reflects the strengthening of Portugal's public finances, including a projected path of declining public debt and budget balances that are considerably stronger than those of comparable countries, supported by a strong political commitment to fiscal prudence," Fitch says.

According to the agency, Portugal's ratings are supported by governance indicators above the median for countries rated "A", as well as institutional strengths linked to membership of the European Union and the euro area. These factors are, however, offset by still-high levels of accumulated public and external debt.

ARCHIVE (18.01.2012). A broker works at a Portuguese bank AP Photo/Armando Franca

Fitch adds that the "prudence" of policies, repeatedly better-than-expected budget performance and persistent current-account surpluses have strengthened the resilience of the Portuguese economy and its ability to "absorb shocks".

The agency expects public debt to fall from 89.7% of GDP in 2025 to 87.0% in 2026 and 82.9% in 2028, supported by the maintenance of primary surpluses and moderate nominal growth. Even so, the ratio is expected to remain above the forecast median of 59.5% of GDP for countries rated "A".

On Thursday, the Minister of State and Finance, Joaquim Miranda Sarmento, said that the fall in the debt-to-GDP ratio "is the result of the work of families and businesses in recent years (source in Portuguese)", stressing that this process "cannot be interrupted and that it is necessary to maintain the pace of public debt reduction". Joaquim Sarmento added that it is necessary "to sharply reduce bureaucracy, which stifles companies and citizens and limits and delays private investment, especially foreign direct investment", which will have "a strong impact on our country's potential GDP", he said.

On X, the finance minister hailed the "excellent news for Portugal, which regains an A+ rating for the first time since March 2011".

This morning, the President of the Republic also welcomed the agency's rating decision. "This is excellent news for the country and an important external recognition of Portugal's performance, the result of a medium- and long-term evolution, sustained by the efforts of the Portuguese people and by a responsible orientation maintained under different governments," António José Seguro writes on the Presidency website (source in Portuguese). "A better rating will improve financing conditions for the state, businesses and families, support investment and job creation and allow more public resources to be directed towards people's needs," the president hopes.

"When the year 2026 comes to be read in retrospect, this will surely be one of its most relevant economic news stories," Seguro adds.

Increase in defence spending puts public finances under pressure

A crane rises above the buildings, with São Jorge Castle and the river Tagus in the background, in Lisbon AP Photo/Armando Franca

Fitch estimates that the budget surplus will fall from 0.7% of GDP in 2025 to 0.1% in 2026, affected by emergency support and reconstruction spending related to storms, by the tax-cut and housing measures set out in the 2026 State Budget, by peak investment linked to the loan component of the Recovery and Resilience Plan (RRP) and by higher spending on wages and pensions.

These effects are expected to be partially offset by higher social contributions, linked to continued employment growth, and by a significant dividend distribution from Caixa Geral de Depósitos, according to the agency.

For 2027 and 2028, Fitch forecasts an average deficit of around 0.4% of GDP. The agency anticipates that demographic ageing and lower migration "will increase spending and put pressure on social contributions", although it notes that the Social Security Financial Stabilisation Fund, with assets equivalent to 13.9% of GDP at the end of 2025, "provides a substantial safety margin".

The cost of housing is also a concern, although the rapid rise in house prices has not yet translated into "significant short-term macro-financial risks"; it may "increase vulnerabilities in the property market and is aggravating pressures on affordability", the agency stresses.

In the first quarter of 2026, residential property prices were about 99% above the level recorded in the fourth quarter of 2019, compared with 31% in the euro area.

Low housing supply and strong demand, linked to high immigration, suggest that pressures in the property market are mainly "structural, limiting the likelihood of a sharp correction in the short term", says Fitch, which suggests that "a solid banking sector should help contain the financial risks related to the property market" and the resulting build-up of household debt.

Another factor to bear in mind is NATO's target of reaching 5% of GDP in defence spending by 2035, which Fitch expects will "add pressure to public finances in the medium term". Even so, the international ratings agency considers that the track record of budgetary policy, relatively stable over successive changes of government, mitigates the risks associated with greater political uncertainty.

World.title: Two people pulled alive by Nepal's search and rescue team 10 days after devastating flash floods
World.content:
Rescuers in Nepal continue to pull people out on Saturday, 10 days after the devastating floods hit along the Nepal-Tibet border, meanwhile thousands of people are still missing.

 

In separate situations, one Chinese man and a woman were found alive by rescue teams.

The woman was found alive in her house buried under thick mud and debris in flood-hit Nuwakot, footage released by Nepal's army shows the woman covered in mud, officials say she has been airlifted to Kathmandu.

In parallel, Nepal's prime minister's office posted on social media that the man was rescued from a hydropower tunnel. He is the third person to be pulled from the Trishuli hydropower project, as two Nepalese workers were rescued on Friday.

Chinese national is seen drinking water after being rescued by soldiers during an ongoing operation at the Trishuli-3A hydropower project in Nepal's Rasuwa district, 05.09.26 Nepal Army via AP/Nepal Army via AP

The man was pulled from a 225-meter tunnel and evacuated in a helicopter by Nepalese military personnel who were working alongside South Korean disaster experts according to Nepal's army.

About 900 workers are still missing and 500 are believed to be trapped in various tunnels across 12 hydropower projects where rescue efforts have focused, according to authorities.

The devasting flash floods which hit the districts of Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading, Gorkha and Tanahun left at least 1,300 people killed, while more than 5,000 remain missing. The disaster was likely caused by a glacier collapse, according to Nepal's disaster management agency.

Specialised teams from China, India, South Korea and the United States have joined search efforts in hope of finding survivors.

World.title: Bosnian Serb war criminal Mladić commemorated in Belgrade, but no state honours
World.content:
A commemoration for former Bosnian Serb army commander and convicted war criminal Ratko Mladić opened on Saturday at the House of the Serbian Army in Belgrade as Serbia faces mounting European pressure over what Brussels has described as his glorification — an accusation Serbia rejects.

 

Mladić died last week while serving a life sentence for genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity during the war in Bosnia. His remains were flown to Serbia from The Hague on a government plane on Thursday.

Serbian army soldiers carried the coffin with Mladić’s body wrapped in the national flag from the plane to an unmarked maroon van, which was then given a police escort down Belgrade’s main motorway.

Serbia's Justice Minister Nenad Vujić — who initially announced that Serbia would give Mladić "all the military and state honours" — was on the plane along with Mladić’s son Darko and two of his former army assistants.

The body was transferred to the military hospital in Belgrade for an autopsy before his coffin is displayed at a church near the Košutnjak cemetery on Monday morning, where he will be buried later in the day, his family announced on Friday.

He will be buried without state or military honours, with no serving officials in attendance including President Aleksandar Vučić, the prime minister and the speaker of parliament, Euronews has learned.

There will be no artillery salutes or ceremonial military presence, and he will not be buried in the Alley of the Greats or the Alley of Distinguished Citizens despite requests to that effect.

Serbian authorities clarified earlier that Saturday's commemoration was not organised by the state, but rather by an association of retired generals. Mladić's family said he would be buried next to his daughter, who died by suicide in the 1990s, according to domestic media outlets.

Belgrade has contributed to covering Mladić's personal expenses and family visits while at the Hague tribunal, and has repeatedly asked for an early release on humanitarian grounds due to his declining health in recent years.

Thousands to gather at funeral

After Bosnia declared independence from Yugoslavia in early 1992 following in the footsteps of Slovenia and Croatia, Bosnian Serb leaders, backed by the government in Belgrade led by Slobodan Milošević, created their own parastate.

The ensuing military offensive led by Mladić — a career Yugoslav army officer who also took part in the fighting in neighbouring Croatia — aimed at ethnically cleansing as much of the country’s territory as possible of the other two ethnic groups, Bosniaks and Croats.

The International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia (ICTY) convicted Mladić of genocide for orchestrating summary executions of more than 8,000 Bosniak men and boys in Srebrenica in July 1995 — considered the worst bloodbath on European soil since the end of World War II.

He was also found guilty of war crimes and crimes against humanity during the siege of Sarajevo, the longest siege of a capital city in modern warfare.

His troops in the surrounding hills terrorised the residents of the Bosnian capital with daily shelling and sniping for nearly four years after the war broke out in early 1992.

Known as the “Butcher of Bosnia,” he became the most notorious figure of the war in the former Yugoslav republic of 3,5 million that left more than 100,000 people dead and over 2 million displaced or seeking refuge abroad before it ended in late 1995 in a US-brokered peace agreement.

FILE: A woman walks next to a barricade made of mortar and damaged vehicles as she makes her way through the frontline neighbourhood of Dobrinja in Sarajevo, 13 November 1994 AP Photo/Jacqueline Arzt

Serbian President Aleksandar Vučić predicted that Mladić’s admirers — who consider him a hero despite his sentence — could come to the funeral in large numbers.

“It will be hard to secure and guarantee security to everybody,” Vučić said. He added that Serbia’s police and the state security agency predicted that “tens of thousands” could attend. “It will be a demanding job for our services and we will use everything at our disposal to provide security.”

“I have spoken to the Mladić family and I wish it all passes in a dignified way,” Vučić added.

The Serbian president later said he would not attend Mladić’s funeral because of a previously scheduled high-level visit.

“I have an official visit on Monday and all day Tuesday by the President of Uzbekistan (Shavkat Mirziyoyev), scheduled four months ago,” Vučić, who is touring the country to showcase infrastructure development, stated on Friday.

“Have I done everything necessary and everything possible for this to proceed in a dignified manner, in a serious and responsible manner, for the state to conduct itself properly? That is exactly what I have done,” he added.

Sparks fly over glorification accusations

Following Mladić’s death last Thursday, thousands of Serbs held vigils and marches in his honour, drawing condemnation from Brussels and elsewhere.

EU Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos on Friday cancelled an upcoming visit to Serbia, a long-standing candidate for membership in the 27-member bloc.

"The glorification surrounding his death is incompatible with the values on which the EU path is built," Kos said on X.

"Ratko Mladić was convicted of genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes," Kos said. “The return of his remains to Belgrade reminds Europe of the darkest pages in our recent history.”

A buyer checks a T-shirt with a picture of former Bosnian Serb wartime general Ratko Mladic displayed on Belgrade's main pedestrian street, 4 September 2026 AP Photo

Vučić responded by stating that Kos’ explanation was "very short but stupid, as usual".

"I suppose we should ban people from showing up, ban the funeral, make cemeteries for dogs," he added.

Earlier on Friday, Kos said the next days ahead of the burial "will be a very important test" for Belgrade.

The Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights Michael O’Flaherty on Friday urged authorities in Serbia and in the Bosnian Serb-run entity of Bosnia to "counter the glorification of convicted war criminals," which is illegal in Bosnia and "is not protected speech under the European Convention on Human Rights."

"I abhor the public glorification of Ratko Mladić, a deceased war criminal convicted for the Srebrenica genocide and crimes against humanity," O'Flaherty said in a statement.

Calls have also multiplied for the European People’s Party (EPP) to cut its ties to the ruling Serbian Progressive Party (SPS).

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen is an EPP member, along with European Parliament President Roberta Metsola and other top officials.

The legacy court in The Hague, now formally known as the International Residual Mechanism for Criminal Tribunals, said it stood “in solidarity with the victims, survivors and their families who suffered the crimes for which Mr Mladić was found guilty.”

It condemned “any actions that glorify those convicted of war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide by international courts.”

Belgian and Irish foreign ministers have both publicly objected to any honours granted to a person convicted of genocide.

Meanwhile, Serbian football club Red Star Belgrade was fined by UEFA for fans chanting in honour of Mladić, who died on the day of their Europa League game last week, which Red Star lost 5-1 against Czech club Viktoria Plzeň.

UEFA said late Friday its judges fined Red Star €90,000 for charges including chants not fit for a sports event plus "racist and/or discriminatory behaviour".

The European footballing body doled out a similar penalty to Bosnia's FK Borac Banjaluka, fining it €39,500 for chants in favour of Mladić and other fan infractions during their Conference League match against Iceland's Vikingur Reykavik.

Red Star is the most decorated football club in the former Yugoslavia, winning the Champions League in 1991.

World.title: US envoys meet with Putin, leave Russia for Kyiv
World.content:
Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff met with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow to try to revive talks to end the war in Ukraine. The US envoys are also scheduled to visit Kyiv on Sunday.

US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff met with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow on Saturday evening.

"The situation is of course not simple," Putin told the US officials in footage aired on Russian state media.

Putin and US envoys held "useful" talks on a range of ideas to end the war in Ukraine, Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov told reporters.

According to Russian media outlets, US envoys left Moscow after the meeting.

Earlier, US President Donald Trump said Kushner and Witkoff were traveling to Russia with a new proposal, but he did not provide any details on the potential peace plan, including whether it involved Ukraine giving territory to Russia as he has previously suggested. Instead, he said, "We have an idea for peace."

In the meeting with Putin, Kushner and Witkoff discussed "substantive plans" for the next steps toward ending the Ukraine war, the White House said, adding that more details would be announced next week.

The envoys "look forward to equally productive meetings tomorrow in Ukraine," a White House official said in a statement.

Russia, Ukraine pause strikes for three days

The Kremlin said Russian forces would pause strikes against Kyiv for three days in conjunction with the peace negotiations.

Putin "ordered that no strikes be carried out against Kyiv for three days, starting at midnight today," Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov told state media.

The order came after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy had already committed to pausing airstrikes for the talks.

"As with previous diplomatic visits by the American side, we will ensure the normal functioning of Russian airspace so that the negotiators can arrive safely. We are concerned about their safety, not about Russia," Zelenskyy said.

US envoys to make first visit to Kyiv

Zelenskyy announced on Friday that Kushner and Witkoff would visit Ukraine on Sunday following talks in Moscow.

Recent media reports have questioned whether the pair would indeed travel to Ukraine. Despite trips to Moscow to meet with Russian officials, the US envoys have not visited Kyiv since Trump's reelection last year.

On Saturday, Zelenskyy said he had been in contact with Kushner and Witkoff.

"I ⁠have ​just spoken ​with the US president’s ​envoys," Zelenskyy said ‌on Telegram.

"From the moment of this conversation, ​we ⁠are ready to observe a ⁠ceasefire ​in airstrikes against the cities involved in the negotiation process."

Trump had promised to end the war in Ukraine, now in its fifth year, on his first day back in office, but has more recently said that the feat was more complicated than expected. In the past, he has blamed Ukraine for the Russian invasion and a "personality problem" between the countries' leaders for the continued fighting.

World.title: German company successfully launches rocket to space
World.content:
Bavaria-based Isar Aerospace managed to launch its Spectrum rocket into orbit, 18 months after its first attempt. This is the first such launch from European soil.

A Spectrum space rocket built by German company Isar Aerospace was launched into space from the Norwegian spaceport at Andoya.

"We're in orbit! And just made European history: This is the first time a privately developed rocket reached orbit from continental Europe," the company wrote on X.

"Germany has spaceflight capabilities," said the country's Ministry for Research, Technology and Space on X, praising a "milestone that impressively demonstrates our country's innovative strength and technical expertise".

This was the German company's second attempt to launch the Spectrum rocket into space. The first attempt, which took place 18 months ago, was unsuccessful.

What is Spectrum rocket?

The Spectrum rocket is designed for small and medium-sized payloads. It carried five smal satellites and an in-flight technological experiment, the company said.

According to Isar Aerospace, the launch was for "both the vehicle's qualification mission and its first flight carrying payload."

The move is believed to bring Europe closer to being able to offer satellite flights from its own territory. Several countries voiced interest in the growing market of commercial space missions, including Britain and Sweden.

The launch of Spectrum follows months of delays Image: Isar Aerospace/dpa/picture alliance

In March, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz visited the launch site of Isar, a Bavaria-based company, showing support for its efforts and for European autonomy at a time when the world order is changing under US President Donald Trump.

Isar is also working on the development of a second launch site, located in Canada.

The company said that while the US launched 198 rockets last year, Europe's tally was just eight. Isar's goal is to produce some 40 rockets a year.

Competition includes SpaceX

Although the rocket is not yet ready for mass production, Isar has already received orders through 2028.

The Spectrum rocket is intended to send both civilian and military satellites into low Earth orbit, meaning a few hundred kilometers above the Earth's surface.

The industry includes Elon Musk's SpaceX and ArianeGroup, a French joint venture between Airbus and Safran that operates a spaceport in French Guiana, located in South America.

For the sake of developing new rockets and extend its testing and launch infrastructure, Isar said last week it received €200 million ($232 million) from the European Space Agency (ESA).

World.title: Why many Syrians feel Assad death sentence isn't enough
World.content:
In July, a Syrian court sentenced former dictator Bashar Assad to death for crimes against his own people. But after 14 years of civil war, many survivors are demanding more when it comes to transitional justice.

Huda Khayti often finds herself returning to the place where she lost almost everything. Khayti, a Syrian women's rights activist, survived a 2013 chemical weapons attack on the east Ghouta region by forces of the former Syrian dictator Bashar Assad.

Her brother was killed by the bombs of the Assad regime and its allies. Her women's center was destroyed along with her home and in 2018, she had to leave her hometown of Douma — a major city in Ghouta — and flee to Idlib, a rebel stronghold in northern Syria.

Today, Khayti regularly visits her hometown, which is about 10 kilometers (about 6 miles) northeast of the country's capital, Damascus. Since the Assad regime was overthrown in late 2024, Khayti has traveled regularly between Idlib and Douma, where she's even working on opening a new women's center.

"Ghouta means so much to me emotionally," she told DW. But every time she returns there, she is also confronted with remnants of the civil war. "When I'm traveling through the country I see traces of war everywhere, so many houses and so much infrastructure destroyed. So much suffering. So much trauma."

In Douma, Huda Khayti visits the grave of her murdered brother Image: privat

Almost two years since the overthrow of the Assad regime, Syria has started a process to examine the crimes of the regime in court. In mid-August a Damascus court sentenced Bashar Assad and other high-ranking members of his regime to death in absentia. Assad is currently living in Russia, where he fled after his government was overthrown. Many senior officials are also there or hiding elsewhere.

Among other things, Assad was found guilty of premeditated murder, torture and depriving individuals of their liberty. The court said these were war crimes and crimes against humanity.

"Of course, this conviction of Assad is a good thing," Khayti said. "Even if it's only on paper. Bashar Assad may have been convicted but he just continues to live his life in Russia — like so many other Syrian criminals who fled to Russia."

Justice served in Syria?

The court's conviction had a big impact in Syria anyway. "The verdict had a lot of echoes by people, they were so happy," said Lina Chawaf, a Syrian journalist, media expert and researcher at Harvard University's Center for Middle Eastern Studies. "Many media celebrated the verdict on the statement day as a victory and consider it as part of transitional justice."

Still, it remains unclear whether there will be any actual punishment following the conviction. Although Russia and Syria agreed on an extradition treaty in 2023, observers say it's unlikely Russia would send Assad, a long-time ally, back to Syria. Additionally, according to the treaty, if the death penalty is likely, that could prevent extradition too.

In August, Syria's Deputy Justice Minister Mustafa al-Qassem said the country had established a commission to cooperate with Interpol and that cooperation with other countries in extraditing fugitive suspects would speed up legal proceedings.

Syria still scarred after 14-year civil war To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Rana Sheikh-Ali, founder of Daret Salam (Peace Circuit in English), which uses technology to build peace and empower women, believes the Assad trial in August should be seen as largely symbolic. From a human rights perspective, she opposes the death penalty, but at the same time she says many locals saw the death sentences as just.

But the prosecution of high-ranking regime members is only one aspect of the transitional justice process.

Transitional justice isn't just about criminal trials. Other aspects include searching for missing people, investigating crimes, deciding on reparations and formulating institutional reforms. With all that, the focus should be on victims and survivors.

Numbers supplied by the Syrian Network for Human Rights indicate just how big the task is. In an article, the advocacy network reports that over 234,805 civilians were killed during the civil war, at least 202,000 of them by the Assad regime and its allies.

In addition, there are also at least 181,312 cases of arbitrary arrest and enforced disappearance to investigate as well as 45,339 deaths resulting from torture. It's thought that the actual numbers are likely far higher. The network has also documented 217 chemical weapons attacks by the Assad regime.

Victim-centered process needed

Women's rights activist Khayti was just a few kilometers from the epicenter of one of those attacks in eastern Ghouta in 2013. "I remember it like it was yesterday," she recounted. "I can't forget the screams of the victims. I kept thinking we were next. I felt that scratchiness in my throat, that burning in my eyes."

For a system of transitional justice that is truly victim-centered, it's not enough to just have survivors act as witnesses in court. "Victims must also participate in every detail related to the transitional justice process," she explained.

Additionally, those who were impacted by the crimes must be able to participate voluntarily and be protected as they do, Sheikh-Ali added. They should be able to talk about their experiences and should also be heard on topics like compensation, financial support and public recognition.

For survivors like Khayti, this means not just making Assad and a few top regime officials the primary targets of justice.

"I also want to see convictions for individuals who wrote reports that led to people ending up in the Saydnaya torture prison," Khayti said. "These individuals are just as guilty as the torturers themselves."

Huda Khayti also runs a women's center in Idlib and works with people in refugee camps on the Turkish border Image: privat

At the moment, though, it's unclear exactly how thoroughly Syria will confront its past.

"Convictions in absentia against Assad and other officials send an important signal after decades of impunity," said Sophie Bischoff, managing director of Adopt a Revolution, a German-Syrian human rights organization that supports civil society initiatives. "But for survivors like Huda Khayti, these sentences remain symbolic as long as those convicted are not actually held accountable — and it's also still not transparent exactly who is to be held accountable and on what legal basis, and who would be granted immunity."

Bischoff also noted that the new Syrian state has yet to fully and comprehensively investigate crimes against humanity and war crimes committed in Syria.

"So far it's primarily been Syrian civil society organizations and human rights activists who have been researching and documenting these cases for years," she told DW. "Systematic state documentation of violent crimes committed during the Assad regime era is only just beginning."

The new Syrian government has created two commissions to work on issues of transitional justice. In late August, one of these — the National Commission for Missing Persons — launched a platform called Athar, where families of the missing can submit information.

The other organization, the National Commission for Transitional Justice, was established in May 2025 but has so far dealt only with crimes committed by the Assad regime. It has not dealt with crimes committed by militias fighting the war or the extremist group known as the "Islamic State".

Return to Syria: Rebuilding and seeking justice in Yarmouk To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Investigating all war crimes

"This falls far short," said Bischoff. "For a comprehensive reckoning and a new beginning in a Syria for all, the war crimes of all warring parties must be included."

For Khayti, the requirement to place victims at the center of the process of transitional justice also has another difficult aspect. Her testimony is being heard, but at the same time she is forced to return to the original trauma.

"It's difficult for me to talk about it and I often feel like I'm reliving it," Khayti explained.

Sheikh-Ali said centering the victims means those impacted play a meaningful role in the process. But as they do so, she added, they should also be protected.

It's also important to remember these events, Khayti added. In Douma, she is working on ways to preserve recollections of the war. "We need to inform younger people about it so that the memory doesn't fade," she said.

In Syria, she said now it's about finding the missing, holding all perpetrators to account, fully investigating all crimes and giving survivors a voice.

"We will continue to be loud," Khayti said. "And we will continue to demand justice."

This article was originally written in German.

World.title: Croatia: Toxic waste protest draws tens of thousands
World.content:
The Zagreb demonstrators demanded that the government come up with a plan to clear illegal toxic waste in 20 days. Prime Minister Plenkovic has promised to tackle the issue.

A protest in Zagreb against Croatia's government drew tens of thousands of people who blamed the government for its lack of action over the illegal storage of toxic waste.

A landfill near the town of Gospic, located some 200 kilometers (124.2 miles) to Zagreb's southwest, is being used to hold toxic waste from several countries, including Germanyand Italy, according to reports.

The demonstration saw signs such as "ecocide equals slow genocide" and "halt waste import," with many of the people in attendance also holding Croatian flags.

The protesters called for all illegal landfills to be cleared due to them polluting groundwater, as well as a new waste management plan across the country within the next 20 days. They also demanded that the government put a temporary ban on waste imports in place.

Protesters waved Croatian flags and demanded better waste management Image: AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

Investigation underway

An investigation in relation to illegal waste dumps has been ongoing since the arrests of 13 people in February 2025, with Europol cooperating with Croatian authorities in the investigation. Four companies are also under investigation.

According to Europol, most of the 35,000 tons of waste had come from Italy, but also from Slovenia and Germany, and consisted of plastic refuse and toxic hospital waste, bringing about a profit of some €4 million ($4.6 million) for the suspects, who had also likely forged documents falsely declaring plastic waste as suitable for recycling.

Local environmental activists dispute the number of waste tons and say 37,000 tons had been illegally dumped in Gospic alone.

Prosecutors also published a report in August that confirmed the Gospic soil contamination, also saying it had spread beyond the site itself.

This presents a "significant risk for the environmentand people's health," the report said, despite the drinking water in Gospic remaining so far unaffected, health authorities said.

Conservative Prime Minister Andrej Plenkovic promised the toxic waste site in Gospic would be covered by mid-October before the waste gets removed from it.

World.title: Masked anti-migrant protesters block UK's Dover terminal
World.content:
Chanting "stop the boats" and wearing balaclavas, the demonstrators blocked traffic at the UK's busiest international ferry port.

Hundreds of masked people blocked traffic at England's port of Dover on Saturday as part of an anti-migrant protest, halting ferry traffic between France and the UK.

Video footage showed demonstrators in balaclavas chanting "stop the boats," in a reference to refugees and migrants who attempt the dangerous English channel crossing in a bid to reach Great Britain.

This came despite the fact that crossing dropped 40% between January and August 2026 compared to the previous year. However, the perceived threat of migrant boats has become a rallying cry for the far-right Reform UK party.

Police said that they were "engaging" with protesters and that normal traffic had resumed at the port after several hours.

Government condemns 'travel disruption'

"The right to peaceful protest is fundamental to our democracy, but we condemn the behavior in Dover and the travel disruption it has caused," said a spokesman for the government of Prime Minister Andy Burnham.

Under Burnham and his predecessor Keir Starmer, migrant crossings have been greatly reduced in part due to closer cooperation with French authorities.

Dover is the UK's biggest international ferry port, handling some 15,000 passengers a day during the summer and welcoming more than a third of the UK's trade goods with the European Union.

Edited by: Srinivas Mazumdaru

World.title: Fact check: Germany's postal voting system isn't rigged
World.content:
As Germany heads into three elections in September, rumors are circulating on social media claiming that postal voting is not secure — claims that have also been made about other elections. Here's why they're wrong.

Stakes are high in Germany's three September state elections. In Saxony-Anhalt, where voters go to the ballot boxes on Sunday, the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) could make history in by winning an outright majority.

The AfD's Saxony-Anhalt branch, which has been classified by the domestic intelligence agency as a "confirmed right-wing extremist organization" , could become Germany's first far-right state government since World War II.

Mail-in voting, or "Briefwahl," has become an increasingly common feature of German elections . But the rise in mail-in ballots has been followed by a renewed wave of speculation and claims questioning the security and integrity of postal vote.

DW Fact check examined a sample of claims circulating online and assessed what the available evidence shows.

Does postal voting manipulate election results?

Claim: Cases of fraud involving postal ballots prove that postal voting is unreliable.

This claim recurrently appeared in posts about postal voting that DW Fact check reviewed on social media platforms including TikTok , X and Facebook .

Some posts point to individual cases of electoral fraud involving postal ballots and present them as evidence that the system as a whole is flawed. One verified account on X using the AfD logo, for example, cited two cases — a mail-in vote being cast on behalf of an elderly woman with dementia, and hundreds of voters in Magdeburg receiving multiple ballots — before calling postal voting defective and demanding immediate reforms.

Social media is rife with posts like this one on X, which cited individual problems with mail-in ballots as evidence that postal voting is fundamentally unreliable Image: X/AfD

DW Fact check: Misleading. Individual cases of fraud, errors or violations do not demonstrate that the entire postal voting system is unreliable or that it has affected the outcome of an election.

The post by the X account with the AfD logo refers to two real incidents, but does so in a misleading way. The claim about an elderly woman may refer to a case in Dessau , where police recently investigated an alleged vote cast on behalf of a 95-year-old woman with "severe dementia" but found no evidence of manipulation. The other incident occurred in Magdeburg, where 440 voters did receive duplicate ballots for the September 6 election ; however, the duplicates were invalidated and could not be used to cast additional valid votes.

Cases of electoral misconduct involving postal ballots have occurred in postal voting, as they have with voting at polling stations. In one case in Dresden, a man manipulated absentee ballots during the 2024 local and state elections, primarily in favor of the far-right Free Saxons party as well as the AfD. And in Bavaria , a former mayor was accused of manipulating postal voting documents in a March 2026 local election.

There have also been documented mistakes, administrative problems and delays in the handling of postal ballots in previous German elections. A 2021 study examining postal voting in German federal elections between 1998 and 2017 found that these weaknesses were primarily related to organization and logistics. Researcher Daniel Hellmann of the Martin Luther University Halle-Wittenberg said, however, that the research was still ongoing.

But such problems are not evidence of widespread fraud or of postal ballots being manipulated on a scale capable of changing an election result.

The 2021 study concluded that postal voting in Germany was secure overall. It found that none of the incidents examined could have changed an election result by even a single seat.

"If problems have occurred, they have generally been reviewed through legal channels and proportionate consequences have been imposed," Lukas Stötzer, an election researcher at the University of Witten/Herdecke in western Germany, told DW. "The postal voting system works and is secure, and that's why it is becoming more popular."

In Saxony-Anhalt, the AfD's lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund has called for postal voting to be restricted to justified exceptional cases. But officials have defended postal voting as a secure and established procedure Image: Annegret Hilse/REUTERS

Postal voting easy to manipulate?

Claim: Postal votes are easily manipulated during counting.

"It can be assumed that postal voting in Saxony-Anhalt will massively distort the election result, This is also relatively easy to do, and the checks on postal voting are laughable," wrote one user on X with about 130,000 followers on August 14.

Some posts have argued that postal votes are easier to manipulate during the counting process Image: X

This claim was also a recurring theme among the posts reviewed by DW Fact check, with some of the content presented in satirical, AI-generated cartoons. The AI-generated video depicted here on TikTok and labelled satire , for example, shows a man involved in counting ballots simply altering the votes from AfD to the center-right CDU party, and then calling a man named "Friedrich" — presumably Chancellor Friedrich Merz — to say that he had "everything under control."

DW Fact check: False. Germany has detailed procedures governing the handling and counting of postal ballots. Postal votes are transported, stored and opened according to established rules, and their counting takes place publicly.

Members of the public are generally allowed to observe the election process, including the counting of votes, without having to demonstrate a particular interest or affiliation. This applies to postal ballot counting as well.

That means election officials do not simply open postal ballots and count them behind closed doors. The process is conducted by election boards, whose work can be observed by members of the public and each parties' representatives.

In Germany, eligible voters can be called upon by local authorities to serve as election workers and are generally required by law to accept the role Image: ABBfoto/picture alliance

In an interview with German public broadcaster ARD Christa Dieckmann, Saxony-Anhalt's state election commissioner, pointed to public observation as an important safeguard. "The best way to ensure the fairness of the election is to come to the polling station as an observer for elections as the basis for choosing a legitimate government," she said.

DW Fact check also encountered numerous claims promoting what has been dubbed the "nursing home theory," which alleges that elderly people who are unable to vote in person may not be casting their ballots freely, but could instead be pressured or influenced by certain political parties or caregivers.

DW Fact check has investigated similar claims in the past, many of which have been promoted by AfD politicians. It has found no substantial evidence to support the broader allegation that postal voting in nursing homes is systematically manipulated or that elderly voters are routinely pressured into voting for particular parties.

A familiar claim beyond Germany

The doubts surrounding postal voting are not unique to Germany. Similar claims have surfaced during elections in other democracies, often becoming entangled with broader political battles over the legitimacy of elections.

During the 2020 US presidential election, President Donald Trump repeatedly claimed that expanded mail-in voting would lead to widespread fraud. Fact-checkers documented and debunked repeated false and exaggerated claims about the security of mail ballots. Ahead of the 2026 midterm elections, the Trump administration is again seeking to impose new restrictions on mail-in ballots, measures that have faced repeated legal challenges.

Fact-check: The truth on burned votes To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Election researcher Stötzer said such claims can become part of a broader political strategy to undermine trust in democratic institutions.

"Right-wing populist parties strategically fuel these doubts," Stötzer said, adding that such claims can later be used to justify electoral law changes that benefit those parties.

He said the immediate impact of such allegations may be limited. But if they are repeated election after election, the longer-term consequences could be more serious.

"Public trust in electoral institutions could suffer," Stötzer said. Election results that are considered undesirable could then routinely be attributed to alleged irregularities in postal voting.

This is a collaborative project between ARD-faktenfinder, and DW Fact check.

World.title: Iran: US hits 3 IRGC-linked oil tankers
World.content:
Published 09/05/2026 Published September 5, 2026 Israel, Hezbollah flare-up in southern Lebanon

Despite a ceasefire that went into effect over two months ago, flare-ups are continuing between Israel and Hezbollah over one strategic hill in southern Lebanon.

Fighting between Israel and Hezbollah, a Shiite political party and paramilitary group supported by Iran, intensified once again earlier this year in the wider context of the US-Iran war. The US, Germany and several Arab countries consider Hezbollah a terrorist organization, whereas the EU only deems Hezbollah's armed wing a terror group.

Israel, Hezbollah agree to truce, US-Iran deal in jeopardy To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

While the fiercest battles are over, the two sides are still in conflict over the Ali Taher hill, which overlooks the city of Nabatiyeh. According to the Lebanese Health Ministry, at least five people have died and 24 have been injured in the fighting since Friday.

The United States, which has mediated peace talks, has wanted Hezbollah to hand the hill over the Lebanese government, but the militant group has refused to withdraw from certain positions north of the Litani river where Ali Taher sits.

There are fears that the fighting could escalate into an all-out battle for Nabatiyeh and lead to more violence across Lebanon, complicating efforts to resolve the war in Iran.

World.title: Germany: From emigration to immigration destination
World.content:
Migration is a sensitive topic in Germany, with public debate dominated by the fear of uncontrolled immigration. But over two centuries, millions of Germans emigrated in search of a better life.

"Why should [they] be suffered to swarm into our Settlements, and by herding together establish their Language and Manners to the Exclusion of ours? [...] [They] will shortly be so numerous [...] and will never adopt our Language or Customs."

These defamatory comments about refugees and asylum-seekers sound as if they might have been made today by the right-wing populist Alternative for Germany party (AfD). Yet in this instance, the people vilified and accused of refusing to integrate are Germans — and the harsh judgement was made in the 18th century by none other than Benjamin Franklin, one of the Founding Fathers of the United States.

The pursuit of happiness and a better life are mentioned in the American Declaration of Independence, which Franklin helped write. Over the centuries, they have been the motivation for countless people to turn their backs on their respective homelands.

Benjamin Franklin, one of the Founding Fathers of the United States, warned against accepting German immigrants Image: Public Domain

The Germans who emigrated to America in Franklin's lifetime were actually fairly limited in number. By 1820, only about 150,000 had successfully made the journey. Often, they were persuaded by compatriots who told tales of their tremendous success in their new homeland and celebrated the prosperity they had supposedly attained in a very short space of time. What most people back home didn't know was that these recruiters received a commission for every migrant.

"The crossing on a sailing ship cost about what a tradesman would earn in a year," said Simone Blaschka of the German Emigration Center in Bremerhaven . "To be able to afford that, families had to sell all their worldly goods."

A journey into the unknown

They would have had no idea what awaited them on board the ship. During the crossing, which took several weeks, they were packed together below deck in a very confined space, plagued by bedbugs, fleas and rats. Many fell sick with dysentery, typhoid, smallpox or scurvy.

In his book "Journey to Pennsylvania in the Year 1750," the schoolmaster and organist Gottlieb Mittelberger described what he had experienced on the voyage: "Many people whimper, sigh and cry piteously for their homes; most of them get home-sick. Many hundred people necessarily die and perish in such misery, and must be cast into the sea."

Many European immigrants who came to the US in the 20th century arrived by boat in New York Image: Raimund Franken/imageBROKER/picture alliance

On arrival in America, Mittelberger wrote, the majority of his fellow passengers were effectively auctioned off. These were people without means who were granted free passage after undertaking to work for years as bonded laborers in exchange. In the US, their contracts were sold off. Mittelberger saw families torn apart and parents forced to sell their children.

An invitation from Russia

As these early migrants were traveling to America, there was simultaneously a big wave of emigration from Germany to the east. People followed the call of the Russian czarina, Catherine the Great, herself a German princess by birth.

On July 22, 1763, she issued a manifesto inviting people to come to Russia, with the aim of cultivating uninhabited regions for arable farming. She promised the new arrivals free transport to their chosen place of residence, land, also free of charge, the first year tax-free, schooling, exemption from military service, and a special political status that would allow them to maintain the German language and, for the most part, govern themselves.

Catherine the Great officially invited Germans to immigrate to Russia in the late 18th century Image: akg-images/picture-alliance

However, in the 19th century the American continent once again became the dream destination. "The German population almost doubled in the 19th century, so you can imagine what the job market was like," said Blaschka from the German Emigration Center. The situation was exacerbated by failed harvests and famines.

"People didn't see any future for themselves or their children, and decided to emigrate," she said. In this way, around 6 million Germans were drawn to the New World.

Migration: A burden or an asset?

Germans were far from the only ones who left their homeland.

"Between the beginning of the 19th century and the World War I, there were probably around 60 million Europeans who left their homes," said Jochen Oltmer, a professor at the Institute for Migration Research and Intercultural Studies in Osnabrück. Then, in the mid-20th century, this trend reversed and Europe went from being a continent of emigration to one of immigration.

Migration researcher Jochen Oltmer has studied the immigration waves to and from Europe in the 19th and 20th centuries Image: Michael Gründel/NOZ

In the 1950s and '60s, the future looked rosy for postwar West Germany and its "economic miracle." From 1956 onward, so-called "guest worker trains" arrived in stations like Stuttgart, Dortmund and Cologne, carrying Italians, Greeks, Spaniards, Portuguese, Yugoslavs and Turks, attracted by the promise of well-paid jobs in the new Federal Republic.

By the time the ban on recruiting foreign labor came into force in 1973, around 14 million people had come to West Germany as "guest workers." Around 3 million stayed permanently.

Yet Germany still did not consider itself an immigration country. "For a very long time, we were dealing with the mindset: It doesn't matter why people came to the Federal Republic; they don't belong, because in any case they'll leave the country again and disappear," said Oltmer.

Between 1956 and 1973, around 14 million 'guest workers' came to Germany from other European countries Image: Hans Heckmann/dpa/picture alliance

In 2025, according to Germany's Federal Statistical Office, more than 30% of Germany's total population had a migrant background. Yet many third- and fourth-generation citizens still don't feel they belong, which has to do with the perspective of the society in which they live.

Who's welcome – and who isn't?

These days, Germany is keen to attract skilled workers, but refugees are only granted asylum if they are politically persecuted in their homeland, or are fleeing war.

As a migration researcher, Oltmer is constantly examining the reasons why some migrants are accepted and others are not. This question was especially relevant in 2015, when refugees came to Germany in very large numbers.

"The attitude was: 'OK, you people from Syria, in light of the Syrian civil war, you are entitled to protection.' But at the same time this society says of people from Afghanistan, 'In your case, we're a bit more sceptical,'" he said.

Germany took in hundreds of thousands of refugees in 2015, above all people fleeing the civil war in Syria Image: Johannes Simon/Getty Images

Yet asylum accounts for barely 10% of immigration to Germany, Oltmer explained. The majority of immigrants are not people fleeing their country. "This means that when it comes to scandalization and the creation of certain negative images, we are seeing a massive distortion of the debate." And the descendants of the German emigrants Benjamin Franklin once reviled as "Palatine boors" have long since perfectly integrated into American society.

In Germany, however, integration is taking much longer. "Many people have no possibility of regularizing their status and obtaining a stable residence permit, even though everyone involved knows they can stay, and will stay," said Oltmer. He believes people urgently need to sit down and clarify how they want German society to look in future.

"It may be a very hard, even hurtful discussion. But it's the only way."
