World.title: Mine explosion in Azerbaijan's Aghdam damages tractor
World.content:
AGHDAM, Azerbaijan, September 6. A tractor hit a mine in the Aghdam district.

The incident occurred in the territory of Sarijali village.

According to reports, the tractor driver was plowing the land in the area when the tractor ran over an anti-tank mine. As a result of the explosion, the tractor was damaged beyond repair.

The tractor driver was not injured in the incident.

Currently, relevant authorities are conducting an investigation at the scene.

World.title: Sweeny exits US Open to end Australia's singles chances
World.content:
Dane Sweeny's gallant US Open campaign has come to a frustrating end with a tough third-round loss to 21st-seeded Italian Luciano Darderi.

Sweeny complained of a hip injury during a 6-4, 6-3, 6-3 defeat to the world number 22 that left Australia without a second-week singles hope in New York for the first time in five years.

Alex de Minaur's shock second-round loss to Botic van de Zandschulp meant Sweeny was Australia's last player standing at Flushing Meadows.

"It's been an amazing week, a career-changing week, but I can't help but feel a bit disappointed just with today's performance," Sweeny said.

"I just wasn't really feeling it, just not really feeling the timing and the rhythm as I have been. I just made a lot of cheap errors and that was quite frustrating.

"I was OK to lose a match, but I really wanted to test him more and bring a good level so I could make an absolute fight out of it.

"Win or lose, I wanted to really make him work for the victory at least and I wasn't able to do that."

The world number 123 only gained a last-minute entry to the US Open after two late withdrawals allowed Tennis Australia to grant Sweeny the reciprocal wildcard it initially handed to Alexei Popyrin.

Dane Sweeny reached the last 32 for the first time at a major. (Getty images/USTA: Dustin Satloff)

Despite his disappointment, Sweeny cashed in on his good fortune.

The 25-year-old turned his first US Open main-draw appearance into a watershed run to the last 32 of a major for the first time.

The Queenslander will walk away with a life-changing cheque for $402,500 and a fresh career-high ranking.

"The financial side of things, that will help with coaching and people you travel with," Sweeny said.

Sweeny is provisionally slated to climb to number 109 in the world.

If he can crack the top 100 by season's end, Sweeny will earn direct entry to the Australian Open for the first time.

"That's exciting too. But that will take care of itself," Sweeny said.

"It's hard not to worry about that because we're indoctrinated to want that low number next to our name, but I can just focus on working hard, focus on improving.

"Particularly just staying really kind to myself and trying to enjoy the journey."

American tilt takes a hit

Past US Open finalists Taylor Fritz, Madison Keys and Amanda Anisimova all crashed out in the third round, dealing a stinging blow to home fans.

Men's ninth seed ​Fritz had yet to drop a set in New York and looked well on his way to another routine victory before Argentina's Francisco Cerundolo found his best tennis to flip the script and win 3-6, 4-6, 6-3, 6-4, 6-4.

It was the earliest exit in four years for the 2024 runner-up, as Cerundolo reached the ​fourth round for the first time.

The American ‌women fared no better as China's Zheng Qinwen fought back from a 5-0 deficit in the decider to beat 2017 runner-up Keys 1-6, 7-6 (7/3), 7-5, collapsing on the court in utter joy as she fights back from a career slump.

Zheng Qinwen celebrates her win over Madison Keys. (Getty Images: Al Bello)

Zheng will next face 2022 champion and former world number one, Iga Świątek, who got past Czech Marie Bouzková 7-6 (7/3), 7-6 (7/3).

Tenth-seeded Anisimova, last ​year's runner-up, was unable to reverse ‌her fortunes in a frustrating year at the majors, with a 6-2, 7-5 defeat by Anastasia Potapova.

Coco Gauff, the 2023 US Open winner, provided the lone bright spot for the Americans when she beat Spain's Cristina Bucșa 6-3, 6-4 in the third round.

AAP/Reuters

World.title: Old working dogs refuse to be put out to pasture
World.content:
Kingsley Vaux's family has been farming at Ongerup, about 400 kilometres south-east of Perth, for more than a century.

By their side are about eight generations of working dogs, with 15-year-old Cassie the last in the line.

"They're normally gone at 10 or 12, but she still seems reasonably healthy although she's gone deaf so we're down to signals," Mr Vaux said.

"It's a bit of a fight to get her to change direction or anything, but she's teaching the young ones a little bit too, so it's still a joy to be working with her."

A seasoned professional

The border collie-huntaway cross may be deaf and arthritic, but her love for sheep work remains strong.

"[She] always wants to do work even though she's hardly capable of it these days, at 15," Mr Vaux said.

"All these jobs she's done before and she knows where they're going."

She is one of many old farm dogs who, far from being put out to pasture, remain "totally faithful" to their masters.

"You can see it in their eyes," Mr Vaux said.

" It's just devotion, isn't it? "

Manners maketh dog

Thirteen-year-old Bundy "loves getting out and amongst it", according to owner Renae Parsons, who relies on working dogs to muster thousands of sheep at her farm in Tenterden, about 330km south-east of Perth.

Bundy as a puppy. (Supplied: Renae Parsons)

The "naturally gifted" kelpie can't do as much as he used to but is still treasured by Ms Parsons.

"He's definitely one in a million," she said.

"If I could find another one like him, I'd grab it in an instant."

On one occasion, in the middle of moving 3,000 sheep, a quick-witted Bundy noticed 300 were missing and nipped off to bring back the laggards on his own.

Renae Parsons says 13-year-old kelpie Bundy is naturally gifted. (ABC Great Southern: Mark Bennett)

But as much as Bundy likes work, there is one thing he won't stand for.

"He doesn't like to be yelled at," Ms Parsons said.

"You can talk firmly, but as soon as you get grumpy, he will go and sit on the ute and won't work.

"So you have to calm down and then he'll come back and start working again."

Better bond, better working dog

Jenny Parsons, who trains and breeds dogs on her Tenterden farm, says this level of care is typical of farming folk, despite their tough reputation.

"A lot of people think that farmers are rough and heartless, but when you look around at all the old dogs that they've still got and absolutely adore … you can tell that most farmers are very, very soft underneath," she said.

Jenny Parsons with her young dog Sherlock says the bond between a dog and trainer is crucial. (ABC Great Southern: Mark Bennett)

In fact, it's this bond that makes for a great working dog.

"They have to want to work for you," she said.

" The better the bond … the bigger the try. "

Special bond

Mr Vaux is emotional walking through the graveyard on his property where each dog has an epithet.

Beth was a talker, Fudge a prankster, Quarter always knew her left from right, and Speckles loved the water.

"It's bloody hard when you leave one, when one leaves you," he said.

"They tug at the heartstrings, even now."

He knows Cassie will end up there one day soon, but for now he's grateful for his "loyal friend".

"She's a good mate, a good friend, and a good worker," he said.

"It's bloody amazing when you can hardly just move a finger and they know what you want to do."

Kingsley Vaux describes his working dog Cassie as a good mate and a good worker. (ABC Great Southern: Mark Bennett)

World.title: Cutting cigarette tax will not create more smokers, Angus Taylor says
World.content:
Opposition Leader Angus Taylor says slashing the tax on a pack of cigarettes by more than 20 dollars will not create more smokers, as the cost of illegal cigarettes is already at that price.

The Coalition has not modelled how its proposed 80 per cent cut to the tobacco excise would affect smoking rates, Shadow Home Affairs Minister Jonno Duniam told ABC's Insiders program, though it has looked at the consequences of similar approaches overseas.

Canada had raised tobacco taxes through the 1980s and 1990s to discourage smoking, but after an explosion in organised crime, Canadian federal and provincial governments slashed tobacco taxes in 1994.

The cuts led to a spike in smoking, particularly among young people, Senator Duniam said, however smoking rates in Canada have ultimately fallen.

"There was a point in time they went up, but over the course of time — as the illicit tobacco trade trailed off — smoking rates went down to where they are now, which is 11 per cent," Senator Duniam said.

"And their policy settings continued that trajectory over that course of time."

Jonno Duniam says Canada's approach ultimately led to lower smoking rates. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

Canada's federal and provincial governments eventually restored pre-1994 tax rates on tobacco, which supporters say allowed a gradual return after the black market had been crushed and law enforcement established.

Critics, however, say it failed to provide a permanent fix, with the illicit black market returning, higher youth smoking rates in the meantime, and lost revenue from the tax cut.

Coalition says crime groups must be disrupted

The tobacco commissioner has estimated about half of all tobacco sales in Australia are now through the black market — fuelling billions in proceeds for crime groups, leading to increased violence particularly in Sydney and Melbourne, and eating into federal government revenue from the tax on tobacco.

Senator Duniam said modelling by the Parliamentary Budget Office his party commissioned on how deeply to cut the tobacco excise found a "real change" in consumer behaviour if the excise was cut by 80 per cent.

He said combined with law enforcement and education, Australia's illicit tobacco trade could be stamped out.

"We should also focus on disrupting the capacity for the illicit market to provide these products. That also causes issues for their capacity to supply, impacts their capacity to offer cheaper prices and the combined package altogether, not just the cut in excise, is what we believe will cripple the illicit tobacco market," Senator Duniam said.

"We want to see the smoking rates in this country go down. In order to do that, a part of the problem is dealing with cheap smokes out there in the community now. Kick off the illegal trade is the only way you can do that."

One Nation, Coalition bank on cigarettes staying uncool There isn't a politician of any stripe who believes the current black market situation is good.

Earlier, Mr Taylor told News24 that to smash organised crime, legal cigarettes needed to be brought to "parity" with illegal tobacco.

"We're confident working with experts, working with the Parliamentary Budget Office, that they can smash that market," Mr Taylor said.

An excise cut of 80 per cent would amount to about $25 being knocked off the price of a pack of 20 cigarettes, bringing those down to about $16 to $26 if the full tax cut is passed on by cigarette retailers.

Asked whether he believed the excise cut would lead to more people picking up smoking, Mr Taylor responded, "No, no I don't [believe that].

"And here's the point. The horse has already bolted on this. The price of cigarettes in this country is already down around $15 a pack or less … anyone can choose to buy that.

"That's the price, it's already happened. So you have got to recognise the reality here."

Mr Taylor rejected that the Coalition had landed on an 80 per cent excise cut to outcompete One Nation's proposed 75 per cent excise cut.

"We decided to go one better than organised crime and criminal gangs in this country. That's who we're competing with here — that's what this is about," he said.

"It needs to be fixed and it needs to be fixed now. And I'll tell you, every arson attack that we see now we will be saying to the government: 'You can fix this.'"

World.title: Labor commits $550m for freeway upgrade in Melbourne's outer west
World.content:
Traffic congestion in Melbourne's outer west is the target of Labor's latest commitment ahead of the state election, with a pledge to spend $550 million upgrading the Western Freeway.

The funds to improve the section of freeway between the fast-growing areas of Melton and Caroline Springs are in addition to $1 billion promised by the Commonwealth government ahead of the 2025 election.

Under the plan, interchanges at Ferris Road, Leakes Road and Hopkins Road would be upgraded, alongside a new half interchange at Mount Cottrell Road giving local traffic direct access on and off the freeway.

"I said as a new premier my first task is to listen to what Victorians' needs are," Premier Ben Carroll said.

"They told me very clearly they wanted a relentless focus on the basics and there was nothing more important than getting our road infrastructure right and making sure hard-working Victorians can spend less time in traffic and get to spend more time with their families."

Premier Ben Carroll says the freeway funding pledge is part of a "relentless focus on the basics". (ABC News)

He said the upgrade would see 30 kilometres of new lanes, with up to four lanes in both directions, and the speed limit would consistently be 100 km/h across the upgraded sections.

Mr Carroll said planning for the project was already underway with the federal money, and the promise represented Victoria "coming to the table as well".

As the November state election approaches, Melton City Council has been advocating for new train stations and major road upgrades to help alleviate pressure on existing railway stations and the busy section of freeway.

Upgrading the Western Freeway is among a suite of road infrastructure improvements the council has been calling for as the area's population increases by 6.61 per cent per annum — more than triple the Melbourne average of 2 per cent.

In documents outlining its advocacy on the issue, the council has stated that "major arterial roads in the City of Melton are not suitable for the existing high volume of traffic".

"They are predominantly of a rural standard with unsealed shoulders, no public lighting, open drains and non-existent bike and pedestrian paths."

World.title: Negotiations over 'Australia's biggest shortcut' near an end
World.content:
Years of complex negotiations with multiple traditional owner groups appear to be nearing an end, paving the way for the long-awaited sealing of the outback highway dubbed "Australia's biggest shortcut".

The Outback Way stretches 2,719 kilometres through central Australia — from Laverton in Western Australia's northern Goldfields to Winton in Queensland.

With more than $1.2 billion committed to sealing the remote route by 2032, one of the project's biggest hurdles has been securing Indigenous Land Use Agreements (ILUAs) in parts of Australia where a permit system is used for visitors.

The ongoing negotiations mean roadworks were put on hold four years ago on WA's side of the border, which stretches 736km from Laverton to the Northern Territory.

The Outback Way in WA begins at Laverton with the Great Central Road. (ABC Goldfields: Jarrod Lucas)

Road progress at 'glacial pace'

The delays prompted WA Liberal MP Rick Wilson to criticise the WA government in federal parliament in June for moving at a "glacial pace".

"There are stretches of this road that do not fall within any native title claims, and still no progress has been made. It's bureaucracy," he said.

WA Liberal MP Rick Wilson's electorate of O'Connor includes the WA stretch of the Outback Way. (ABC Goldfields: Jarrod Lucas)

A spokesperson for WA Transport Minister Rita Saffioti defended the approach.

"Ensuring all approvals and registered ILUAs are in place will ensure the long-term success of the project, which has a key focus on delivering training, employment and economic opportunities for local and Aboriginal people and businesses," the statement said.

The WA section of the Outback Way stretches 736km along the Great Central Road. (Supplied: Goldfields-Esperance Development Council)

Remote communities support road

In this remote part of WA, known as the Ngaanyatjarra Lands, three main groups represent the people of the Yilka, Nangaanya-ku and Yarnangu.

This week, Main Roads did not say how advanced its discussions were with traditional land owner groups, only that they were continuing.

Ngaanyatjarra Council major projects advisor Ralph Addis described the Outback Way as "nationally significant" with "complex opportunities and challenges".

"We're hearing early next year [for construction] … we think the earliest works can start, the better for all concerned," he said.

Outback Highway Development Council chairman Pat Hill, who is also Shire of Laverton president, echoed those sentiments.

Pat Hill has been chairman of the Outback Highway Development Council since 1997. (ABC Goldfields: Jarrod Lucas)

"The communities out there have all had input, negotiating with Main Roads and the state government," he said.

"From what I've heard it will be starting just after Christmas … the sooner the better, obviously."

Studies reveal next phase

New documents show Main Roads has completed a clearing assessment and biological survey to seal a 171km section of the road.

Under the plan, 660 hectares of native vegetation would be cleared.

The assessments did not identify any significant impacts to threatened flora or fauna.

The reports now form part of a formal planning and approvals process Main Roads has begun alongside the Department of Water and Environmental Regulation.

The Outback Way stretches 2,719km from Laverton in WA's northern Goldfields to Winton in Queensland. (Supplied)

A social impact assessment by the Goldfields-Esperance Development Commission has also been completed, which questions if infrastructure along the route can support an influx of travellers.

It also raises the question of how to preserve culturally significant sites, with the loss of the current permitting system once it becomes a public road.

Other concerns include an increased risk of communicable disease, access to non-Opal fuel undermining petrol sniffing prevention and increased police enforcement.

Goldfields-Esperance Development Commission chief executive Kris Starcevich (left) after the completion of a social impact assessment for the Outback Way project. (Supplied: Facebook/Ngaanyatjarra Council Group)

Protecting places of significance

The Great Central Road currently averages 30-60 vehicles a day, but traffic volumes are estimated to increase 300 per cent over a decade once it is sealed, including a significant rise in heavy vehicle movements.

Mr Addis said the biggest concern for traditional land owners along the route remained the protection of culturally significant sites.

There are concerns about visitor behaviour involving photography and social media, including the photography of people, places or culturally sensitive features without consent.

The Outback Way cuts through some of the most remote parts of Australia. (ABC)

"People are concerned about making sure the extra volume of people coming through the lands is both supported and properly managed so people can enjoy the experience but not damage the local environment and cultural places," Mr Addis said.

Yilka Talintji Aboriginal Corporation chairman Harvey Murray was contacted for comment.

World.title: Germany's Isar rocket launches from arctic Norway and reaches orbit
World.content:
Germany's Isar Aerospace has launched a rocket into orbit from Norway as Europe races to boost its ability to economically send satellites into space independently of the United States.

Isar's 28 metre-long two-stage Spectrum rocket blasted off from Andoya spaceport, north of the Arctic Circle, the company said.

"We're in orbit! And just made European history: This is the first time a privately developed rocket reached orbit from continental Europe," the company said on X.

Isar Aerospace is aiming to further build space capacity. (Supplied: Isar Aerospace)

About 10 minutes into the mission dubbed "Onward and Upward", the video transmission cut out after the rocket exceeded maximum range for connection.

"Germany has spaceflight capabilities," the Ministry for Research, Technology and Space posted on X, hailing a "milestone that impressively demonstrates our country's innovative strength and technical expertise".

European breakthrough in 'turbulent times'

The event was a breakthrough for the European launch industry, giving the continent better access to space, Norway's Minister of Trade and Industry Cecilie Myrseth said in a statement.

"The fact that we can now launch satellites from Andoeya strengthens Norwegian and European security in the turbulent times we live in," she said.

The launch followed months of delays, caused by either technical or safety issues.

Orbital space rocket explodes 40 seconds after take-off German startup Isar Aerospace says this was an initial test as part of a project aimed at kickstarting satellite launches from Europe.

It was Isar's second launch, coming 18 months after the company's first rocket plunged into the sea and exploded in a fiery spectacle shortly after take-off from the same site.

Once ready for serial production, the Spectrum will be tasked with sending civilian and military satellites into low-Earth orbit a few hundred kilometres above the ground.

The Spectrum can haul about 1 tonne of payload, and Isar says its plant near Munich will be able to make more than 30 of the rockets per year.

While France's Arianespace has long operated from French Guiana, Europe is betting on competition between Isar and other companies to more cheaply launch satellites in future, as Elon Musk's SpaceX has done in the United States.

"We need capacity. We need independence," German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said in March while visiting the Andoya facility with Norway's prime minister.

"For far too long we have relied on other delivery systems and other nations around the world."

Mr Merz spoke at the International Aerospace Exhibition in Berlin, held in June.

"Space is not only crucial for our security, but it is also becoming an increasingly important part of our economic sphere," he said.

Europe seeks to build autonomy

The launch came at a time US President Donald Trump has badly shaken European trust in the NATO alliance, with Europe worrying about its dependence on America, including in space launch capabilities.

German Defence Minister Boris Pistorius has announced a €35 billion ($56 billion) drive by 2030 to build out space capacity.

Global players in the satellite launch market include Elon Musk's SpaceX, which launches from the US, and French ArianeGroup, which uses a spaceport in South America's French Guiana.

Rocket Moon crash Part of a SpaceX rocket has crashed into the Moon, with the impact likely to be seen from Earth.

SpaceX, a company spanning rockets, satellites and AI, in June listed on the Nasdaq exchange in a record initial public offering.

Sweden, with its Esrange launch site, and Britain with its SaxaVord Spaceport in the Scottish Shetland Islands, are the nearest rivals to the Norwegian site, all of which aim to give Europe greater autonomy in space flights.

Isar last week said it had secured about €200 million ($323 million) from the European Space Agency to help fund development of new rockets and expand its testing and launch infrastructure.

The German company is also developing a second launch site in Canada.

AFP/Reuters

World.title: Meet the Rural Women's Award finalists for 2026
World.content:
Rural leaders from across the country will come together in Canberra this week to celebrate the achievements of women driving change outside the big cities.

Seven state and territory finalists are in the running for the national 2026 AgriFutures Rural Women's Award, which will be announced at a gala event on Tuesday night, September 8.

First established by ABC Rural in 1994, the award supports and recognises women who are making a difference in the bush.

State and territory finalists receive a $15,000 grant for their project, business or program, and the national winner takes home an additional $20,000.

Kristie Ivone – New South Wales/ACT

In the Murray River cities of Albury–Wodonga, a plethora of languages are being taught by native speakers: Spanish, Italian, Arabic, Swedish and even Swahili.

The Boas Language Academy, founded by Kristie Ivone in September 2024, trains migrants to teach their own languages and share their culture with others.

"There was an appetite for language education in the community," Ms Ivone said.

"I also knew that we had this amazing dynamic and highly talented multicultural community locally who I think had underutilised skills and experience."

Ms Ivone decided to open up her city to the wider world through language after a cancer diagnosis.

"I think in my life language and language skills have been a key to some of the best opportunities that I've had in my life personally," Ms Ivone said.

Boas has delivered over 29 language courses in the past two years.

Becky Dickinson – Victoria

Mixed animal veterinarian Becky Dickinson from Warragul in Gippsland is passionate about training the next generation of rural vets.

She founded Veterinary Support Services in 2022 to provide mentoring, training and networking pathways to early-career veterinarians.

Becky Dickinson is passionate about training the next generation of rural vets. (Supplied: AgriFutures)

Ms Dickinson told the Victorian Country Hour that being a new vet in rural areas is tough and isolating.

"I decided there's a bit of a gap here, in terms of a lack of a structured postgraduate pathway for our rural vets," she said.

"It's a very isolating job working independently right from the outset out of uni. This can get them into situations they're not really ready for."

Ms Dickinson is using her state award funds to help secure a resilient rural veterinary workforce for Australia's livestock industries.

Angie Nisbet – Queensland

Fifth-generation beef producer from remote North-West Queensland Angie Nisbet used her own experience with skin cancer and melanoma, and her motivation to make a difference for others.

The death of her best friend to skin cancer and her sister's melanoma diagnosis inspired Ms Nisbet to co-found FarmHer Hands, which makes colourful sun-safe gloves for farmers.

Angie Nisbet makes colourful sun-safe gloves for farmers to help prevent skin damage. (Supplied: AgriFutures)

Speaking to the ABC in March, Ms Nisbet said helping farmers prevent skin damage was key to reducing soaring rates of melanoma and skin cancer.

"The gloves are such a great conversation starter," Ms Nisbet said.

"The patterns are really bright and fun, and I think that's really important, especially when you're out 12 hours a day mustering cattle, or out in the hot sun.

"It needs to be encouraged to give that first-year jackaroo or jillaroo some gloves or an option at least to cover up and look after themselves."

FarmHer Hands is leading the AgriSkin Project — a national initiative focused on early intervention and improving access to skin health services in rural Australia.

Narelle Zanker – South Australia

Narelle Zanker is a dairy farmer, former teacher and co-founder of Dairy Adventures, an agritourism venture bringing the story of dairy farming to life on the family's 4,000-acre property just outside Mannum, South Australia.

Narelle Zanker is bringing the story of dairy farming to life. (Supplied: AgriFutures)

Raised on the land and shaped by four years in the classroom teaching from ELC to Year 11, Ms Zanker returned to her family farm to combine her twin passions for education and agriculture.

In September 2024, she co-founded Dairy Adventures, the only experience of its kind in South Australia, welcoming visitors of all ages for hands-on encounters with daily farm life, from bottle-feeding calves and touring the dairy to meeting pet cow Elvis.

In its first year, Dairy Adventures attracted more than 1,000 visitors and earned a Silver Medal at the 2025 South Australian Tourism Awards.

With the support of the AgriFutures Rural Women's Award and the Westpac $15,000 grant, Narelle is expanding the farm's visitor spaces, developing educational spaces, activities and signage on the farm, and delivering educational resources in collaboration with Dairy Australia.

Angela Teale – Western Australia

Angela Teale is an aerospace engineer, co-founder and Strategic Advisor of Starsite Australia — a company bringing world-class space infrastructure to regional Western Australia.

Her career began in the US Air Force and has spanned over two decades at the leading edge of the global space sector.

She moved to Geraldton in 2015, and what looked like a career-limiting sea change turned out to be anything but.

Angela Teale is bringing world-class space infrastructure to regional Western Australia. (Supplied: AgriFutures)

In 2022, she and her husband co-founded Starsite. Their Mullewa site is now part of the world's first commercial network dedicated to lunar communications, in partnership with KSAT, operational by the end of 2026.

As the recipient of the 2026 AgriFutures Rural Women's Award, Ms Teale is committed to building real STEM pathways into the space industry for regional and Indigenous communities across Western Australia.

Kelly Shotton – Northern Territory

Kelly Shotton is a station hand, qualified pilot and founder of BoreWatch – an app transforming how remote cattle stations monitor and manage their water infrastructure.

Raised on a sheep and cropping farm in Rochester, Victoria, Ms Shotton completed an electrical apprenticeship before taking a station role with Consolidated Pastoral Company at 25.

She found her calling in the industry and never looked back.

Kelly Shotton is a station hand, qualified pilot and founder of BoreWatch. (Supplied: AgriFutures)

Now based in Darwin as senior head pilot for CPC, she developed BoreWatch from a practical need to streamline bore-run reporting on remote stations, and recognised its potential far beyond her own operation.

With the support of the AgriFutures Rural Women's Award and the Westpac $15,000 grant, Ms Shotton is investing in app development to commercialise BoreWatch and make it accessible to stations across Australia.

Amy Vickers – Tasmania

Amy Vickers spent 26 years in the Royal Australian Navy, rising to Chief Petty Officer — and when her service ended with a medical discharge, she faced the question every veteran knows: "What now?"

The answer came unexpectedly, through a gifted horse named Alby on her property in Gladstone, Tasmania.

Amy Vickers spent 26 years in the Royal Australian Navy. (Supplied: AgriFutures)

That connection became the spark for Well Beyond Service, a rural retreat program helping those who have served in defence and emergency services rediscover identity and purpose after service life.

Through nature, animals, art, therapy and genuine community, Well Beyond Service is earning national recognition for its impact on some of Australia's most dedicated people.

World.title: Hawkesbury's Helping Hands charity marks 15 years of service
World.content:
Single mother Linda Strickland was at home in Sydney's north-west with her eight-year-old daughter one night when she heard someone getting into the bins in her backyard.

Her daughter Cassidy asked why someone was desperate enough to go through their bins to find food.

"How do I explain to her that we allow, we can let people be that hungry?" Ms Strickland said.

" I had blinkers on. I had no idea that people were that hungry. "

Hawkesbury's Helping Hands started out with Cassidy and her mother Linda making meals at home for people experiencing homelessness in the park. (Supplied: Linda Strickland)

The Windsor pair decided they had to do something about it. Linda and Cassidy made some meals, put them in plastic containers, and went to the local park where they knew people experiencing homelessness were staying.

That night, 15 years ago, Linda and Cassidy co-founded the charity Hawkesbury's Helping Hands (or HHH), which has since grown from those warm meals at the park into a warehouse that provides hampers and basic essentials for hundreds across Sydney's most disaster-prone region.

The charity handles up to 30 pallets a day during busy times, which are either Christmas or a major disaster. (ABC News: Declan Bowring)

Helping where disaster is no stranger

The mum-and-daughter team has since become the face of disaster response in the Hawkesbury, which in recent years has battled through more than its fair share of major events, including the 79-day Gospers Mountain bushfire in 2019–20 and five major floods between 2020 and 2022.

They have received two visits from prime ministers, by Scott Morrison in March 2022 and once by Anthony Albanese in July 2022 when the area was hit three times in the same year.

Ms Strickland remembered being called up in the middle of the night when the first flood hit in February 2020 off the back of the Black Summer bushfires. She said years of being a service with connections in the community meant they were ready to step up.

Scott Morrison visited HHH while he was prime minister when flooding hit the Hawkesbury in March 2022. (ABC News)

"I was called in the middle of the night to set up an evacuation centre because, being a homelessness service, we had air mattresses, we had pet supplies, we had snacks," Ms Strickland said.

"We were already prepared."

" Now we are prepared even better because five floods has taught us a lot. "

Outside of major natural disasters, the charity of around 20 volunteers has been a lifeline for the community during droughts, the COVID-19 pandemic and the ongoing cost-of-living crisis.

High in the warehouse, air mattresses and sleeping bags are pre-wrapped for the next major disaster. (ABC News: Declan Bowring)

At their busiest, which was usually around Christmas when some other charities were not operating, Ms Strickland said they were moving between 20 and 30 pallets of food a day, which is donated by food relief charities and supermarkets.

This week, the charity turns 15. Ms Strickland said Hawkesbury's Helping Hands' clientele had grown from people experiencing homelessness to working families doing it tough, some of whom travel well outside their area to receive support.

The charity receives donated food from supermarkets and food relief organisations. (ABC News: Declan Bowring)

"There can be two-income families who still can't afford to eat, meet their mortgage, meet their rent," Ms Strickland said.

"Interestingly enough, our fastest-rising demographic is actually The Hills, which most people always consider an affluent area."

No direct government funding

People like mother-of-three Paula Maher, who also looks after her two grandchildren, know how much of a difference the charity makes.

She came into Hawkesbury Helping Hands and left with a hamper that could sort out meals for the best part of a week.

Paula Maher says the charity goes a long way when finances are tough. (702 ABC Sydney: Declan Bowring)

"Rent payments, car payments, water bills, electricity, everything's just haywire at the moment," Ms Maher said.

" When you don't have the money for the food you just come here to Linda's and she provides you with everything that she can. "

Despite the high-profile visits from politicians during a crisis, Ms Strickland said the charity had never been directly funded by government and was instead funded through community donations and business sponsorships.

Linda Strickland hopes HHH can keep going for at least another 15 years. (ABC News: Declan Bowring)

Politicians from both sides of the aisle admire the charity's work.

"HHH shows up week after week to give people affordable access to food and basics, but in times of disaster and crisis the team is extraordinarily responsive," said Labor MP Susan Templeman, whose federal seat of Macquarie includes the Hawkesbury.

"As a local charity, they understand the unique geography and the people of the Hawkesbury region."

Ms Templeman said she provided a federal grant for the organisation in 2024 aimed at their volunteers and that federal funding of at least $20 million had been given to food relief providers who were among those that donated supplies to HHH.

" The benefits of federal funding to organisations like Foodbank, Second Bite, and OzHarvest flows through to communities thanks to the work of local charities like HHH. "

Liberal NSW Member for Hawkesbury Robyn Preston said the charity made a real impact for people who did not know where their next meal might come from.

"When basic necessities are not even an option, Linda and her team of amazing volunteers fill the gap, giving practical support, reinstating dignity, showing respect and continued compassion," Ms Preston said.

"That's the difference that has earned Hawkesbury's Helping Hands the high regard that the community has for the services they provide."

Supermarkets and food relief charities supply food to the HHH building. (ABC News: Declan Bowring)

Looking ahead to the next 15 years

Floods don't always move slowly, prepare now Floods can devastate large areas and it's important to know the risk of flooding at your home. Make sure your property is prepared because floods can happen quickly.

Ms Strickland said the charity was preparing for a major El Niño event that may bring hot days to the Hawkesbury by opening up her warehouse space as a relaxation zone with fans and couches for people who could not escape the heat.

The charity has made room for this by acquiring a neighbouring warehouse room where dozens of pre-wrapped crates filled with air mattresses and sleeping bags await the next disaster.

Ms Strickland said the charity was also gearing up for the next flood and had recently been given flood-proof bags that could contain half the goods of a house and stay submerged for four weeks.

“I can see myself being here for another 15 years," Ms Strickland said.

"Whether I'm here or not, because it's not about me, we have amazing volunteers.

"I think Hawkesbury's Helping Hands is a much-needed place."

World.title: Les Kiss knows his strongest Wallabies side. It’s time to pick it, and stay with it
World.content:
SportRugby UnionWallabies Opinion Les Kiss knows his strongest Wallabies side. It’s time to pick it, and stay with it Peter FitzSimons Columnist and author September 6, 2026 — 11:04am

September 6, 2026 — 11:04am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The good news is that this 28-28 draw in Mendoza against Los Pumas meant that after last week’s win for the Goodies, the Wallabies have won the series in Argentina – the first undefeated tour of that fine country in 47 years – and have now gone five Tests without defeat. The bad news is that it was an exceedingly scrappy match. It was chalk and cheese when compared to the All Blacks and Springboks Test match played in Johannesburg earlier in the morning. Loading That 29-24 victory to the Boks featured unremitting intensity and staggering skill levels. This contest in Mendoza was stop-start-drop and all over the place. Ultimately for the Wallabies, this was one that got away, but we’ll get to that.



The “Argentinian Wave” that came 13 minutes into the match told the story of the first 20 minutes. Even the locals looked a bit bored as both sides went error for error, with the only upside for the Wallabies being that our errors were so egregious – knock-ons, forward passes, penalties, lost lineouts, opposition up-and-under kicks that were allowed to bounce with none of our blokes calling “MINE!” – that at least we were able to test our defensive capacity, and it was strong ... for 35 minutes. Wallabies captain Harry Wilson receives the Puma Trophy from Argentine Rugby Union president Felix Paez Molina. Getty Images At that point, somehow, the Wallabies were leading 14-0 after great tries by skipper Harry Wilson and winger Max Jorgensen – the second when Carter Gordon came on and took over the five-eighth spot. (Our back-line always seems to operate best when he is on the field, and he is the one coach Les Kiss must go back to.) Alas, between that 35-minute mark and the half-time break we conceded our usual two tries to sloppy defence, and were lucky not to let in a third when fullback Tom Wright foolishly led with a forearm, giving Los Pumas a penalty. We were only able to hold on, in extremis, after the resumption of some great defence.



So here, as the second half began, was the test of the Test …. Would the locals rise, with the crowd behind them, as Argentines on their own turf are ever wont to do, or would the Wallabies continue their renaissance under new coach Les Kiss to record their fifth win on the trot? Fraser McReight and Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii celebrate McReight’s try against Argentina. Getty Images Again, the Wallabies forwards proved their lethality from in close when, after a forward rush, the always excellent back-rower Fraser McReight scored shortly after the break. Alas, just as had happened in the first half, the Pumas quickly struck back with two tries of their own after our defence again proved porous. But wait!



A penalty try to the Wallabies with 10 minutes to go, which also saw Argentina have a second man yellow-carded in two minutes, saw the score at 28-all with the Wallabies having a huge advantage. Fifteen men on thirteen men, surely, surely, it would be a matter of mathematics beating geography, and we could beat the locals? Related Article International rugby Injury worry for star playmaker after Wallabies botch chance against 13-man Pumas Alas, it was not to be. The locals simply kept the ball in the forwards where it was eight on eight, and the one time we did get the ball in the open, our fullback Tom Wright knocked it on after a loose pass. It was all so deeply frustrating, but on the other hand, the Wallabies didn’t really deserve to win it after such a scrappy effort. Look, I get Les Kiss wanting to try different combinations and build depth as we approach the Springboks and All Blacks. But 14 changes to the squad of 23 was excessive, and it showed. It was the Wallabies’ poorest effort this year, and frustrating. The upside is that by now, Les Kiss surely knows who his strongest Test side is. It’s time to pick it, and stay with it for the rest of the year. The Wallabies have great talent between them. But now Kiss has to make a firm decision about who is the core of next year’s World Cup side, and stick with them.

World.title: Health watchdog must put patient welfare first and foremost
World.content:
NationalAHPRA Editorial Health watchdog must put patient welfare first and foremost The Herald's View Editorial September 6, 2026 — 10:00am

September 6, 2026 — 10:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Australian consumers rely heavily on effective regulators across many industry sectors. This is especially important in healthcare where negligence or incompetence can result in disfigurement, long-term pain and even death; proactive and effective watchdogs are vital to safeguarding patients’ interests. Patients claim the Australian Healthcare Practitioner Regulation Agency has failing to adequately investigate allegations of medical negligence and misconduct. iStock It is disappointing then that one of the nation’s most important supervisory bodies, the Australian Healthcare Practitioner Regulation Agency (AHPRA), is once more in the spotlight. As health editor, Kate Aubusson, reports in today’s Sun-Herald many injured, chronically ill and traumatised patients have accused AHPRA of failing to adequately investigate allegations of gross negligence and misconduct by doctors, nurses and allied healthcare professionals.



They report a worrying lack of transparency in the agency’s complaints handling; cases are sometimes dismissed without investigation, and no explanation is offered as to why. Related Article Exclusive

Healthcare ‘Patients want answers’: Why the health practitioner watchdog needs to show it’s working Earlier this year the ABC’s Four Corners detailed how the agency failed to act on multiple complaints about surgeries performed by renowned Melbourne gynaecologist Simon Gordon. While Gordon says he always acted “ethically and responsibly”, expert colleagues say AHPRA “dropped the ball” when it took no action on the complaints. Today’s report describes how patients received pro forma letters from AHPRA in response to detailed and often deeply personal testimonials. Patients also complain of an alarming lack of trauma-informed communication with agency staff.



This is not the first time AHPRA’s performance has been called into question. In 2021 and 2022 the Cosmetic Cowboys series of investigative reports by this masthead– along with reporting by 60 Minutes and Four Corners – documented scores of cases where people suffered horrific disfigurement and life-threatening complications after cosmetic procedures. The investigation exposed widespread malpractice and predatory marketing within Australia’s multibillion-dollar cosmetic surgery industry. Following those reports hundreds of people joined a class action demanding compensation for botched cosmetic surgery. These revelations put AHPRA under intense scrutiny and raised doubts about its capacity to protect patients.



At the time, consumer affairs expert and former chair of the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission Allan Fels warned the agency was “ineffective in protecting the public from very dangerous practices in cosmetic surgery”. Health practitioners are often poorly served by the AHRPA’s long-winded investigations. Those subject to a lengthy probe face psychological distress, loss of income and reputational damage – even when complaints are eventually dismissed. A recent review concluded that dissatisfaction with the agency’s complaints handling was felt “equally deeply” by both patients and practitioners. That’s no surprise considering the average duration of investigations was found to have increased by 52 per cent between 2018-19 and 2022-23. One in four of the agency’s investigations dragged on for over two years without resolution. AHPRA works alongside 15 national boards to ensure hundreds of thousands of health practitioners across the nation are suitably trained, qualified and safe to practise; this masthead acknowledges this is a challenging remit.



The regulator’s five-year reform strategy to better protect the public is encouraging. Work already under way is welcome, including the publication of historical findings of sexual misconduct against practitioners on AHPRA’s public register. But there is no justification for keeping patients who lodge complaints with the agency in the dark. The lack of transparency of AHPRA’s investigations risks damaging the community’s trust in our health system. Jordan Baker sends a newsletter to subscribers each week. Sign up to receive her Note from the Editor.

World.title: Why Lebanese farmers chose a small NSW town to grow cherries
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

There are three key values that have remained consistent across three generations of the Ali family: they all hate Sydney, they love the town of Young, and they grow cherries. The late Mostapha Ali, his son Bassam and his grandson Mohammed were and are all cherry farmers in the town of Young on the NSW South-Western Slopes, part of a growing contingent of Lebanese farmers there. And despite their growing numbers and their work to build a community there, including opening a school and a mosque, it still feels strange to hear Lebanese-tinged Arabic spoken in such a small town. Young is as far from the migrant centres of Sydney as you can get, physically and spiritually distant from the imaginings of the immigrant dream in Australia, and yet the Lebanese community is thriving there. Second generation farmer Bassam Ali, 52, is following in his father’s footsteps working the family cherry orchard in Young, NSW. KATE GERAGHTY The Ali patriarch bought a cherry farm in 1990 and sought to maintain its cherry output while blending in some Lebanese techniques and crops; his work in some ways was a cultural statement as much as it was a farm. “Dad was an old-school farmer. He used to grow pomegranates and olives in his village. So when he came to Young, he picked farming back up,” the eldest son, Bassam said.



“And we have laid roots here. Young is a special place.” Along with a clutch of families, they have knitted together a unique community with roots in Lebanon, Sydney and Young itself, their work and lives a living tapestry of the unique opportunities migration can present to families and their long-held traditions. But why Lebanese families have come to Young is a question with a sprawling answer, touching on the nature of Lebanese migration to Australia, their dormant traditions and the peace they sought. Third-generation farmer Mohammed Ali inspects cherry trees on the family property. KATE GERAGHTY A history of change Atop his dirt bike, Mohammed Ali shoots through the orchard his grandfather built, bobbling as his bike flies over mounds and holes in the ground. “She wants to go, but I am holding her back,” he says after drifting to stop, throwing up plumes of dirt. Mohammed is one of the dozens of grandchildren Moustapha saw born and brought up in Young.



The 25-year-old has seen the orchard transform into a vibrant and busy farm, its cherry trees stretching into the horizon. Much like his uncles and aunties, he was put to work as far back as he can remember, his grandfather organising the crop and the family effort. “He was a straight shooter,” Mohammed says of his grandfather. “He was a well-respected, hard-working farmer who you’d never want to cross.” Mostapha Ali arrived in Sydney in 1977, in the wake of a brutal civil war that was shredding his home. He came from a long line of north Lebanese farmers who worked their patches of land with old knowledge. Mohammed Ali during an inspection on his motorbike. KATE GERAGHTY In Young, Lebanese farmers found a perfect place to apply skills and knowledge honed over thousands of years. KATE GERAGHTY He had seven children living in western Sydney but he was eventually enticed to return to his roots in Young after several getaways picking fruit in the regions. And Young presented a perfect opportunity. Its abundant cherry farming provided ready-made infrastructure for the family to step into.



He bought a cherry farm on the outskirts of the town and put his kids to work ploughing the ground and trimming the trees. And he applied old Lebanese techniques to the Australian land, including digging trenches around the trees and filling them with water. The technique was used for thousands of years in rural Lebanon to ensure a sapling remains hydrated. “We’d dig the trenches by hand. It’s an old technique, but a good one. It was more natural, no chemicals. My father was a simple but dedicated farmer,” Bassam said. “Its thousands of years of knowledge in stuff like that. They just knew how it worked.” Despite adopting improvements in technology and technique, the family has held on to its inherited knowledge, tying it to their roots in rural Lebanese villages. Where are you from? Across town, Mahmoud Khodr explains his own farming philosophy: “If you had a son, wouldn’t you take care of him? A farm is like a baby. You have to feed it and take care of it.” Khodr is standing in the middle of his cherry farm, his son snipping off branches from the trees behind him. He says he bought the farm when it was in disrepair and slowly brought it back to life, moving his family out to the town 17 years ago.



“I came here for the first time with my in-laws and I fell in love with it. It smelt like the village from back home. It has that same energy.” While data can tell us the country migrants are coming from, it struggles to tell us the culture or lifestyle they’re leaving behind and what they are seeking in Australia. Lebanese migrants in Australia can be roughly split between rural communities from north Lebanon and metropolitan communities from major cities such as Beirut and Tripoli. Mahmoud Khodr and son Ali among the cherry trees on their property Lynton Orchard in Young. KATE GERAGHTY Mahmoud Khodr says he bought the farm when it was in a state of disrepair and has brought it back to life, KATE GERAGHTY Those who came from the rural communities arrived domino-style, one major family following another. Their unfamiliarity with city living led them to follow their families and their communities, to live with them and near them, unfurling into the migrant hubs we know now in western Sydney. But for many who left a rich life of farming behind, there was a yearning that remained unquenched by the hectic lifestyle in Sydney. While some adapted, working in fruit markets and opening grocery shops, some looked longingly at Australia’s rural communities.

World.title: She was given up for dead, then a faint cry came from the depths of the mud
World.content:
WorldAsiaFloods She was given up for dead, then a faint cry came from the depths of the mud Mujib Mashal , Binod Ghimire and Sajal Pradhan September 6, 2026 — 9:22am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Betrawati: Days after Chandika Shrestha’s family carried out her last rites, expecting never to find her body, a faint noise came from a house along the ravaged riverside in northern Nepal. The three-story structure was almost entirely buried, with only its roof and the tip of its top windows peeking out above the sludge. But that wasn’t enough to muffle the defiant plea for help. Shrestha was alive. Chandika Shrestha was rescued on Saturday from a house that was almost completely buried. Nepal Police In the 10 days since devastating floods wiped out the town around her, Shrestha had clung to life under the debris. The group of locals who heard her cry on Saturday (Kathmandu time) rushed to find emergency workers. Some crawled through the mud to reach an opening in the house. Others cleared a path with shovels. They gave her water, and by early afternoon Shrestha had been airlifted in a white helicopter to a hospital in Kathmandu, Nepal’s capital.



“We don’t have words to describe what this means, for how happy we are,” her nephew, Surendra Lal Shrestha, said outside the hospital. Chandika Shrestha’s recovery was the second improbable rescue of the day. A Chinese national rescued by soldiers during an ongoing operation at the Trishuli-3A hydropower project in Nepal’s Rasuwa district. Nepal Army via AP The Nepali army said earlier on Saturday that a joint rescue team had found a Chinese worker trapped inside a 225-metre tunnel in the Upper Trishuli-1 hydropower project. Both the Chinese worker, whose name authorities did not immediately confirm, and Shrestha managed to stay alive well beyond the 72-hour window after which rescuers say the chances of surviving a natural disaster usually drop off. At least 1300 people were killed in the floods last month, when a glacial collapse in the Himalayas sent tsunami-like waves through valleys along the border of Nepal and the Tibet region of China. An additional 5000 people are missing.



Emergency workers have in recent days focused their efforts on the several power stations that make up Nepal’s budding hydropower industry, like the one in which the Chinese man was found. The hope is that workers trapped in them may have been better able to shelter from the force of the floods than the thousands of people living alongside the rivers, who bore the brunt of the deluge’s force. Shrestha – despite living immediately beside the river in one of the towns most devastated by the floods – defied those odds. Loading Reporters from The New York Times spent much of Friday in the town, Betrawati, which was almost entirely wiped out by the floods. Rescuers there had given up trying to find survivors among most of the ruins. There is no trace of the bazaar that once comprised about 200 shops on either side of the river. There is nothing of the two bridges that connected both sides, or the Ram temple the locals frequented. The two-story building that once housed the police station was ripped from its roots and deposited on its side.



In the two wards that straddle the river, nearly 300 people are missing, officials say. Ganesh Kumar Nepal, a ward chair, said workers had been stationed in the area of Shrestha’s house for search and rescue. They had visited the house earlier but had not found her, perhaps because they did not check properly, he said. Related Article Floods ‘Survivable pockets’: Australian tunnel expert arrives in Nepal as two people rescued after 10 days As night fell on the town on Friday, the electricity had not yet been restored to the elevated houses that survived. The town was quiet, with just the sound of crickets and the roaring of the river. News of Shrestha’s survival injected the town with renewed hope. People rushed to the riverbank opposite the house where Shrestha was found, eager to observe the rescue operation. Shrestha’s son, Ashish Shrestha, who was at the hospital with her after the rescue, said his mother was being treated for an infection in one leg. Three generations of the Shrestha family had run a clothing shop in the town before the floods, Shailendra Kumar Shrestha, Shrestha’s brother, said. She had often been the one to make trips to Kathmandu, where the family bought material, Shailendra Shrestha said, as he waited outside the hospital where his sister was being treated.



But Chandika Shrestha was at home when the floods arrived. When the walls of water and mud descended on the town, her husband, Ananda Lal Shrestha, ran into the streets, urging people to flee, Chandika Shrestha’s brother said. She made it to a higher floor of the house, but her husband did not have enough time. He is still missing. A rescue team at the house where Chandika Shrestha was found in Betrawati. Lam Yik Fei/The New York Times Local officials and residents who observed the rescue said they believed the house had been carried about 200 metres downstream of its original location. Exact details of how rescuers first found Shrestha are unclear, but officials said they had been told that a group of locals was investigating what remained of the house when they heard the faint cry. Shailendra Shrestha said the locals had also heard the sound of clanking plates. The notion that someone could have survived inside the house was so far-fetched, he said, that the group had at first taken the noises for evidence of a ghost.



“It is generally not a place with many ghosts,” he said. “But things could have changed since this week, I don’t know.” Related Article Floods At first, the smell is overwhelming. Then, they open the book of the dead Chandika Shrestha’s nephew said rescue efforts had been complicated by how deep the sludge was. The government had sent a helicopter to survey the town within days of the disaster, but rescuers on the ground had great difficulty navigating the area, with workers sinking into the mud. He said that many had lost hope when corpses – most in such a damaged state that they were difficult to identify – started appearing in the area a week after the floods. The family had checked morgues even 128 kilometres downstream, looking for Shrestha and her husband, but they had not found a trace. So on Thursday, the family came to a difficult decision. Resigned to the probability that the bodies of Shrestha and her husband would be forever lost, they gathered for a symbolic cremation, substituting sacred effigies for the loved ones they were sure had died. About 60 relatives came together for the observance.





This article originally appeared in The New York Times. Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: Australian wildcard’s unlikely US Open run comes to end on day of upsets
World.content:
SportTennisUS Open Australian wildcard’s unlikely US Open run comes to end on day of upsets Marc McGowan September 6, 2026 — 9:02am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Dane Sweeny’s unlikely US Open run as the last Australian standing is over. The 25-year-old wildcard from the Sunshine Coast had never won a grand slam match before this year’s Australian Open, and backed that up by venturing into the third round in a career-best effort in New York this week. Australia’s Dane Sweeny fought hard before going down in straight sets. AP Photo/Kirsty Wigglesworth Sweeny upset Italy’s world No.14 Lorenzo Musetti to make it this far – but a second straight seeded Italian proved too much as Luciano Darderi eliminated the Australian 6-4, 6-3, 6-3 in two hours and 13 minutes. Sweeny’s second-round victory over Musetti was not only his maiden top-20 scalp, but also his first against a top-50 opponent at just his fourth attempt, guaranteeing him life-changing prizemoney of more than $400,000.



Related Article US Open De Minaur dumped from US Open in straight sets as Kyrgios cocaine ban revealed This is all still very new for the 123rd-ranked Australian, who remains without an apparel sponsor, and the reward for his pair of US Open wins will be a career-high ranking of No.109 once the tournament ends. Sweeny has about three months to make his top-100 debut in time to earn direct acceptance into next year’s Australian Open, but he would be a certain wildcard recipient if not. On this occasion, he scored Tennis Australia’s reciprocal wildcard with the United States Tennis Association after a series of withdrawals enabled Alexei Popyrin to sneak into the draw. Sweeny made the most of his fortune, starting with an upset of eccentric Frenchman Corentin Moutet in the first round. It was tough going from the outset against 22nd-ranked Darderi.



Sweeny handed an early advantage to the barrel-chested Italian with a loose third game on serve, including a missed volley and double fault before his jumping backhand drive volley thudded into the net. He almost slipped two breaks behind, but escaped that peril, then turned the screws on Darderi, who staved off a break-back point with some excellent serving. The 21st seed was also 15-30 in his next service game, as Sweeny began to settle into the contest, but he did enough to secure the opening set. Italy’s Luciano Darderi eliminated Sweeny. AP Photo/Kirsty Wigglesworth Sweeny’s approach was obvious from the outset: take the ball early, be aggressive, defend like his life depended on it, and finish points at the net where possible. His aggressive counter-punching meant he had to cop an inflated number of unforced errors – some of them missed by a fair way – but he was happy to pay that price to give himself a chance.



But after a competitive first set, Sweeny dug himself a hole with consecutive errors from 30-30 to immediately concede a break in the second. The 25-year-old Australian could have fallen away but instead grabbed the break straight back, starting with a terrific chase-down followed by an angled backhand winner to the opposite service box. Darderi was incensed and picked up an audible obscenity warning, which angered him more. Sweeny continued to fight as Darderi argued with the chair umpire for the next few minutes about his warning. Unsurprisingly, at Sweeny’s height, he doesn’t get many cheap points on serve, particularly against an opponent with Darderi’s power. That led to him being in lots of pressure moments while serving, and back-to-back misses from 30-all proved his undoing as he fell 3-2 behind.



The key moment came in the next game, on another 30-all point, as Sweeny tried to draw level again. Darderi survived a riveting 33-shot rally with an inside-out forehand blast that finally broke through the Australian’s defences. Sweeny provided some spectacular moments, but could not snatch a set off his Italian rival. AP Photo/Kirsty Wigglesworth He double-faulted afterwards but won the next two points to go 4-2 up, then broke Sweeny again a few games later to go two sets up. Sweeny refused to quit – that is not in his DNA – and earned a break point in the opening game of the third set. A frenzied volley exchange followed between the players, which Darderi won despite Sweeny launching himself at the shot that beat him.



Related Article US Open Joint joy: Williams sisters fall just short in US Open doubles comeback This one hurt him, and he spent the next few minutes nursing a sore right elbow. Anyone who watches enough of Sweeny knows he is not afraid to dive across the court to stay in points; he typically plays with scabs on his arms and legs from doing so. Darderi again escaped, then broke Sweeny with a superb backhand lob winner to go 2-0 up. That could have, not for the first time, broken Sweeny’s spirit. Instead, he figuratively rolled up his sleeves and kept fighting. Darderi shanked an overhead at the net to gift Sweeny a third break-back point, then ballooned a backhand long to breathe life into the Australian battler’s cause.



But it was always difficult for Sweeny to hold serve. He won barely half the points on his first serve for the match, which was never going to be a winning formula against Darderi, one of six Italians ranked in the top 50. Coco Gauff is hunting a second US Open title. AP Photo/Yuki Iwamura Sweeny dropped serve for a sixth time to go 3-1 down, and his gallant New York run soon came to a close. Coco Gauff, the 2024 winner, advanced to the fourth round on Sunday (AEST) as she continues to spearhead the host nation’s title hopes, but fellow Americans Taylor Fritz, Amanda Anisimova and Madison Keys were all shock losers.



Roland-Garros runner-up Flavio Cobolli also exited the US Open early, losing 6-7 (4-7), 6-3, 6-0, 6-3 to Belgian rising star Alexander Blockx. But grand slam champions Iga Swiatek and Mirra Andreeva dodged the carnage to move into the last 16. Watch the US Open live on 9GO!, 9NOW and Stan Sport. World.title: Three children injured in jumping castle accident as 80km/h winds hit Sydney
World.content:
Updated NationalNSWEmergency services Three children injured in jumping castle accident as 80km/h winds hit Sydney Max Maddison Updated September 6, 2026 — 7:47am ,first published 4:41pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Three young children had to be rushed to hospital after powerful winds lifted a jumping castle into the air in Sydney’s inner south as wild weather cut power to thousands of homes across Sydney, Newcastle and the Central Coast. An Ausgrid spokeswoman said crews were still working to restore power to approximately 1400 homes as of 7am on Sunday morning with services expected to be restored by midday. Three children were injured when a jumping castle became airborne in Banksia, in Sydney’s south, amid ferocious wind gusts on Saturday. Nine News The outages followed a cool change that swept through NSW, with wind gusts surpassing 80km/h recorded at Sydney Airport late on Saturday afternoon. Temperatures in Sydney had hovered around 30 degrees, accompanied by strong north-westerly winds. At the height of the outages, about 40,000 Ausgrid customers were left without power after high winds damaged one of the company’s substations in Sydney’s west. Another 50,000 customers on Endeavour Energy’s network were also left without power.



Emergency services were called to Gardiner Park in Banksia, about 12 kilometres south of the CBD, about 1.20pm on Saturday after the jumping castle became airborne, a NSW Ambulance spokeswoman said. The children were taken to Sydney Children’s Hospital after being treated by paramedics at the scene. A preschool-aged boy and girl suffered head injuries, while a baby was treated for minor injuries. A woman was also taken to hospital with minor injuries, the spokeswoman said. All three children were in a stable condition. Loading This was the second incident involving an airborne jumping castle recorded in a matter of hours on Saturday. Two children were injured at a party near Geelong in Victoria in the morning. Both children were taken to hospital with injuries to their upper bodies and were in a stable condition. Greater Western Sydney and the Blue Mountains were the areas worst hit by the wild winds.



“There’s currently over 250 fault sites. Crews are currently working to make damaged areas safe before restoration work can commence,” an Endeavour Energy spokeswoman said. The company’s website estimated that power would not be restored until the early hours of Sunday morning. In a statement, an Ausgrid spokeswoman said most customers were expected to have their power restored by 7pm with the remainder by 11pm. “There are currently approximately 40,000 customers without power after strong winds moved through Sydney and the Central Coast this afternoon,” she said. “Hardest-hit areas include Bankstown, Milperra and Revesby where high winds have caused some damage to one of our substations.”



Outages were being experienced right across Sydney, including in Mosman, St Ives, Bellevue Hill, Rosebery and Summer Hill. Get alerts on breaking news as it happens.

World.title: Les Kiss knows his strongest Wallabies side. It’s time to pick it, and stay with it
World.content:
SportRugby UnionWallabies Opinion Les Kiss knows his strongest Wallabies side. It’s time to pick it, and stay with it Peter FitzSimons Columnist and author September 6, 2026 — 11:04am

September 6, 2026 — 11:04am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The good news is that this 28-28 draw in Mendoza against Los Pumas meant that after last week’s win for the Goodies, the Wallabies have won the series in Argentina – the first undefeated tour of that fine country in 47 years – and have now gone five Tests without defeat. The bad news is that it was an exceedingly scrappy match. It was chalk and cheese when compared to the All Blacks and Springboks Test match played in Johannesburg earlier in the morning. Loading That 29-24 victory to the Boks featured unremitting intensity and staggering skill levels. This contest in Mendoza was stop-start-drop and all over the place. Ultimately for the Wallabies, this was one that got away, but we’ll get to that.



The “Argentinian Wave” that came 13 minutes into the match told the story of the first 20 minutes. Even the locals looked a bit bored as both sides went error for error, with the only upside for the Wallabies being that our errors were so egregious – knock-ons, forward passes, penalties, lost lineouts, opposition up-and-under kicks that were allowed to bounce with none of our blokes calling “MINE!” – that at least we were able to test our defensive capacity, and it was strong ... for 35 minutes. Wallabies captain Harry Wilson receives the Puma Trophy from Argentine Rugby Union president Felix Paez Molina. Getty Images At that point, somehow, the Wallabies were leading 14-0 after great tries by skipper Harry Wilson and winger Max Jorgensen – the second when Carter Gordon came on and took over the five-eighth spot. (Our back-line always seems to operate best when he is on the field, and he is the one coach Les Kiss must go back to.) Alas, between that 35-minute mark and the half-time break we conceded our usual two tries to sloppy defence, and were lucky not to let in a third when fullback Tom Wright foolishly led with a forearm, giving Los Pumas a penalty. We were only able to hold on, in extremis, after the resumption of some great defence.



So here, as the second half began, was the test of the Test …. Would the locals rise, with the crowd behind them, as Argentines on their own turf are ever wont to do, or would the Wallabies continue their renaissance under new coach Les Kiss to record their fifth win on the trot? Fraser McReight and Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii celebrate McReight’s try against Argentina. Getty Images Again, the Wallabies forwards proved their lethality from in close when, after a forward rush, the always excellent back-rower Fraser McReight scored shortly after the break. Alas, just as had happened in the first half, the Pumas quickly struck back with two tries of their own after our defence again proved porous. But wait!



A penalty try to the Wallabies with 10 minutes to go, which also saw Argentina have a second man yellow-carded in two minutes, saw the score at 28-all with the Wallabies having a huge advantage. Fifteen men on thirteen men, surely, surely, it would be a matter of mathematics beating geography, and we could beat the locals? Related Article International rugby Injury worry for star playmaker after Wallabies botch chance against 13-man Pumas Alas, it was not to be. The locals simply kept the ball in the forwards where it was eight on eight, and the one time we did get the ball in the open, our fullback Tom Wright knocked it on after a loose pass. It was all so deeply frustrating, but on the other hand, the Wallabies didn’t really deserve to win it after such a scrappy effort. Look, I get Les Kiss wanting to try different combinations and build depth as we approach the Springboks and All Blacks. But 14 changes to the squad of 23 was excessive, and it showed. It was the Wallabies’ poorest effort this year, and frustrating. The upside is that by now, Les Kiss surely knows who his strongest Test side is. It’s time to pick it, and stay with it for the rest of the year. The Wallabies have great talent between them. But now Kiss has to make a firm decision about who is the core of next year’s World Cup side, and stick with them.
