World.title: Health watchdog must put patient welfare first and foremost
World.content:
NationalAHPRA Editorial Health watchdog must put patient welfare first and foremost The Herald's View Editorial September 6, 2026 — 10:00am

September 6, 2026 — 10:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Australian consumers rely heavily on effective regulators across many industry sectors. This is especially important in healthcare where negligence or incompetence can result in disfigurement, long-term pain and even death; proactive and effective watchdogs are vital to safeguarding patients’ interests. Patients claim the Australian Healthcare Practitioner Regulation Agency has failing to adequately investigate allegations of medical negligence and misconduct. iStock It is disappointing then that one of the nation’s most important supervisory bodies, the Australian Healthcare Practitioner Regulation Agency (AHPRA), is once more in the spotlight. As health editor, Kate Aubusson, reports in today’s Sun-Herald many injured, chronically ill and traumatised patients have accused AHPRA of failing to adequately investigate allegations of gross negligence and misconduct by doctors, nurses and allied healthcare professionals.



They report a worrying lack of transparency in the agency’s complaints handling; cases are sometimes dismissed without investigation, and no explanation is offered as to why. Related Article Exclusive

Healthcare ‘Patients want answers’: Why the health practitioner watchdog needs to show it’s working Earlier this year the ABC’s Four Corners detailed how the agency failed to act on multiple complaints about surgeries performed by renowned Melbourne gynaecologist Simon Gordon. While Gordon says he always acted “ethically and responsibly”, expert colleagues say AHPRA “dropped the ball” when it took no action on the complaints. Today’s report describes how patients received pro forma letters from AHPRA in response to detailed and often deeply personal testimonials. Patients also complain of an alarming lack of trauma-informed communication with agency staff.



This is not the first time AHPRA’s performance has been called into question. In 2021 and 2022 the Cosmetic Cowboys series of investigative reports by this masthead– along with reporting by 60 Minutes and Four Corners – documented scores of cases where people suffered horrific disfigurement and life-threatening complications after cosmetic procedures. The investigation exposed widespread malpractice and predatory marketing within Australia’s multibillion-dollar cosmetic surgery industry. Following those reports hundreds of people joined a class action demanding compensation for botched cosmetic surgery. These revelations put AHPRA under intense scrutiny and raised doubts about its capacity to protect patients.



At the time, consumer affairs expert and former chair of the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission Allan Fels warned the agency was “ineffective in protecting the public from very dangerous practices in cosmetic surgery”. Health practitioners are often poorly served by the AHRPA’s long-winded investigations. Those subject to a lengthy probe face psychological distress, loss of income and reputational damage – even when complaints are eventually dismissed. A recent review concluded that dissatisfaction with the agency’s complaints handling was felt “equally deeply” by both patients and practitioners. That’s no surprise considering the average duration of investigations was found to have increased by 52 per cent between 2018-19 and 2022-23. One in four of the agency’s investigations dragged on for over two years without resolution. AHPRA works alongside 15 national boards to ensure hundreds of thousands of health practitioners across the nation are suitably trained, qualified and safe to practise; this masthead acknowledges this is a challenging remit.



The regulator’s five-year reform strategy to better protect the public is encouraging. Work already under way is welcome, including the publication of historical findings of sexual misconduct against practitioners on AHPRA’s public register. But there is no justification for keeping patients who lodge complaints with the agency in the dark. The lack of transparency of AHPRA’s investigations risks damaging the community’s trust in our health system. Jordan Baker sends a newsletter to subscribers each week. Sign up to receive her Note from the Editor.

World.title: Why Lebanese farmers chose a small NSW town to grow cherries
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

There are three key values that have remained consistent across three generations of the Ali family: they all hate Sydney, they love the town of Young, and they grow cherries. The late Mostapha Ali, his son Bassam and his grandson Mohammed were and are all cherry farmers in the town of Young on the NSW South-Western Slopes, part of a growing contingent of Lebanese farmers there. And despite their growing numbers and their work to build a community there, including opening a school and a mosque, it still feels strange to hear Lebanese-tinged Arabic spoken in such a small town. Young is as far from the migrant centres of Sydney as you can get, physically and spiritually distant from the imaginings of the immigrant dream in Australia, and yet the Lebanese community is thriving there. Second generation farmer Bassam Ali, 52, is following in his father’s footsteps working the family cherry orchard in Young, NSW. KATE GERAGHTY The Ali patriarch bought a cherry farm in 1990 and sought to maintain its cherry output while blending in some Lebanese techniques and crops; his work in some ways was a cultural statement as much as it was a farm. “Dad was an old-school farmer. He used to grow pomegranates and olives in his village. So when he came to Young, he picked farming back up,” the eldest son, Bassam said.



“And we have laid roots here. Young is a special place.” Along with a clutch of families, they have knitted together a unique community with roots in Lebanon, Sydney and Young itself, their work and lives a living tapestry of the unique opportunities migration can present to families and their long-held traditions. But why Lebanese families have come to Young is a question with a sprawling answer, touching on the nature of Lebanese migration to Australia, their dormant traditions and the peace they sought. Third-generation farmer Mohammed Ali inspects cherry trees on the family property. KATE GERAGHTY A history of change Atop his dirt bike, Mohammed Ali shoots through the orchard his grandfather built, bobbling as his bike flies over mounds and holes in the ground. “She wants to go, but I am holding her back,” he says after drifting to stop, throwing up plumes of dirt. Mohammed is one of the dozens of grandchildren Moustapha saw born and brought up in Young.



The 25-year-old has seen the orchard transform into a vibrant and busy farm, its cherry trees stretching into the horizon. Much like his uncles and aunties, he was put to work as far back as he can remember, his grandfather organising the crop and the family effort. “He was a straight shooter,” Mohammed says of his grandfather. “He was a well-respected, hard-working farmer who you’d never want to cross.” Mostapha Ali arrived in Sydney in 1977, in the wake of a brutal civil war that was shredding his home. He came from a long line of north Lebanese farmers who worked their patches of land with old knowledge. Mohammed Ali during an inspection on his motorbike. KATE GERAGHTY In Young, Lebanese farmers found a perfect place to apply skills and knowledge honed over thousands of years. KATE GERAGHTY He had seven children living in western Sydney but he was eventually enticed to return to his roots in Young after several getaways picking fruit in the regions. And Young presented a perfect opportunity. Its abundant cherry farming provided ready-made infrastructure for the family to step into.



He bought a cherry farm on the outskirts of the town and put his kids to work ploughing the ground and trimming the trees. And he applied old Lebanese techniques to the Australian land, including digging trenches around the trees and filling them with water. The technique was used for thousands of years in rural Lebanon to ensure a sapling remains hydrated. “We’d dig the trenches by hand. It’s an old technique, but a good one. It was more natural, no chemicals. My father was a simple but dedicated farmer,” Bassam said. “Its thousands of years of knowledge in stuff like that. They just knew how it worked.” Despite adopting improvements in technology and technique, the family has held on to its inherited knowledge, tying it to their roots in rural Lebanese villages. Where are you from? Across town, Mahmoud Khodr explains his own farming philosophy: “If you had a son, wouldn’t you take care of him? A farm is like a baby. You have to feed it and take care of it.” Khodr is standing in the middle of his cherry farm, his son snipping off branches from the trees behind him. He says he bought the farm when it was in disrepair and slowly brought it back to life, moving his family out to the town 17 years ago.



“I came here for the first time with my in-laws and I fell in love with it. It smelt like the village from back home. It has that same energy.” While data can tell us the country migrants are coming from, it struggles to tell us the culture or lifestyle they’re leaving behind and what they are seeking in Australia. Lebanese migrants in Australia can be roughly split between rural communities from north Lebanon and metropolitan communities from major cities such as Beirut and Tripoli. Mahmoud Khodr and son Ali among the cherry trees on their property Lynton Orchard in Young. KATE GERAGHTY Mahmoud Khodr says he bought the farm when it was in a state of disrepair and has brought it back to life, KATE GERAGHTY Those who came from the rural communities arrived domino-style, one major family following another. Their unfamiliarity with city living led them to follow their families and their communities, to live with them and near them, unfurling into the migrant hubs we know now in western Sydney. But for many who left a rich life of farming behind, there was a yearning that remained unquenched by the hectic lifestyle in Sydney. While some adapted, working in fruit markets and opening grocery shops, some looked longingly at Australia’s rural communities.

World.title: She was given up for dead, then a faint cry came from the depths of the mud
World.content:
WorldAsiaFloods She was given up for dead, then a faint cry came from the depths of the mud Mujib Mashal , Binod Ghimire and Sajal Pradhan September 6, 2026 — 9:22am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Betrawati: Days after Chandika Shrestha’s family carried out her last rites, expecting never to find her body, a faint noise came from a house along the ravaged riverside in northern Nepal. The three-story structure was almost entirely buried, with only its roof and the tip of its top windows peeking out above the sludge. But that wasn’t enough to muffle the defiant plea for help. Shrestha was alive. Chandika Shrestha was rescued on Saturday from a house that was almost completely buried. Nepal Police In the 10 days since devastating floods wiped out the town around her, Shrestha had clung to life under the debris. The group of locals who heard her cry on Saturday (Kathmandu time) rushed to find emergency workers. Some crawled through the mud to reach an opening in the house. Others cleared a path with shovels. They gave her water, and by early afternoon Shrestha had been airlifted in a white helicopter to a hospital in Kathmandu, Nepal’s capital.



“We don’t have words to describe what this means, for how happy we are,” her nephew, Surendra Lal Shrestha, said outside the hospital. Chandika Shrestha’s recovery was the second improbable rescue of the day. A Chinese national rescued by soldiers during an ongoing operation at the Trishuli-3A hydropower project in Nepal’s Rasuwa district. Nepal Army via AP The Nepali army said earlier on Saturday that a joint rescue team had found a Chinese worker trapped inside a 225-metre tunnel in the Upper Trishuli-1 hydropower project. Both the Chinese worker, whose name authorities did not immediately confirm, and Shrestha managed to stay alive well beyond the 72-hour window after which rescuers say the chances of surviving a natural disaster usually drop off. At least 1300 people were killed in the floods last month, when a glacial collapse in the Himalayas sent tsunami-like waves through valleys along the border of Nepal and the Tibet region of China. An additional 5000 people are missing.



Emergency workers have in recent days focused their efforts on the several power stations that make up Nepal’s budding hydropower industry, like the one in which the Chinese man was found. The hope is that workers trapped in them may have been better able to shelter from the force of the floods than the thousands of people living alongside the rivers, who bore the brunt of the deluge’s force. Shrestha – despite living immediately beside the river in one of the towns most devastated by the floods – defied those odds. Loading Reporters from The New York Times spent much of Friday in the town, Betrawati, which was almost entirely wiped out by the floods. Rescuers there had given up trying to find survivors among most of the ruins. There is no trace of the bazaar that once comprised about 200 shops on either side of the river. There is nothing of the two bridges that connected both sides, or the Ram temple the locals frequented. The two-story building that once housed the police station was ripped from its roots and deposited on its side.



In the two wards that straddle the river, nearly 300 people are missing, officials say. Ganesh Kumar Nepal, a ward chair, said workers had been stationed in the area of Shrestha’s house for search and rescue. They had visited the house earlier but had not found her, perhaps because they did not check properly, he said. Related Article Floods ‘Survivable pockets’: Australian tunnel expert arrives in Nepal as two people rescued after 10 days As night fell on the town on Friday, the electricity had not yet been restored to the elevated houses that survived. The town was quiet, with just the sound of crickets and the roaring of the river. News of Shrestha’s survival injected the town with renewed hope. People rushed to the riverbank opposite the house where Shrestha was found, eager to observe the rescue operation. Shrestha’s son, Ashish Shrestha, who was at the hospital with her after the rescue, said his mother was being treated for an infection in one leg. Three generations of the Shrestha family had run a clothing shop in the town before the floods, Shailendra Kumar Shrestha, Shrestha’s brother, said. She had often been the one to make trips to Kathmandu, where the family bought material, Shailendra Shrestha said, as he waited outside the hospital where his sister was being treated.



But Chandika Shrestha was at home when the floods arrived. When the walls of water and mud descended on the town, her husband, Ananda Lal Shrestha, ran into the streets, urging people to flee, Chandika Shrestha’s brother said. She made it to a higher floor of the house, but her husband did not have enough time. He is still missing. A rescue team at the house where Chandika Shrestha was found in Betrawati. Lam Yik Fei/The New York Times Local officials and residents who observed the rescue said they believed the house had been carried about 200 metres downstream of its original location. Exact details of how rescuers first found Shrestha are unclear, but officials said they had been told that a group of locals was investigating what remained of the house when they heard the faint cry. Shailendra Shrestha said the locals had also heard the sound of clanking plates. The notion that someone could have survived inside the house was so far-fetched, he said, that the group had at first taken the noises for evidence of a ghost.



“It is generally not a place with many ghosts,” he said. “But things could have changed since this week, I don’t know.” Related Article Floods At first, the smell is overwhelming. Then, they open the book of the dead Chandika Shrestha’s nephew said rescue efforts had been complicated by how deep the sludge was. The government had sent a helicopter to survey the town within days of the disaster, but rescuers on the ground had great difficulty navigating the area, with workers sinking into the mud. He said that many had lost hope when corpses – most in such a damaged state that they were difficult to identify – started appearing in the area a week after the floods. The family had checked morgues even 128 kilometres downstream, looking for Shrestha and her husband, but they had not found a trace. So on Thursday, the family came to a difficult decision. Resigned to the probability that the bodies of Shrestha and her husband would be forever lost, they gathered for a symbolic cremation, substituting sacred effigies for the loved ones they were sure had died. About 60 relatives came together for the observance.





This article originally appeared in The New York Times. Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: Australian wildcard’s unlikely US Open run comes to end on day of upsets
World.content:
SportTennisUS Open Australian wildcard’s unlikely US Open run comes to end on day of upsets Marc McGowan September 6, 2026 — 9:02am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Dane Sweeny’s unlikely US Open run as the last Australian standing is over. The 25-year-old wildcard from the Sunshine Coast had never won a grand slam match before this year’s Australian Open, and backed that up by venturing into the third round in a career-best effort in New York this week. Australia’s Dane Sweeny fought hard before going down in straight sets. AP Photo/Kirsty Wigglesworth Sweeny upset Italy’s world No.14 Lorenzo Musetti to make it this far – but a second straight seeded Italian proved too much as Luciano Darderi eliminated the Australian 6-4, 6-3, 6-3 in two hours and 13 minutes. Sweeny’s second-round victory over Musetti was not only his maiden top-20 scalp, but also his first against a top-50 opponent at just his fourth attempt, guaranteeing him life-changing prizemoney of more than $400,000.



Related Article US Open De Minaur dumped from US Open in straight sets as Kyrgios cocaine ban revealed This is all still very new for the 123rd-ranked Australian, who remains without an apparel sponsor, and the reward for his pair of US Open wins will be a career-high ranking of No.109 once the tournament ends. Sweeny has about three months to make his top-100 debut in time to earn direct acceptance into next year’s Australian Open, but he would be a certain wildcard recipient if not. On this occasion, he scored Tennis Australia’s reciprocal wildcard with the United States Tennis Association after a series of withdrawals enabled Alexei Popyrin to sneak into the draw. Sweeny made the most of his fortune, starting with an upset of eccentric Frenchman Corentin Moutet in the first round. It was tough going from the outset against 22nd-ranked Darderi.



Sweeny handed an early advantage to the barrel-chested Italian with a loose third game on serve, including a missed volley and double fault before his jumping backhand drive volley thudded into the net. He almost slipped two breaks behind, but escaped that peril, then turned the screws on Darderi, who staved off a break-back point with some excellent serving. The 21st seed was also 15-30 in his next service game, as Sweeny began to settle into the contest, but he did enough to secure the opening set. Italy’s Luciano Darderi eliminated Sweeny. AP Photo/Kirsty Wigglesworth Sweeny’s approach was obvious from the outset: take the ball early, be aggressive, defend like his life depended on it, and finish points at the net where possible. His aggressive counter-punching meant he had to cop an inflated number of unforced errors – some of them missed by a fair way – but he was happy to pay that price to give himself a chance.



But after a competitive first set, Sweeny dug himself a hole with consecutive errors from 30-30 to immediately concede a break in the second. The 25-year-old Australian could have fallen away but instead grabbed the break straight back, starting with a terrific chase-down followed by an angled backhand winner to the opposite service box. Darderi was incensed and picked up an audible obscenity warning, which angered him more. Sweeny continued to fight as Darderi argued with the chair umpire for the next few minutes about his warning. Unsurprisingly, at Sweeny’s height, he doesn’t get many cheap points on serve, particularly against an opponent with Darderi’s power. That led to him being in lots of pressure moments while serving, and back-to-back misses from 30-all proved his undoing as he fell 3-2 behind.



The key moment came in the next game, on another 30-all point, as Sweeny tried to draw level again. Darderi survived a riveting 33-shot rally with an inside-out forehand blast that finally broke through the Australian’s defences. Sweeny provided some spectacular moments, but could not snatch a set off his Italian rival. AP Photo/Kirsty Wigglesworth He double-faulted afterwards but won the next two points to go 4-2 up, then broke Sweeny again a few games later to go two sets up. Sweeny refused to quit – that is not in his DNA – and earned a break point in the opening game of the third set. A frenzied volley exchange followed between the players, which Darderi won despite Sweeny launching himself at the shot that beat him.



Related Article US Open Joint joy: Williams sisters fall just short in US Open doubles comeback This one hurt him, and he spent the next few minutes nursing a sore right elbow. Anyone who watches enough of Sweeny knows he is not afraid to dive across the court to stay in points; he typically plays with scabs on his arms and legs from doing so. Darderi again escaped, then broke Sweeny with a superb backhand lob winner to go 2-0 up. That could have, not for the first time, broken Sweeny’s spirit. Instead, he figuratively rolled up his sleeves and kept fighting. Darderi shanked an overhead at the net to gift Sweeny a third break-back point, then ballooned a backhand long to breathe life into the Australian battler’s cause.



But it was always difficult for Sweeny to hold serve. He won barely half the points on his first serve for the match, which was never going to be a winning formula against Darderi, one of six Italians ranked in the top 50. Coco Gauff is hunting a second US Open title. AP Photo/Yuki Iwamura Sweeny dropped serve for a sixth time to go 3-1 down, and his gallant New York run soon came to a close. Coco Gauff, the 2024 winner, advanced to the fourth round on Sunday (AEST) as she continues to spearhead the host nation’s title hopes, but fellow Americans Taylor Fritz, Amanda Anisimova and Madison Keys were all shock losers.



Roland-Garros runner-up Flavio Cobolli also exited the US Open early, losing 6-7 (4-7), 6-3, 6-0, 6-3 to Belgian rising star Alexander Blockx. But grand slam champions Iga Swiatek and Mirra Andreeva dodged the carnage to move into the last 16. Watch the US Open live on 9GO!, 9NOW and Stan Sport. World.title: Three children injured in jumping castle accident as 80km/h winds hit Sydney
World.content:
Updated NationalNSWEmergency services Three children injured in jumping castle accident as 80km/h winds hit Sydney Max Maddison Updated September 6, 2026 — 7:47am ,first published 4:41pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Three young children had to be rushed to hospital after powerful winds lifted a jumping castle into the air in Sydney’s inner south as wild weather cut power to thousands of homes across Sydney, Newcastle and the Central Coast. An Ausgrid spokeswoman said crews were still working to restore power to approximately 1400 homes as of 7am on Sunday morning with services expected to be restored by midday. Three children were injured when a jumping castle became airborne in Banksia, in Sydney’s south, amid ferocious wind gusts on Saturday. Nine News The outages followed a cool change that swept through NSW, with wind gusts surpassing 80km/h recorded at Sydney Airport late on Saturday afternoon. Temperatures in Sydney had hovered around 30 degrees, accompanied by strong north-westerly winds. At the height of the outages, about 40,000 Ausgrid customers were left without power after high winds damaged one of the company’s substations in Sydney’s west. Another 50,000 customers on Endeavour Energy’s network were also left without power.



Emergency services were called to Gardiner Park in Banksia, about 12 kilometres south of the CBD, about 1.20pm on Saturday after the jumping castle became airborne, a NSW Ambulance spokeswoman said. The children were taken to Sydney Children’s Hospital after being treated by paramedics at the scene. A preschool-aged boy and girl suffered head injuries, while a baby was treated for minor injuries. A woman was also taken to hospital with minor injuries, the spokeswoman said. All three children were in a stable condition. Loading This was the second incident involving an airborne jumping castle recorded in a matter of hours on Saturday. Two children were injured at a party near Geelong in Victoria in the morning. Both children were taken to hospital with injuries to their upper bodies and were in a stable condition. Greater Western Sydney and the Blue Mountains were the areas worst hit by the wild winds.



“There’s currently over 250 fault sites. Crews are currently working to make damaged areas safe before restoration work can commence,” an Endeavour Energy spokeswoman said. The company’s website estimated that power would not be restored until the early hours of Sunday morning. In a statement, an Ausgrid spokeswoman said most customers were expected to have their power restored by 7pm with the remainder by 11pm. “There are currently approximately 40,000 customers without power after strong winds moved through Sydney and the Central Coast this afternoon,” she said. “Hardest-hit areas include Bankstown, Milperra and Revesby where high winds have caused some damage to one of our substations.”



Outages were being experienced right across Sydney, including in Mosman, St Ives, Bellevue Hill, Rosebery and Summer Hill. Get alerts on breaking news as it happens.

World.title: ACT unveils election climate policy, vows to scrap net zero target and repeal Zero Carbon Act
World.content:
The ACT party has vowed to get rid of the net zero emissions target, repeal the Zero Carbon Act and cut carbon tax if elected.

Its climate policy is largely a repeat of what it brought to the 2023 election campaign, and promises not to "kneecap New Zealand's prosperity for the sake of political virtue signalling".

ACT leader David Seymour said the country's approach to dealing with climate change was broken and sending the country broke.

"A small trading nation can't ignore climate policy, but overdoing it backfires and puts unnecessary costs on Kiwi businesses and households," he said.

ACT's policy was "grounded in economic reality" and would reduce emissions without imposing costs on New Zealanders that trading partners were unwilling to bear, Seymour said.

The policy includes:

repealing the Zero Carbon Act and scrapping the target of net zero emissions by 2050, instead benchmarking New Zealand's emissions cap against major trading partners

cutting the Carbon Tax by removing the Government's minimum price for Emissions Trading Scheme auctions

introducing a carbon tax refund, returning 100 per cent of net carbon auction revenue to New Zealanders

opposing new climate taxes, including a tax on agricultural emissions

discouraging productive farms being converted into carbon forests and requiring forest owners to carry long-term costs and risks of their forests

offering "carbon assistance" to businesses that can demonstrate a competitive disadvantage against overseas producers if those competitors have lower or no carbon costs

ACT climate change spokesperson Simon Court said ACT would also seek a "better deal" for New Zealand under the Paris Agreement.

New Zealand has pledged to halve its emissions by 2030.

"New Zealand produces a tiny share of global emissions," Court said.

"We should play our part, but there is no virtue in sacrificing jobs, household incomes and productive land so politicians can boast about being more ambitious than everyone else."

Court said ACT's climate policy would reward efficient local businesses, rather than push production offshore.

"If a New Zealand business can produce steel, cement, aluminium or food more efficiently than its overseas competitors, closing that business is an economic own goal and an environmental one too," he said.

"ACT will cut unnecessary costs, protect Kiwi jobs, give carbon revenue back to households and let innovation deliver cleaner solutions."

World.title: Greens vow to break up supermarket duopoly, set up publicly owned 'KiwiMart'
World.content:
The Green Party is campaigning on establishing a publicly owned supermarket chain to break up the duopoly and drive down food prices.

The initiative is part of its 'Affordable Kai' policy which would cost more than $6 billion over four years, and included expanding the school lunch programme.

Co-leader Chlöe Swarbrick said successive governments had failed to lure an existing chain to New Zealand to introduce competition in the sector, which is dominated by Foodstuffs and Woolworths.

"That's why today we are announcing the real solution: a supermarket owned by all New Zealanders, for all New Zealanders," she said.

"We're not short of supermarkets, we're short of competition. As experts have noted, divestment - that is, buying already existing stores - is key to breaking up the duopoly."

The publicly owned chain, KiwiMart, would be mandated to prioritise affordability.

Co-leader Marama Davidson said it was unacceptable that people were going without food because they could not afford it, given New Zealand produces enough to feed 40 million people.

"Government has abdicated its responsibilities and left it to the market, in fact literally, the supermarket," she said.

Foodstuffs and Woolworths would be forced to sell 120 stores and two distribution centres into public ownership which would require new legislation, Swarbrick said.

The party said its plan would cost about $2.8b.

Parliamentary Library modelling estimated it would cost $1.3b to buy the stores and distribution centres, and $1.5b to establish KiwiMart, it said.

Swarbrick said KiwiMart would start with 15 percent market share.

A publicly owned supermarket was not a new idea, Swarbrick said.

"This is something that has been identified by experts and economists, the likes of Consumer New Zealand as a consumer advocacy group, who have identified that as a small country at the bottom of the world, that it does make sense to have a publicly owned supermarket as a third competitor," she said.

"We are proud to say it's something that the Greens are taking to the election to actually increase affordability for New Zealanders. "

The Greens' full Affordable Kai policy also includes:

restoring and permanently funding the school lunch programme Ka Ora, Ka Ako and expanding it to 150,000 more children ($2.2b)

increasing food bank funding from $8 million to $25m ($72m) doubling the cap on Work and Income food grants ($388m)

a $150m annual Fair Food Fund for community-led food security initiatives ($600m)

increasing funding, penalties and powers for the Commerce Commission, including a mandatory pricing accuracy code with automatic compensation when shoppers are overcharged ($104m)

banning supermarket price gouging and extending that to include other "uncompetitive" sectors like energy and fuel

a National Food Strategy, including legislating the right to adequate and nutritious food.

Davidson said the policy would rebuild parts of the food system the current government had "run down".

World.title: Weather: Rain and snow warnings issued as trough crosses central NZ
World.content:
The upper South Island is being lashed by heavy rain, with up to 200 millimetres expected in the ranges.

MetService says a large trough will cross central New Zealand on Sunday and early Monday, bringing heavy rain and potentially snow to mountain passes.

An orange-level warning is in place for Grey and Buller Districts, and Nelson Lakes, from 9am Sunday until 1am Monday.

The MetService warning issued at 9:17am said residents should expect "a further 100 to 140 mm of rain about the ranges on top of what has already fallen," and 50-70 mm elsewhere.

It said peak intensities of up to 25mm/h were expected this afternoon and early evening.

At the same time, it issued a heavy rain warning for the Tararua Range, effective from 5pm Sunday until 3pm Monday, with up to 150 millimetres expected overnight.

It said there is a "minimal chance" of the either warning being upgraded, but urged people to avoid low-lying areas.

"Streams and rivers may rise rapidly. Surface flooding, slips, and difficult driving conditions possible."

Rain watches were in place for the Westland ranges north of Mt Cook until 10pm, Tasman west of Takaka until 3am Monday, and the Canterbury High Country north of Mt Cook and southwestern Marlborough until 4am Monday.

Watches will come into force for northern Taranaki at 6pm, southern and eastern Wellington and Wairarapa away from the ranges at 11pm, and the Ruahine Range at 3am Monday.

Road snowfall warnings

By 10am Sunday, MetService had issued road snowfall warnings for five mountain passes in the South Island.

It says rain may fall as snow on both the Lindis Pass (SH8) and the Crown Range Road between 11am and 4pm.

Further north, rain is expected to turn to snow about the summits of Arthur's Pass and Porters Pass (both SH73) from 9pm Sunday until early Monday morning.

World.title: Rugby: Ardie Savea heading home as All Blacks rue missed chances in third test defeat
World.content:
All Blacks coach Dave Rennie was both disappointed and frustrated with the third test defeat to the Springboks, but he believes they're "close" to beating the World Champions.

The All Blacks started well in front of about 90,000 fans in Soweto and took and early 7-0 lead - something they weren't able to do in the first two tests.

However, the Springboks worked their way back into the match and levelled the score 12-12 by halftime.

The host's scrum dominance and seemingly unstoppable lineout mauls helped them take the lead midway through the second half and never relinquish it.

It was again a contrast of styles with the All Blacks trying to play at a high tempo with ball in hand and run the Springboks ragged in the Johannesburg Highveld, while the hosts took every opportunity to go to set piece and employ their power game.

Ultimately it was power that prevailed over pace as South Africa took a 2-1 lead in the four-match series. The final score was 29-24 to the Springboks.

Dave Rennie is disappointed but believes there's not much between the two sides. Photosport NZ Ltd / www.photosport.nz

Rennie said the All Blacks weren't accurate enough to win.

"We were able to play a high-tempo first half and we saw a lot of their big men struggling and we're keen to try and make that pay in the second half," Rennie said.

"But we made a few errors which slows the game down to a scrum and then often a penalty in field position for them."

With penalties coming thick and fast for the Springboks at scrum and maul time, Rennie said his side struggled to get their game going.

"There was a period where, just after we'd hit the lead, they sort of dominated us at set-piece and won all the scraps and had all the momentum for that period and obviously got reasonably well in front."

Rennie said the All Blacks need to be more ruthless when presented with opportunities to score.

"It's frustrating because there's a lot of effort out there and we just, maybe we weren't quite clinical enough first half and then couldn't wrestle momentum back when it mattered second half."

Adding injury to insult, All Blacks captain Ardie Savea was forced from the field with what appeared to be a serious shoulder injury after scoring the tourist's first two tries of the game.

Ardie Savea scores a try. Photosport NZ Ltd / www.photosport.nz

Rennie said Savea will miss the fourth and final test in Baltimore, where the All Blacks will try and salvage a series draw.

"Yes, his shoulder. I'm not sure whether it's dislocated, he certainly won't be travelling to the United States."

Rennie said losing Savea was a blow, but not the reason the All Blacks lost.

"I mean, he was massive, wasn't he? But Wallace [replacement loose forward Wallace Sititi] come on and played well, so we're certainly not going to use that as an excuse."

Two other All Blacks will also be heading home and have been ruled out of the match in the US, with midfielder Quinn Tupaea suffering a knee injury and loose forward Luke Jacobson, who took over as skipper when Savea went off, injuring a tendon in his elbow, which will require further investigation when he's back in New Zealand.

Return to play timeframes for the trio are yet to be determined.

The Springboks' scrum was again one of their strongest weapons, and after accusing them of "walking" the scrum around in the second test at Cape Town, Rennie said they were simply better than the All Blacks in Soweto.

"I think they got rewarded for dominance at times, so no issues with that," he said.

While disappointed, Rennie isn't dejected, and he believes the All Blacks aren't far away from beating the Springboks.

"I don't reckon there's much in it. I didn't think there was much in the first test, which we won convincingly in the end, according to the scoreboard.

"So it's key moments. You know, like a big moment today was [wing] Will Jordan kicking it dead. That's just unlucky," Rennie said.

"It was a good option, but you come back for a scrum, which is a penalty to a maul where they drive however many metres to score. They made hay when they had momentum tonight. We probably didn't do that enough."

Rennie also lamented some penalties his side conceded at crucial times, and said they will need to be better if they want to win the fourth and final test against the Springboks, in the US city of Baltimore next weekend.

"I think discipline hurt us at times. They're the world champions for a reason. They are very good up front, and they played a bit of footy tonight.

"We probably made a few errors that allowed them to play and I thought they were a lot stronger in that area than they had been in the first two tests."

The most dominant part of the Springboks' performance was the maul, with the All Blacks consistently struggling to stop their lineout drives.

Xavier Numia and Leroy Carter after the loss. Photosport NZ Ltd / www.photosport.nz

Rennie said they must find a solution before the fourth test, but said it's not beyond their grasp.

"The key thing is you've got to get in front of it," he said.

"The one they scored off, we competed, and then we scrambled to try and get in front of it and they kept rolling through us.

"It was really the only one that troubled us today and we've got to be able to stay in front of it. If we're going up [and competing at lineouts], we still need to stay in front of it. So, yeah, it's disappointing."

Wing Leroy Carter had a high work rate and played a key role in two of the All Blacks' four tries but made some glaring errors on defence with two missed tackles leading directly to Springboks tries.

Rennie was loath to single the winger out and said it wasn't just Carter who missed tackles.

"You know, a big fella misses a tackle around the fringe and no one notices, your winger misses a tackle out wide and they score," Rennie said.

"I feel for Leroy, he's a bloody good man. He's a very good defender and I'm sure he's hurting about that.

"I mean, our job, once they'd scored, was to try and bounce back and try and take control of possession, but they were able to dominate the next sort of 10 minutes and that was pivotal."

Rennie said he couldn't fault the effort of Carter and all his players and said they're bitterly disappointed with the result.

He said they will be determined to make amends in next weekend's fourth test in the US.

"Our boys worked bloody hard tonight," Rennie said.

"When you've lost a test, it's easier to reflect on all the negative things. I can guarantee you the room's pretty gutted. I just walked in there before, and there's a lot of heads down.

World.title: National promises low deposits for more first home buyers
World.content:
National is promising to help more people buy their first home by expanding access to the government's low-deposit scheme, if it's re-elected.

The existing First Home Loan scheme run by Kāinga Ora allows buyers to purchase their first home with a 5 percent deposit, rather than 20 percent which most banks require.

If elected, National would increase the income threshold so anyone earning less than $300,000 combined could access it - whether that was single income or combined income.

Housing spokesperson Chris Bishop said many would-be first home buyers could afford to service a mortgage, but struggled to get together a deposit.

Chris Bishop. RNZ / Mark Papalii

The scheme's current cap of $95,000 for single buyers with no dependents, or $150,000 for multiple buyers or single buyers with dependents, was too restrictive, he said.

The caps were last updated in 2022.

"Right now, a junior doctor on $100,000 can't access the scheme. Nor can a young couple, like an electrician on $85,000 and a teacher on $78,000, or two friends who have just graduated from police college and are earning $77,000 each," he said.

Around half of first-home buyers earned more than $146,000, said Bishop.

"So, while a combined income of $150,000 might sound like a lot of money, the reality is that plenty of young couples now earn more than that but still struggle to save for a 20 percent deposit while juggling the cost of rent, food, and childcare.

"National's changes will address those pressures and build on the work we have done in government to support more people into home ownership."

The loans are issued by some banks and other lenders, and underwritten by Kāinga Ora, allowing lenders to provide loans it otherwise would not.

Bishop said National's long term goal was to boost the home ownership rate to 74 percent, up from 66 percent currently.

He said the policy would see "thousands" more applicants accessing the scheme, but would not give a specific number.

Of 25,000 first home buyers last year, 4000 accessed the scheme, Bishop said.

"We do expect by widening the eligibility, thousands more will use it."

The coalition in 2024 scrapped Labour's First Home Grant, which gave eligible applicants up to $10,000 towards purchasing their first home. https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics/517499/government-confirms-first-home-grants-to-be-scrapped

Bishop said National's policy was more effective.

"Giving people an amount of money in cash... was a very blunt and ineffective way of actually helping," he said.

"This goes to the biggest barrier that we see that young people face getting into the housing market which is getting that deposit together."

The party estimated widening access to the First Home Loan scheme would cost between $4 million and $6m, funded from existing baselines.

The scheme cost $14.5m to administer during FY2024/25 which included the cost of the government subsidising Lenders Mortgage Insurance, it said.

World.title: 'Absolute chaos' at Gisborne Hospital ED as nurses struggle with staffing shortages
World.content:
A nurse at Gisborne Hospital says the emergency department (ED) is in a state of "absolute chaos" due to ongoing staffing shortages and the surge of winter illnesses.

The New Zealand Nurses Organisation (NZNO) said EDs across the country are under strain.

Meanwhile, flu data shows hospitalisations have been climbing steeply nationwide for over a month.

More than 30 ED nurses from Gisborne Hospital are striking for an hour on Wednesday over unsafe staffing levels.

NZNO union delegate and Gisborne Hospital ED nurse Clara Dolman-Tuhou said the "absolute chaos" was not sustainable.

"It's placing both the patient safety and the staff wellbeing at risk, the staff are absolutely exhausted doing back-to-back 12 hour shifts," she said.

"You got nurses running from here, there and everywhere, you can see the strain, you can see the tiredness from everybody and you can also feel the worry."

She said there'd been an influx of patients with influenza, as well as patients with respiratory syncytial virus - or RSV - particularly in children.

Patients with underlying conditions were being hit the most, and some were ending up with pneumonia, she added.

The hospital had lost 10 senior nurses over the past year, and what Health NZ (HNZ) was offering to replace those roles was "definitely not good enough", Dolman-Tuhou said..

HNZ had offered 1.4 full time equivalent (FTE) nurses in permanent roles, 0.8 FTE for a six-month fixed-term position and 0.8 FTE for a health care assistant.

Dolman-Tuhou said two new nurses had been hired so far this year.

NZNO union delegate and Waikato hospital ED nurse Tracy Chisholm said it was also running way over capacity, and that it hadn't been unusual to see over 300 presentations to ED in a 24-hour period.

NZNO union delegate and Waikato hospital ED nurse Tracy Chisholm. RNZ / Natalie Akoorie

She said patients could be waiting for more than eight to 10 hours.

"These waiting rooms are full, we have a cupboard with extra chairs in it so when we run out of chairs for the waiting room, we can find more chairs for people to sit in, or people sit in wheelchairs.

"Some people just get so tired and exhausted that they'll end up lying on the floor of an emergency department waiting room," Chisholm said.

There was no capacity to isolate patients with influenza A from other patients, she said.

"If you came in with a broken leg, you might be sitting in a room [with someone] who's coughing because they have influenza A".

Chisholm said the hospital got permission from HNZ to hire 10 FTE nurses following the death of a patient in an ED toilet in late June.

She said it took time to advertise and hire, and these staff wouldn't be ready for this winter.

It was reported on Saturday that a second patient also died in an ED toilet.

Chisholm said attempts to move staff around to support areas facing high demand were not working.

"If you rob from Peter to pay Paul, you're kinda just moving the chairs on the Titanic."

Health NZ responds to strike action

Health New Zealand said it had been notified by NZNO that nursing staff planned to take industrial action in Gisborne Hospital's Emergency Department.

"Safeguarding patient care is our priority. If the strike goes ahead, the emergency department will remain open and appropriate measures will be put in place to maintain patient and staff safety and provide service continuity.

"Tairāwhiti is in an ongoing process looking at emergency department nursing staffing levels to ensure we have the right workforce capability, capacity and skill mix to deliver safe, high-quality patient care.

"This has been a collaborative process with the NZNO organiser and delegates. There have been several opportunities for feedback throughout and we remain committed to working in good faith as this process continues."

Winter was always a busy time, the spokesperson said, and August demand was very high combined with increased sick leave among clinical staff.

"Our nurses, doctors and wider healthcare teams continue to do an outstanding job caring for patients and our community.

"Despite pressures, patients with the most urgent clinical needs continue to be prioritised and seen first, as we actively manage demand through established escalation processes, staff redeployment and by maximising flow through the hospital, including increasing resourced bed availability."

Last week Auckland's Middlemore Hospital saw what was described by an ED doctor as an "appalling" late night surge of patients.

World.title: A contempt of privilege: Parliament's Clerk explains
World.content:
Parliament's finding that officials from MBIE had committed a contempt of Parliament's privilege received a lot of news coverage, but in the aftermath, confusion may remain as to what the privilege was that they contravened, how the contempt was decided and what the possible punishments even were.

And why did they go down in flames when politicians seem to get away with similar behaviours?

The House put those and other questions to the Clerk of the House of Representatives, Dr David Wilson. Part of his role is to act as a specialist advisor to Parliament on its rules.

A contempt of privilege: Parliament’s Clerk explains The House Download MP3 13m

Broadly speaking, what is privilege?

"Well, it's perhaps an unfortunate term because it suggests some sort of entitlements or wealth or something like that.

It's none of those things.

"It is really just the rules and protections that are available to Parliament collectively, to the House of Representatives, not to individual members, but to them as a collective, that enable them to do their jobs thoroughly and honestly and without fear.

"And so I guess the best-known privilege that Members of Parliament (MPs) have is freedom of speech-that they're free to say almost anything they like in the House and there can be no legal consequence.

"In fact, the only consequences can be ones imposed by the House itself."

And there are also other privileges that help MPs do their job, including the one at the centre of this, which is different?

"It is. Really.

"It is a fundamental principle that Parliament is entitled to receive truthful answers to its questions.

"That is because it exists to hold the government to account. One of Parliament's primary roles, apart from making laws, is to scrutinise the government, and it can only do that if it can be sure that the government (both ministers and public servants) will tell the truth when they answer those questions.

"When we talk about the government, we're not just talking about the ministers, but also the whole machinery behind them, the senior public servants who also have to turn up to Parliament to answer questions.

"Generally, they do it twice a year. One is the Estimates process, where the government is setting out its budget and asking Parliament to agree to fund it, and the other is the Annual Reviews, where the performance of departments is scrutinised, usually by questioning the chief executive and other senior officials."

So, they may be in a room for half an hour or some hours with a select committee, who will have sent them hundreds of questions beforehand, will ask dozens of questions in the room, and then follow up with lots of questions afterwards - all of which they are expected to answer truthfully?

"Yeah, that's exactly how it works. And, [the] questioning of officials has got longer over recent years, as Parliaments have put more time and attention on that. But the obligation to tell the truth is always the same. The whole system falls down if people don't.

"Regardless of whether an answer might be embarrassing or might paint the government or a minister in a poor light, or the department itself, they're still required to give a truthful answer to the question.

"And that's where it kind of fell down earlier this year when, after a select committee hearing, the committee felt that they hadn't been told everything that they should have been told (in response to questions), so they did the next thing you'd do, which is… To raise a 'matter of privilege' with the Speaker."

The Speaker is the gatekeeper on these things - what does he do, and how does that work?

"So any member (and only members) can raise matters of privilege with the Speaker, and that's effectively making a complaint by saying 'I think one of the rules of Parliament have been infringed'."

"The Speaker's role is to look at that and [ask whether] on the face of it - does there appear to be an issue here that warrants investigation?

"They don't make any judgement about whether someone has done something wrong, for example, but on the face of it, if the allegations here could be true, then is this something that should be investigated?

"And they also give some weight to the seriousness of the matter, because there are lots of minor technical breaches that happen from time to time, particularly in the heat of Question Time.

"But where it appears to be a serious one, then the Speaker refers the matter to the Privileges Committee.

"And they do that by saying so in the House, so that all members and the public can hear what's happened. Applications, as I say, are also turned down, and that's just done in private between the Speaker and the member who complained."

So, the Speaker doesn't tell the rest of us that someone complained, but he decided not to do anything about it?

"That's right, and that's been the invariable practice of Speakers over the years."

If the Speaker decides that there may be a case to answer, then the Privileges Committee is convened?

"That's right.

"So it doesn't meet routinely because (unlike a lot of other select committees), it doesn't have a routine workload.

"Mostly, it just meets to consider these privilege matters, and there might be a handful of them in a Parliament.

"Sometimes there are none, but perhaps three or four would be normal. The committee has senior MPs on it and, by convention, is chaired by the Attorney General, and although it often has a government majority, generally it operates on a consensus basis."

It's quite fun to watch, and anyone can go along and observe.… It almost feels like a court, doesn't it?

"Yeah, it does have some similarities, and that may be one of the reasons the Attorney General chairs it.

"Of course, it isn't a court of any kind. I know that Parliament is sometimes referred to as the 'highest court', but it isn't a court; it is the supreme lawmaking body.

"The Privileges Committee does carry out a quasi-judicial function, which is why it has some powers that other committees don't have.

"For example, it can compel people to attend and answer questions. Other committees can't do that - they can only ask the Speaker to do it for them.

"It doesn't really have to use that (in the same way that other committees don't need to), because generally just the force of the expectation to be there is sufficient.

"But it is a committee that will quite often make adverse findings and therefore needs to put them to the people the findings are about before they're released. So those are some of the ways its practice is a little bit different to other committees.

And then whatever its findings are, it writes a report, and it returns that to the House, and then the House (as it has this week) debates that report?

"That's right. Like all committees, the Privileges Committee can make some findings and recommendations, but it is actually up to the House what happens.

"So if there's some sort of sanction that is proposed, it is the House that decides whether to uphold that.

"In this particular case, the House was simply asked to 'note the report' and the sanction was found to be the finding of contempt. No further sanction was proposed.

Apart from anything else, it must be pretty awful to have your name discussed in Parliament [in this way].

"No doubt it is, and members are generally pretty careful about that because they know that the people they are speaking about can't speak back.

"So they're pretty restrained in talking about public servants, or members of the public, as a general rule.

"But part of their role in scrutinising the government might sometimes be to critique the work that departments do, and particularly the chief executives.

In terms of the kind of recommendations the committee can make, despite what some people say, it cannot imprison anybody. That's been ruled out in legislation. It doesn't have a lot of options, does it?

"When you're talking about making recommendations about people who are not Members of Parliament. Really, it is a matter of telling the person off, reprimanding them, maybe having them apologise.

"There have, over the years, been a few unique penalties proposed.

"There was once a courier firm that was said to have transported some confidential committee documents, I think, to a journalist.

"They wouldn't say who had given them the documents to provide, and so that courier firm was banned from deliveries to Parliament for a period of time. But that's an unusual case.

"Most of these privileges cases have involved Members of Parliament.

"In the past, they used to involve journalists quite often because of the conflict between confidential Parliamentary information and journalists' duty to report on interesting news stories.

"That's not so common these days, and with members of the Press Gallery, I guess, there is an additional sanction available because they're only in the Press Gallery for as long as the Speaker will allow them to have access to Parliament.

"But for general members of the public or public servants, yeah, there are a smaller range of sanctions available.

"Technically, it is possible to fine people up to $1,000. That's only been done once. That was against TVNZ some years ago, and it's really a symbolic punishment. It's highly unlikely to ever be levied against an individual."

A Privileges Committee hearing aimed at a government agency is quite rare, isn't it?

"Yeah, it is. It's very unusual. In preparing for this particular case (because I go along and advise the Privileges Committee each time), I looked back at other times that public sector agencies had been in front of the committee, and I could only find three.

"New Zealand Post in 2003 for a somewhat similar issue. They were accused of having deliberately misled a committee, but ultimately found not to have because it was probably more of a misunderstanding.

"TVNZ in 2006, which was found guilty of contempt and was actually fined. And then Maritime New Zealand in 2015, and in that instance, the committee found there was no case to answer. So it is pretty unusual.

For anyone who watches Question Time and who regularly shouts at the television in response to ministers from any government not quite answering questions properly, not quite telling the full truth, or even potentially full-on lying. Why don't they get brought before the Privileges Committee, or why aren't complaints made that 'minister so-and-so said something patently not true, and he's misleading the House'?

"I think there's a few reasons.

"One is: often answers to questions reflect different opinions, and the Speaker is not there to choose whose [opinion] is right and whose is wrong.

"The Speaker has got no way of knowing that. And there are different interpretations of answers. So sometimes those issues do get raised with the Speaker.

"I think the other thing is that Speakers really - over the whole time the Parliament has existed - have said that in order to be found to have deliberately misled the House (it's quite a high bar), there needs to be knowledge that what you're saying is incorrect and that you're setting out to be misleading.

"And often [for things said] in the heat of debate, Speakers have found it's difficult to sustain both those [requirements]. People might be wrong, but not have given much preparation to answers, particularly to supplementary questions.

"I suppose they're a bit lenient on it, but it is actually the same rule that applies in the case we're talking about now that has just been in front of the Privileges Committee, and Members of Parliament have occasionally been held to account for that.

"There was one in the last Parliament where a minister gave an incorrect answer and then didn't come back to the House to correct it for a period of time. And the committee was critical of that, although they in that case didn't find that contempt had occurred."

I suppose in order to successfully bring a case, you also need to have the majority support of the Committee, and that must be quite difficult to achieve when the committee numbers are somewhat split?

"The Committee, as I say, often has a government majority, but it's very rare for it to vote on anything. It does try to reach a consensus, and I think that reflects the function it's carrying out, which is sitting in judgement on other people's conduct.

"I think the Privileges Committee isn't inherently a particularly political environment, although of course the members are politicians, and you can never entirely separate those things, and nor should you try. But that is one of the barriers, I suppose.

"The other one is - some member has actually got to raise a complaint, and the Speaker does have that gatekeeping role of thinking, well, on the face of it, is there an issue here, and is it a serious enough one to warrant going to the Privileges Committee?"

World.title: Rugby: Springboks outmuscle All Blacks to win third test, take 2-1 series lead
World.content:
The Springboks have beaten the All Blacks 29-24 in the third test in Soweto to take a 2-1 lead in the four-match series.

The Springboks again started well, but the All Blacks absorbed the pressure and began to apply their own. With the All Blacks close to the line the hosts' first-five Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu knocked the ball down and was yellow carded for a professional foul.

The All Blacks made the most of the extra man, with captain Ardie Savea barging over from close range for the first try of the match after some good work from hooker Asafo Aumua.

Love kicked the conversion to give New Zealand a 7-0 lead after about 10 minutes at FNB Stadium in Johannesburg.

The Springboks were back to 15 men in the 20th minute with Feinberg-Mngomezulu re-entering the game, and the hosts would score moments later with wing Kurt-Lee Arendse going over in the right-hand corner. Feinberg-Mngomezulu missed the conversion, leaving the score 7-5 to the All Blacks midway through the first half.

The All Blacks struck back with another try to Savea after a break down the left edge by wing Leroy Carter, the skipper picking up a loose ball before diving over for his second try of the match. The conversion was unsuccessful, with the score 12-5 to the All Blacks after 27 minutes.

All Blacks winger Leroy Carter in action against the Springboks. Photosport

Savea though would leave the field soon after with what appeared to be a shoulder injury, dealing a sizable blow to the tourists. He was replaced by Wallace Sititi, with openside flanker Luke Jacobson taking over as captain.

The All Blacks had a player sent to the sin bin in the 37th minute with Love yellow carded for being offside when the Springboks were hot on attack in the All Blacks' 22.

The hosts would score from the resulting five-metre scrum, referee Nika Amashukeli awarding a penalty try under the posts after the All Blacks infringed with the Springboks scrum marching towards the try line. That made the score 12-12 just minutes before halftime, and that's how it would remain going into the break.

Love rejoined the game early in the second half, and he almost kicked a penalty from more than 40m out but pushed his attempt just wide.

The Springboks were dominating at scrum time as they were in the first half, but the All Blacks were hanging in there and scored the next try after wing Leroy Carter regathered a Will Jordan kick before passing back to Jordan, who scored the All Blacks third try of the night.

All Blacks winger Will Jordan scores against the Springboks. Photosport

Love missed the conversion with the score 17-12 to the All Blacks with just over 20 minutes to go.

Their lead was short-lived however as the Springboks hit back almost immediately with midfielder Jesse Kriel storming over after Carter missed a one-on-one tackle.

Feinberg-Mngomezulu added the extras to put South Africa back in front 19-17.

The Springboks' scrum was again dominant, and the hosts were winning consistent penalties at scrum time, making it hard for the All Blacks to build any momentum.

Another scrum penalty led to an attacking lineout for the hosts, and the All Blacks were powerless to stop the ensuing maul as Springboks hooker Malcolm Marx dived over for a try in the 65th minute to extend their lead to 26-17 with the help of another conversion.

Referee Nika Amashukeli talks to Ardie Savea. Photosport

The All Blacks gave away another penalty inside their own half, lock Fabian Holland pinged for an illegal clean out, and South Africa kicked the three points to push out to a 12-point lead (29-17) with just 10 minutes to go.

The crowd by this stage was in full party mode, and the noise inside the 90,000 capacity FNB Stadium was deafening as they began to sing the name of Springboks coach Rassie Erasmus.

The hosts had their tails up and continued to win penalties at the breakdown, the All Blacks running out of time to fight their way back into the game.

The All Blacks needed to be the next to score, but it was South Africa who made all the play with the tourists barely hanging on.

The All Blacks never gave up and they finally cracked the Springboks' defence after the fulltime siren, with replacement front rower Samisoni Taukei'aho scoring a consolation try, but it wasn't enough as the hosts held on for a 29-24 victory and a 2-1 series lead.

The best the All Blacks can now hope for is a drawn series, with game four in the US city of Baltimore next weekend.

World.title: How the Panthers and Warriors can win the NRL minor premiership
World.content:
The NRL minor premiership is still up for grabs heading into the final day of the home-and-away season, with the New Zealand Warriors on top and the Penrith Panthers ready to pounce.

The Warriors moved to outright first with a narrow win in Auckland on Saturday, but the Panthers only need a slender win on Sunday afternoon to reclaim top spot, where they have spent much of the 2026 season.

The Warriors and Panthers will finish in the top two, and in practical terms there is little different between the two spots entering the finals series.

Both sides will host two matches in the finals, including qualifying finals next week.

But the minor premier does get a monetary prize, and confidence heading into finals footy, knowing they finished on top of the pile after 27 gruelling rounds of rugby league.

Here is how the Warriors and Panthers can win the minor premiership, and what happens when first and second are level on points, and point differential.

NRL top two

1st: New Zealand Warriors — 42, points for 728, points against 418, point differential +310

2nd: Penrith Panthers — 40, points for 645, points against 337, point differential +308

How the Warriors can become minor premiers

Panthers fail to beat Wests Tigers

Panthers defeat Tigers by one point

With a nail-biting one-point win over Manly yesterday in Auckland, the New Zealand Warriors put themselves in outright first on the NRL ladder.

ABC NRL Daily podcast Andrew Moore and the ABC NRL team bring you your daily dose of NRL conversation. The team give you the context and depth beyond the headlines.

But their fate is out of their hands.

If the Tigers cause an upset and defeat the Panthers this afternoon, then the Warriors will win the minor premiership.

If the Panthers beat the Tigers, they will draw level on points with the Warriors, and then the minor premiership will be decided by point differential.

The Warriors hold a very narrow two-point advantage over the Panthers in the points differential — Warriors +310, Panthers +308.

That means if the Panthers can only manage a one-point win over the Tigers at Western Sydney Stadium, then the Warriors would finish first by having a superior points differential +310-+309.

How the Panthers can become minor premiers

Defeat Wests Tigers by two or more points

The first thing the Panthers must do is beat Wests Tigers.

Then, how much they beat the Tigers by will decide who finishes first and second on the NRL ladder.

The Panthers will finish as minor premiers if they beat the Warriors by two or more points.

If two teams finish on the same points and have the same points differential, the NRL splits the two sides based on a tiebreaker: points for divided by points against, then multiplied by 100 (Points for / points against x 100).

If this tiebreaker is needed, then the Panthers will finish higher as their defence this year has conceded much less than the Warriors, greatly assisting that tiebreaker maths equation.

Who will the Panthers and Warriors face in the first week of finals?

By finishing in the top two, the Warriors and Panthers have earned the right to host two matches in the finals.

Each will host qualifying finals in week one. If they win, they will host a preliminary final in week three.

If the Panthers or Warriors lose in week one, they then host a cut-throat semifinal in week two against a side that was victorious in week one elimination finals played between the teams that finished fifth-eighth.

In week one, whoever finishes first will host the Sydney Roosters (4th) and the team that finishes second will host the Dolphins (3rd).

The NRL will announce dates and times for week one of the final once all matches in round 27 finish.

World.title: Wallabies escape with draw against Pumas after late penalty try
World.content:
The Wallabies have snatched a 28-28 draw with Argentina in Mendoza after they were awarded a penalty try with 10 minutes remaining in the Test.

Trailing 28-21, the Wallabies were on the attack inside the Pumas' 22 when the home side's fullback Santiago Carreras deliberately knocked the ball on in defence.

Referee James Doleman felt he had no other option but to award the Wallabies a penalty try.

Carreras was shown a yellow card for his infringement only a minute after teammate Lucio Cinti committed the same offence and was sent from the field for 10 minutes.

The Pumas were reduced to 13 players but the Wallabies failed to take advantage.

They could not break the deadlock in the shadows of full-time, but still secured a history-making 1-0 series win.

The Wallabies had previously never won a multi-Test series on Argentine soil.

The result also left new coach Les Kiss with an unbeaten record (three wins and a draw) since taking over from Joe Schmidt.

It was an unconvincing performance from the Wallabies, who had led 14-0 following converted tries to captain Harry Wilson and Max Jorgensen in the first half.

The Pumas responded before the half-time break with tries to skipper Pablo Matera and Ignacio Mendy, both of which were converted by Carreras.

The Wallabies and Pumas could not be split on the scoreboard in Mendoza. (Getty Images: Alejandro Pagni)

It was 14-14 at half-time, before the Wallabies broke the deadlock with Fraser McReight's try from close range in the 47th minute.

Ryan Lonergan added the extras but it was a short-lived lead after the Pumas responded through converted tries to Ignacio Ruiz and Matera.

The Pumas held their advantage until Carreras's indiscretion late in the match.

The Wallabies, who won the opening Test 27-21 in Jujuy last week, now have three weeks to prepare for their next clash.

They face world champions South Africa in Perth on September 27.
